title: Generality of nest, which fails depending on the number of rows. Applying nest to tibble of 0 rows
description:
The beauty of tidyverse is that operations apply two tables of any dimensions with zero rows and or zero columns.

However, nesting leads to a non-general behaviour

```r
x = tibble(a = character(), b = character(), c = character())
x |> nest(data = -a) |> pull(data)
list()
```

Here `data` is an empty list, while it should be a zero-row tibble

```r
# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: b <chr>, c <chr>
```

Nest and unnest are not anymore inverse of each other

```r
x |> nest(data = -a) |> unnest(data) 
# A tibble: 0 × 2
# ℹ 2 variables: a <chr>, data <???>
```

The current behaviour makes building pipelines with diverse input hard. For example, if I want to nest and unnest, I would get an error

```r
 x = tibble(a = character(), b = character(), c = character())
x |> nest(data = -a) |> unnest(data) |> nest(b)

Error in nest(.data, !!!cols, .by = { : In expression named `data`:
Caused by error:
! Can't subset columns that don't exist.
✖ Column `b` doesn't exist.
```

The above operation fails depending on the number of rows, which I believe should not be the case.

title: Inverse of drop_na?
description:
I love drop_na. While working on a particular project, however, I tried to reach for the inverse, which I incorrectly assumed existed and would hypothetically return rows with NA, e.g.:

```
library(tidyr)
df <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, NA), y = c("a", NA, "b"))
df %>% only_na(y)
```
instead of:

```
df %>% filter(is.na(y))
```

Since tidyverse functions tend to come in pairs (count/uncount, replace_na/na_if, separate/unite), can we have `only_na` or `keep_na` or something? Or is this too fringe a use case?

title: `full_seq.numeric()` should set `finite = TRUE`
description:
Right now you just get an error

```r
> tidyr::full_seq(c(1, Inf), 1L)
Error in if (any(((x - rng[1])%%period > tol) & (period - (x - rng[1])%%period >  : 
  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

You most likely don't want to create an infinite sequence anyways.

This would be somewhat useful with the Date method in particular, as a way to generate a full sequence along the following start/end intervals:

``` r
start <- as.Date(c("2019-01-05", "2019-01-10", "2019-01-11", "2019-01-14"))
end <- as.Date(c("2019-01-07", NA, "2019-01-14", NA))
end[is.na(end)] <- Inf

# `end = Inf` means "hasn't ended yet"
df <- tibble::tibble(start = start, end = end)
df
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   start      end       
#>   <date>     <date>    
#> 1 2019-01-05 2019-01-07
#> 2 2019-01-10 Inf       
#> 3 2019-01-11 2019-01-14
#> 4 2019-01-14 Inf

# Want a full sequence along range of start/end excluding infinite values
# `finite = TRUE` gives you the right range
range <- .Date(range(as.numeric(c(df$start, df$end)), finite = TRUE))
range
#> [1] "2019-01-05" "2019-01-14"

seq(range[1], range[2], by = 1)
#>  [1] "2019-01-05" "2019-01-06" "2019-01-07" "2019-01-08" "2019-01-09"
#>  [6] "2019-01-10" "2019-01-11" "2019-01-12" "2019-01-13" "2019-01-14"

# Ideally you'd just do:
# tidyr::full_seq(c(start, end), period = 1)
```

title: unnest_wider / _longer fails if list contains objects.
description:
Consider this example

```r
m <- tibble::as_tibble(mtcars[1,]) %>% 
  mutate(ls_col=list(
    list(
      a=c(1:10), 
      b=lm(cyl~gear))
    )
  )
```

Where I have a nested column that has 2 elements, one of which is an object (`lm` in this case). When trying to unnest elements to columns (`unnest_wider`) or rows (`unnest_longer`), `tidyr` complains.

```r
m %>% tidyr::unnest_wider(ls_col)
# Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `lm` object
# Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace

m %>% tidyr::unnest_longer(ls_col)
# Error: `x` must be a vector, not a `lm` object
# Call `rlang::last_error()` to see a backtrace
```

Strangely, we can get the correct behavior if we use plain `unnest`.

```r
m %>% tidyr::unnest(ls_col)
# # A tibble: 2 x 12
# mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs    am  gear  carb ls_col
```

I am not sure if this is intended behavior and whether there are possible workarounds.

title: A good two stage pivot example
description:
Real life example that came up in my wife's work

Could be added to https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/articles/pivot.html#longer-then-wider

This is more of an advanced pivot that can also be accomplished in one step if you know how to use df-cols.

``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(
  patient = c("bob", "ann", "joe"),
  A_start = c(1, 2, 3),
  A_stop = c(NA, 6, 9),
  B_start = c(3, NA, 1),
  B_stop = c(6, NA, 2),
  C_start = c(1, 5, 3),
  C_stop = c(2, 6, NA)
)

# Want the treatment name in a column, but want to keep start/stop columns
df
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   patient A_start A_stop B_start B_stop C_start C_stop
#>   <chr>     <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 bob           1     NA       3      6       1      2
#> 2 ann           2      6      NA     NA       5      6
#> 3 joe           3      9       1      2       3     NA

# Two stage pivot
df %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -patient, 
    names_to = c("treatment", "endpoint"),
    names_sep = "_"
  ) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = endpoint, 
    values_from = value
  )
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   patient treatment start  stop
#>   <chr>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 bob     A             1    NA
#> 2 bob     B             3     6
#> 3 bob     C             1     2
#> 4 ann     A             2     6
#> 5 ann     B            NA    NA
#> 6 ann     C             5     6
#> 7 joe     A             3     9
#> 8 joe     B             1     2
#> 9 joe     C             3    NA

# One pivot
df %>%
  pack(
    A = c(A_start, A_stop), 
    B = c(B_start, B_stop), 
    C = c(C_start, C_stop), 
    .names_sep = "_"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(A, B, C),
    names_to = "treatment",
  ) %>%
  unpack(value)
#> # A tibble: 9 × 4
#>   patient treatment start  stop
#>   <chr>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 bob     A             1    NA
#> 2 bob     B             3     6
#> 3 bob     C             1     2
#> 4 ann     A             2     6
#> 5 ann     B            NA    NA
#> 6 ann     C             5     6
#> 7 joe     A             3     9
#> 8 joe     B             1     2
#> 9 joe     C             3    NA
```

title: `unite()` and `separate()`'s third argument could be more consistent
description:
The third argument in `unite()` can be symbols or strings, but the third argument in `separate()` must be strings. I expected them to be complements, though I realize they are described as almost complements in `?unite`. 

---

`separate(x, c(y, z))` will produce an error.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df_uni <- data.frame(x = paste0(1:3, "_", letters[1:3]))
df_uni
#>     x
#> 1 1_a
#> 2 2_b
#> 3 3_c

df_sep <- data.frame(y = 1:3, z = letters[1:3])
df_sep
#>   y z
#> 1 1 a
#> 2 2 b
#> 3 3 c

## unite()'s argument col can be symbols
df_sep |> 
  unite(x, c(y, z))
#>     x
#> 1 1_a
#> 2 2_b
#> 3 3_c

## separate()'s argument into cannot be symbols
df_uni |> 
  separate(x, c(y, z))
#> Error in str_separate(value, into = into, sep = sep, convert = convert, : object 'y' not found

## Argument into must be strings
df_uni |> 
  separate(x, c("y", "z"))
#>   y z
#> 1 1 a
#> 2 2 b
#> 3 3 c
```

title: `complete`'s documentation includes slightly confusing examples with `expand()`
description:
In https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/main/R/complete.R
the documentation uses #' @inheritParams expand

but these descriptions of expand's arguments (see below) include explicit examples e.g. `expand(df, x, y, z)` so it can be confusing when someone is trying to figure out `complete`. Is it worth either deleting the specific example or adding both examples?
expand(df, x, y, z) or complete(df, x, y, z) or neither?

"Specification of columns to expand. Columns can be atomic vectors or lists.

To find all unique combinations of x, y and z, including those not present in the data, supply each variable as a separate argument: expand(df, x, y, z).

To find only the combinations that occur in the data, use nesting: expand(df, nesting(x, y, z)).

You can combine the two forms. For example, expand(df, nesting(school_id, student_id), date) would produce a row for each present school-student combination for all possible dates.

When used with factors, expand() uses the full set of levels, not just those that appear in the data. If you want to use only the values seen in the data, use forcats::fct_drop()."

title: Can we somehow have `nest(.by = )`?
description:
`dplyr::nest_by(data, x, y)` is somewhat useful because I like that the variables you specify are the ones that end up _outside_ the nesting. The equivalent `nest(data, -c(x, y))` has always felt very awkward to me.

But really we'd like to pick one of `nest()`, `nest_by()` and `group_nest()` and deprecate the others.

It feels like tidyr is the right place for `nest()` to live, but it would be nice if we could somehow bring that `by` behavior over.

Maybe it is something like `nest(.data, ..., .by = NULL/everything())`? Then you could do `nest(data, .by = c(x, y))` to get the `nest_by()` behavior. I still think you could use the `...` in combination with `.by`, we'd just have to think about exactly how that would work (and can you duplicate variables in both `.by` and `...`?)

We'd have to consider if this conflicts with the current behavior of `nest(data)` with no `...`, which currently nests everything (rather than nothing, as might be expected by `nest(data, .by = c(x, y))`)

Consider how this conflicts with dplyr `.by`, and if that would be confusing or not. It might not be, because they seem to be very similar concepts.

title: `df_unchop()` and `NULL` recycling
description:
`df_unchop()` has fairly complicated `NULL` recycling handling that is different from the rest of tidyr.

https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/831bf7462316155e5c7271d4e62baa2bd12b3fe3/R/chop.R#L159-L164

This makes the implementation rather complicated, as we can't use the typical recycling rules of assuming that `NULL` elements are size `0` and don't recycle against anything other than other size `0` and size `1` elements.

This in turn affects `unchop()` and `unnest()` directly (at the very least).

It is also inconsistent with other tidyr functions like `unnest_longer()`, which do treat `NULL` this way.

Basically, most of tidyr treats `NULL` elements as if they were `unspecified(0)`, in terms of both common size and common type determination, except `df_unchop()`.

```r
library(tidyr)

# WITH NULL:

# Size 0 in `x`, size 2 in `y`
df <- tibble(x = list(NULL), y = list(tibble(a = 1:2)))
df
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   x      y               
#>   <list> <list>          
#> 1 <NULL> <tibble [2 × 1]>

# Since it was `NULL` we force it to work (THIS SEEMS WEIRD)
unnest(df, c(x, y))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   x         a
#>   <lgl> <int>
#> 1 NA        1
#> 2 NA        2

# But it doesn't work in `unnest_longer()` because `NULL` became a 0 row df
unnest_longer(df, c(x, y))
#> Error in `unchop()` at tidyr/R/unnest-longer.R:130:2:
#> ! In row 1, can't recycle input of size 0 to size 2.


# WITH EMPTY TYPED ELEMENT

# Size 0 in `x`, size 2 in `y`
df <- tibble(x = list(integer()), y = list(tibble(a = 1:2)))
df
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>   x         y               
#>   <list>    <list>          
#> 1 <int [0]> <tibble [2 × 1]>

# It isn't `NULL`, so tidyverse recycling kicks in
unnest(df, c(x, y))
#> Error in `unchop()` at tidyr/R/unnest.R:180:2:
#> ! In row 1, can't recycle input of size 0 to size 2.

unnest_longer(df, c(x, y))
#> Error in `unchop()` at tidyr/R/unnest-longer.R:130:2:
#> ! In row 1, can't recycle input of size 0 to size 2.
```

It is probably worth considering treating `NULL` like size 0 elements, as this would greatly simplify the implementation and make it more consistent with other tidyr verbs. This really only affects `unnest()` when you unnest multiple columns simultaneously, so hopefully it doesn't affect much code in the wild.

title: unnest_wider() fails when list columns have additional classes and missing values
description:
I recently upgraded from `1.1.4` to `1.2.0` and ran into an error with `unnest_wider()`. It now fails with a type conversion error when two occurrences overlap:

1. the list column to be unnested is composed of list(s) with at least one empty object (`NULL` or `list()`).
2. the list column to be unnested is composed of list(s) with an additional class.

``` r

#> Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 4.1.2
library(tibble)

x <- list(a = 1, b = NULL)
df <- tibble::tibble(c = 1, d = list(x))
str(df)
#> tibble [1 × 2] (S3: tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
#>  $ c: num 1
#>  $ d:List of 1
#>   ..$ :List of 2
#>   .. ..$ a: num 1
#>   .. ..$ b: NULL

#> # A tibble: 1 × 3
#>       c     a b    
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <lgl>

df <- tibble::tibble(c = 1, d = list(x))
```

description:
Moving from Slack.

I just used `separate_wider_regex()` on a tibble created with parsermd on the section headings from a chapter from R Packages.

It turns out I needed to specify `names_sep` and `too_few`, but those user errors interact with each other in a way that makes it harder to figure out what's wrong.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

x <- tribble(
  ~ sec_h1, ~ sec_h2,
  "Intro {intro}", NA,
  "First cool thing {first-cool-thing}", NA,
  "First cool thing {first-cool-thing}", "First cool details {first-cool-details}",
  "Second cool thing", NA
)
x |> 
  separate_wider_regex(
    everything(),
    c("text" = "[^\\{]*", " [{]", label = ".*", "[}]"),
    too_few = "debug"
  )
#> Warning: Debug mode activated: adding variables `sec_h1_ok`, `sec_h1_matches`, and
#> `sec_h1_remainder`.
#> Warning: Debug mode activated: adding variables `sec_h2_ok`, `sec_h2_matches`, and
#> `sec_h2_remainder`.
#> Error in `unpack()`:
#> ! Names must be unique.
#> ✖ These names are duplicated:
#>   * "text" at locations 1 and 7.
#>   * "label" at locations 2 and 8.
#> ℹ Use argument `names_repair` to specify repair strategy.
```

I think I should be getting scolded first and foremost for not specifying `names_sep`, which is actually required since `cols = everything()`. That is the root cause of the `unpack()` error but the suggested remedy is off-base.

I'd probably also be happy with some default choice of `names_sep` (related #1367).

Until you get the naming stuff straightened out, you can't see the cool `too_few = "debug"` diagnostics.

title: Should `hoist()` be converting to a bare data frame, and then calling `reconstruct_tibble()`?
description:
You can currently generate a corrupt grouped-df because of the way `append_df()` works here:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df <- tibble(
  id = c("x", "y", "z"),
  data = list(
    tibble(a = 1:2, b = 2:3),
    tibble(a = 2:3, b = 3:4),
    tibble(a = 3:4, b = 4:5)
  )
)

gdf <- group_by(df, id)

hoist(df, data, "a")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   id    a         data            
#>   <chr> <list>    <list>          
#> 1 x     <int [2]> <tibble [2 × 1]>
#> 2 y     <int [2]> <tibble [2 × 1]>
#> 3 z     <int [2]> <tibble [2 × 1]>

hoist(gdf, data, "a")
#> Error in `validate_grouped_df()`:
#> ! The `groups` attribute is not a data frame with its last column called `.rows`.
```

This is not a new bug, as tidyr 1.2.0 and 1.1.4 both show this issue.

(Side note that hoisting out a column followed by an `unchop()` or `unnest()` is a really neat pattern if you don't need everything from `data`)

title: `append_df()` is broken with duplicated names
description:
Used by things like `hoist()`, `extract()`, and `separate()`

``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(
  x = 1:3, 
  y = list(list(x = 3, a = 2), list(x = 4, a = 3), list(x = 5, a = 4)), 
  z = 1:3
)

# Typically hoisted column is placed right before column it comes from
hoist(df, y, "a")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>       x     a y                    z
#>   <int> <dbl> <list>           <int>
#> 1     1     2 <named list [1]>     1
#> 2     2     3 <named list [1]>     2
#> 3     3     4 <named list [1]>     3

# It gets a little weird if the column already existed
hoist(df, y, "x")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   y                    x     z
#>   <list>           <dbl> <int>
#> 1 <named list [1]>     3     1
#> 2 <named list [1]>     4     2
#> 3 <named list [1]>     5     3
```


``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(x = 1:3, y = c("a-b", "c-d", "e-f"), z = 1:3, w = 1:3)

# Typically new columns replace `col` or go right after it
separate(df, y, into = c("new1", "new2"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>       x new1  new2      z     w
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <int> <int>
#> 1     1 a     b         1     1
#> 2     2 c     d         2     2
#> 3     3 e     f         3     3
separate(df, y, into = c("new1", "new2"), remove = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>       x y     new1  new2      z     w
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <int> <int>
#> 1     1 a-b   a     b         1     1
#> 2     2 c-d   c     d         2     2
#> 3     3 e-f   e     f         3     3

# Things get weird if you are replacing a name that already exists
separate(df, y, into = c("x", "new"))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>       z x     new       w
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <int>
#> 1     1 a     b         1
#> 2     2 c     d         2
#> 3     3 e     f         3
separate(df, y, into = c("x", "new"), remove = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   y         z x     new       w
#>   <chr> <int> <chr> <chr> <int>
#> 1 a-b       1 a     b         1
#> 2 c-d       2 c     d         2
#> 3 e-f       3 e     f         3
```

title: Should `unnest_longer()` have `keep_empty`?
description:
From https://community.rstudio.com/t/unnest-longer-drops-lists-rows-with-character-0/132748

Original example:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

my_df <- tibble(
  txt = c(
    "chestnut, pear, kiwi, peanut",
    "grapes, banana"
  )
)

#Extract all nuts
my_df <- my_df %>% 
  mutate(nuts = str_extract_all(txt, regex("\\w*nut\\w*"))) %>% 
  mutate(index = row_number(), .before=1)

#Row index 2 has nuts <chr [0]>
my_df
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   index txt                          nuts     
#>   <int> <chr>                        <list>   
#> 1     1 chestnut, pear, kiwi, peanut <chr [2]>
#> 2     2 grapes, banana               <chr [0]>

#unnest
my_df_long <- my_df %>% 
  unnest_longer(nuts, values_to = "nuts_long")

#Row index 2 is now missing
my_df_long
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   index txt                          nuts_long
#>   <int> <chr>                        <chr>    
#> 1     1 chestnut, pear, kiwi, peanut chestnut 
#> 2     1 chestnut, pear, kiwi, peanut peanut
```

<sup>Created on 2022-03-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

Minimal reprex:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

df <- tibble(
  x = list("a", character())
)
df
#> # A tibble: 2 × 1
#>   x        
#>   <list>   
#> 1 <chr [1]>
#> 2 <chr [0]>

unnest_longer(df, x)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   x    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 a

unnest(df, x, keep_empty = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 1
#>   x    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 a    
#> 2 <NA>
```

<sup>Created on 2022-03-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

It may be as simple as passing `keep_empty` through to the `unchop()` call in `unnest_longer()`, but I'd need to think about it critically to make sure

title: `unnest_longer()` uses a mix of `keep_empty = TRUE` and `keep_empty = FALSE`
description:
Currently it keeps `NULL` elements, but drops empty vectors like `integer()`.

It should work like `unchop(keep_empty = FALSE)` which drops both `NULL` and `integer()`.

This is heavily related to #1339. I imagine that to be able to add `keep_empty` to `unnest_longer()` we will have to resolve this. I think it requires changes to `tidyr:::elt_to_long()`'s handling of `NULL`. When `keep_empty = FALSE` (the default) it should probably use `unspecified(0L)` and an empty vector for the `index` if needed. The current behavior looks to be what should happen for `keep_empty = TRUE`. 

Fixing this is probably a small breaking change. But I think it is definitely worth it for package consistency.

``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(
  x = list(NULL, 1L, integer())
)

df
#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>   x        
#>   <list>   
#> 1 <NULL>   
#> 2 <int [1]>
#> 3 <int [0]>

# Inconsistent:
# Keeps the `NULL` as `NA`.
# Drops the `integer()`.
unnest_longer(df, x)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1    NA
#> 2     1

# Consistent with our definition of "empty".
# - Drops `NULL`
# - Drops `integer()` (size 0 vectors)
unchop(df, x)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1     1

# - Keeps `NULL` as NA
# - Keeps `integer()` as NA
unchop(df, x, keep_empty = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>       x
#>   <int>
#> 1    NA
#> 2     1
#> 3    NA
```

title: `expand_grid()` evaluation environment
description:
``` r
library(tidyr)
data <- tibble(foo=1)
foo <- bar <- 1:2

expand_grid(data, new = bar)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>     foo   new
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     1     2

expand_grid(data, new = foo)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>     foo   new
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1
```

This puzzled me then hit me that it behaves like a mutating function and this works :


``` r
expand_grid(data, new = .env$foo)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>     foo   new
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     1     2

expand_grid(data, new = !!foo)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>     foo   new
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     1     2
```

I'm not sure if the current behaviour is intended but it's undocumented. As far as I'm concerned I wouldn't mind have the dots evaluated outside of the data.

title: Remove temporary backwards compat support for `list()` in `names_ptypes` and `values_ptypes` of `pivot_longer()`
description:
See #1291 for even more details.

When we moved from default values of `names/values_ptypes = list()` to `names/values_ptypes = NULL` and allowed `names_ptypes = list()` to mean "use a list ptype for all columns", this caused breakage in extension packages that extended `pivot_longer()` and still had `list()` as their default value for these arguments.

So we temporarily special cased a value of `list()` for these two arguments to be identical to `NULL` to give the extension packages time to update to the new default. Documentation was updated to mention this special casing, and to state that it was temporary.

We'd like to remove this special casing once the packages are updated so that `names_ptypes = list()` will again mean "use a list ptype for all columns".

This issue tracks the status of the known packages that have this issue. Once they are all fixed, we can remove the special casing from the code and documentation:

- [x] dbplyr https://github.com/tidyverse/dbplyr/pull/744
- [x] sf https://github.com/r-spatial/sf/pull/1895
- [x] sparklyr https://github.com/sparklyr/sparklyr/pull/3221
- [x] tidyseurat https://github.com/stemangiola/tidyseurat/pull/49

Once these issues are all resolved, revert everything done in this PR https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/pull/1297

title: [Feature request] Teach `pivot_longer` to be aware of experimental design
description:
I mostly work with experimental datasets, and data collection software frequently output wide datasets, that we need to `pivot_longer()`. Sometimes the names of both within- and between-participant conditions, as well as the trial number are present in the names.

``` r
library(tidyr)

# Legend:
#  - `wcx` stands for within-participants condition number x
#  - `bcx` stands for between-participants condition number x
#  - `tx` stands for trial number x
as_expected <- data.frame(pp = 1:2,
                          wc1_bc1_t1 = c(1, NA), wc1_bc1_t2 = c(1, NA),
                          wc2_bc1_t1 = c(1, NA), wc2_bc1_t2 = c(1, NA),
                          wc1_bc2_t1 = c(NA, 1), wc1_bc2_t2 = c(NA, 1),
                          wc2_bc2_t1 = c(NA, 1), wc2_bc2_t2 = c(NA, 1))
```

We usually want the output of `pivot_longer()` to have one row per trial that each participant was *expected* to perform. This means that we want the output to have as many rows as the number of participants `Np`, times the number of trials (`nt`) per within-participant conditions (`wc`) but not per between-participant conditions (`bc`). Meaning we want `nrow(dataset)` to equal `Np * nt * wc` (but not `Np * nt * wc * bc`).

``` r
# In this case we want eight rows (2 Np * 2 nt * 2 nwc)
```

When participants performed all the trials they were *expected* to perform we can get to what we want just by setting `values_drop_na = TRUE` in the `pivot_longer()` call.

``` r
expected <- pivot_longer(as_expected, -pp,
                         names_sep = "_", names_to = c("wc", "bc", "t"),
                         values_drop_na = TRUE)
expected_nrows <- length(unique(expected$pp)) * length(unique(expected$t)) *
                  length(unique(expected$wc))
print(nrow(expected) == expected_nrows)
#> [1] TRUE
print(expected)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>      pp wc    bc    t     value
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1     1 wc1   bc1   t1        1
#> 2     1 wc1   bc1   t2        1
#> 3     1 wc2   bc1   t1        1
#> 4     1 wc2   bc1   t2        1
#> 5     2 wc1   bc2   t1        1
#> 6     2 wc1   bc2   t2        1
#> 7     2 wc2   bc2   t1        1
#> 8     2 wc2   bc2   t2        1
```

However, sometimes, individual participants can have some missing values in one or more trials they were *expected* to perform but for some reason they didn't.

``` r
unexpected_na <- data.frame(pp = 1:2,
                            wc1_bc1_t1 = c(1, NA), wc1_bc1_t2 = c(1, NA),
                            wc2_bc1_t1 = c(1, NA), wc2_bc1_t2 = c(NA, NA),
                            wc1_bc2_t1 = c(NA, 1), wc1_bc2_t2 = c(NA, 1),
                            wc2_bc2_t1 = c(NA, 1), wc2_bc2_t2 = c(NA, 1))
```

If we set `values_drop_na = TRUE` then we lose some of those rows (making those missing values implicit as the manual warns us).

``` r
# This way we lose a row for participant one we wanted to keep.
option1 <- pivot_longer(unexpected_na, -pp,
                        names_sep = "_", names_to = c("wc", "bc", "t"),
                        values_drop_na = TRUE)
print(nrow(option1) == expected_nrows)
#> [1] FALSE
print(option1)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 5
#>      pp wc    bc    t     value
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1     1 wc1   bc1   t1        1
#> 2     1 wc1   bc1   t2        1
#> 3     1 wc2   bc1   t1        1
#> 4     2 wc1   bc2   t1        1
#> 5     2 wc1   bc2   t2        1
#> 6     2 wc2   bc2   t1        1
#> 7     2 wc2   bc2   t2        1
```

If we set `values_drop_na = FALSE` we get to make those missing values explicit, but we also have to keep all the missing values for the trials they were NOT expected to perform (i.e., the trials for the between-participant conditions they were not assigned to).

``` r
# This way we keep four extra rows per participant.
option2 <- pivot_longer(unexpected_na, -pp,
                        names_sep = "_", names_to = c("wc", "bc", "t"),
                        values_drop_na = FALSE)
print(nrow(option2) == expected_nrows)
#> [1] FALSE
print(option2)
#> # A tibble: 16 × 5
#>       pp wc    bc    t     value
#>    <int> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl>
#>  1     1 wc1   bc1   t1        1
#>  2     1 wc1   bc1   t2        1
#>  3     1 wc2   bc1   t1        1
#>  4     1 wc2   bc1   t2       NA
#>  5     1 wc1   bc2   t1       NA
#>  6     1 wc1   bc2   t2       NA
#>  7     1 wc2   bc2   t1       NA
#>  8     1 wc2   bc2   t2       NA
#>  9     2 wc1   bc1   t1       NA
#> 10     2 wc1   bc1   t2       NA
#> 11     2 wc2   bc1   t1       NA
#> 12     2 wc2   bc1   t2       NA
#> 13     2 wc1   bc2   t1        1
#> 14     2 wc1   bc2   t2        1
#> 15     2 wc2   bc2   t1        1
#> 16     2 wc2   bc2   t2        1
``` 

Do you think we could add an option to instruct `pivot_longer` to `values_drop_na` only for the between-participant conditions?
I don't know how such a feature could be implemented...
I reason if we have an argument where we can specify the between participants conditions, `pivot_longer` could then be taught not to remove rows for which there are non-NA values for any level of those conditions.
`pivot_longer()` should probably return an error if there are more than one non-NA values for more than one level of those conditions as that is by definition impossible for between-participant conditions.
``` r
# In essence this means ensuring the folowing tiblle is always empty:
#data %>%
#expand(nesting(participant_id, between_condX, between_condY, between_cond...),
#       within_conds, trial_number) %>%
# dplyr::anti_join(data)

# Which is the case for the expected dataset.
expected %>% expand(nesting(pp, bc), wc, t) %>% dplyr::anti_join(expected)
#> Joining, by = c("pp", "bc", "wc", "t")
#> # A tibble: 0 × 4
#> # … with 4 variables: pp <int>, bc <chr>, wc <chr>, t <chr>

# But not for the one with unexpected NAs
option1 %>% expand(nesting(pp, bc), wc, t) %>% dplyr::anti_join(option1)
#> Joining, by = c("pp", "bc", "wc", "t")
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>      pp bc    wc    t    
#>   <int> <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 bc1   wc2   t2
```

<sup>Created on 2022-11-14 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I apologize for the long-winded explanation but it is my first time opening a issue here and I didn't know how else to explain it.
My greatest gratitude to everyone working in `tidyverse` and specifically `tidyr`!

title: [Feature request] consider allowing dataframe-columns in `pivot_wider()`
description:
I realise this wouldn't open up a huge number of new possibilities, but it could make the output slightly more manageable when `values_from` selects many columns:

``` r
library(tidyverse)

# Hacky mockup of functionality. An actual implementation would 
# also handle multiple selections in `names_from`
pivot_wider2 <- function(data, values_from, ...) {
  
  vals_from <- data |> 
    select({{ values_from }}) |> 
    colnames()
  
  pivoted <- pivot_wider(data, ..., values_from = {{ values_from }})
  new_cols <- setdiff(colnames(pivoted), colnames(data))
  
  for (col in vals_from) {
    pivoted <- pivoted |> 
      mutate(
        "{col}" := across(str_subset(new_cols, glue::glue("^{fixed(col)}"))) |> 
          rename_with(~ str_remove(., glue::glue("^{fixed(col)}_"))),
        .keep = "unused"
      )
  }
  
  pivoted
  
}

us_rent_income |> 
  pivot_wider2(
    names_from = variable,
    values_from = c(estimate, moe),
    names_vary = "slowest"
  )
```

title: `hoist()` on a zero length list-of col should utilize the ptype
description:
Taken from: https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/997#issuecomment-984865044

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# no hoist column is returned at all
mtcars %>%
  group_nest(cyl) %>% # this gives us a list-of `data` col
  slice(0) %>%
  hoist(data, "mpg")
# A tibble: 0 x 2
# ... with 1 variable: cyl <dbl>
```

It ideally should instead return:

```r
mtcars %>%
  group_nest(cyl) %>%
  slice(0) %>%
  hoist(data, "mpg")
# A tibble: 0 x 2
# ... with 2 variables: cyl <dbl>, mpg <dbl>
```

This currently doesn't work for two reasons:

- This double `map()` should take into account the fact that `x` might be a list-of col, in which case applying the plucker to each list element could always result in the same type of plucked result. If the list elements are list-ofs or data.frames, then I think every plucked result should always have the type of `pluck(<ptype>, ...)`, but this isn't fully thought through. https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/511fc0f17ce3f0e6985e46918ecca2176fb95033/R/rectangle.R#L197-L201
- Even if we fix the above point, https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/1203, would force `pluck(<ptype>, ...)` to always return `NULL`, which makes fixing the above point useless right now

title: Should `*_wider()` have option to list new columns?
description:
I don't love that when you read code like this:

```R
locations <- gmaps_cities |> 
  unnest_wider(json) |> 
  select(-status) |> 
  unnest_longer(results) |> 
  unnest_wider(results)
```

You have no idea what columns you'll end up with, and if the data structure changes, this code will continue to work just giving you new columns names that will cause a potentially confusing downstream failure.

It might be nice if you could specify the column names you expect:

```R
locations <- gmaps_cities |> 
  unnest_wider(json, new = c("results", "status")) |> 
  select(-status) |> 
  unnest_longer(results) |> 
  unnest_wider(results, new = c("city", "address_components", "formatted_address", "geometry", "place_id", "types"))
```

OTOH, it seems unlikely that people would actually do this with out some helper that would automatically add to their code and we'd need to carefully think through the semantics of these columns (i.e. it feels like it shouldn't error if there were additional columns not included in the list?)

title: Consider moving the dots in `pivot_wider()` and `pivot_longer()`
description:
We'd move them up front, like:

```r
pivot_longer(
  data,
  cols,
  ...,
  cols_vary = "fastest",
  names_to = "name",
  names_prefix = NULL,
  names_sep = NULL,
  names_pattern = NULL,
  names_ptypes = NULL,
  names_transform = NULL,
  names_repair = "check_unique",
  values_to = "value",
  values_drop_na = FALSE,
  values_ptypes = NULL,
  values_transform = NULL
)

pivot_wider(
  data,
  ...,
  id_cols = NULL,
  id_expand = FALSE,
  names_from = name,
  names_prefix = "",
  names_sep = "_",
  names_glue = NULL,
  names_sort = FALSE,
  names_vary = "fastest",
  names_expand = FALSE,
  names_repair = "check_unique",
  values_from = value,
  values_fill = NULL,
  values_fn = NULL,
  unused_fn = NULL
)
```

This has two big benefits:

- Allows us to add more optional arguments to the generic without fear of breaking packages that have written methods for these generics. As long as the optional arguments come after the `...` in the generic, then there won't be a CRAN check warning.

- Forces users to specify the optional arguments by name. This is nice because we can add new optional arguments in any order without fear of breaking any positional arguments. This is particularly important for package code, where reliance on positional argument ordering can cause a CRAN failure

See https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/pull/1347#issuecomment-1095147941 for more details and some motivation

This would be a breaking change for anyone who is currently relying on positional arguments. But the `cols_vary` addition is _already_ a breaking change for the same reason, so it seems like a nice time to change this too.

title: Memory usage with separate very high and not released
description:
Hi

I am loading a tsv-file of 51 Mb. I am quite astonished that RStudio uses 8Gb of RAM for this.
When I keep working, this RAM usage even increases more and more, making RStudio slower and slower.

This is the script (the tsv-file can be dowloaded [here ](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/estat-navtree-portlet-prod/BulkDownloadListing?file=data/naio_10_cp15.tsv.gz)(a Eurostat data file).

```r
library(tidyverse)
supply <- read.table("naio_10_cp15.tsv",   sep = '\t', header = TRUE, fill = TRUE)  %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  pivot_longer(2:last_col(), names_to = "Year", values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(Value = as.numeric(Value),
         Year = as.numeric(str_replace(Year, "X","" ))) %>%
  rename(X1 = 1) %>%
  separate(X1, into = c("X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "X5"), sep = ",")
```
The last line takes very long and increases the memory usage on my Windows computer to around 8Gb. 

if I save the data in a RDS-file and load the table in a new R session, RAM is around 1.4 Gb instead of 8 Gb.

I tried garbage cleaning with gc(), but this had no effect.
I ran the script in the RGui and in RStudio with the same effect.
If I remove the data frame with `rm(supply),` the RAM usage gets a little bit less, but still around 7.5 Gb.

I am using R.40.4 on Windows 10 with 32Gb RAM.


Cheers
Renger

title: pivot doesn't preserve attributes
description:
It seems most (I tested filter, select, left_join, mutate, head) dplyr functions happily (and nicely) copy over attributes with metadata. For some reason, pivot functions do not:

> new_tibble(tibble(a=3,b=4),metadata="test") %>% validate_tibble() %>% attr("metadata")
[1] "test"
but:
>new_tibble(tibble(a=3,b=4),metadata="test") %>% validate_tibble() %>% pivot_longer(cols=c(a,b)) %>% attr("metadata")
NULL

This may be related to the discussions about extending tibbles, but I feel redefining the class adds lots of complexity for a simple user attribute (and I honestly couldn't make much sense of github.com/tidyverse/tibble/issues/275, and it being open means it is still not clarified I guess).

title: speed-up `separate` by extracting unique values first
description:
`separate` is surprisingly slow in common simple situations - where the column to be separated has few unique values but the  tibble has many rows.

In such cases, it's WAY faster to extract unique values first, `separate` then `right_join`. In fact, I don't see the downside of doing it always - even when all rows are (almost completely) unique, this extract/separate/right_join procedure is equally slow as just calling `separate` directly.

Consider following code handling two extremes - one unique value and (almost) no repeat values in a tibble of 1M rows:

```r
# separating a column with one unique value (in a tibble with 1M rows)
tmp = tibble(name = rep("foo_bar",1e6))
system.time(tmp %>% separate(name, into = c("foo","bar"), sep ='_')) # 11.293 on my computer
system.time(tmp %>% select(name) %>% 
              distinct() %>% 
              separate(name, into = c("foo","bar"), sep ='_',remove = F) %>% 
              right_join(tmp,by='name'))  # 0.078 on my computer
# 100x speed-up!

# separating a column with almost no repeating values (in a tibble with 1M rows)
set.seed(43)
random.10mers = replicate(2e6,paste0(letters[sample(1:26, 10, replace = T)],collapse = ''))
tmp = tibble(foo = random.10mers[1:1e6], bar = random.10mers[(1e6+1):2e6]) %>% 
  transmute(name = paste(foo,bar,sep = "_"))
system.time(tmp %>% separate(name, into = c("foo","bar"), sep ='_')) # 15.010 on my computer
system.time(tmp %>% select(name) %>% 
              distinct() %>% 
              separate(name, into = c("foo","bar"), sep ='_',remove = F) %>% 
              right_join(tmp,by='name')) # 14.883 on my computer
# no (significant) slow-down
```


---

It might be related to PR [#1304](https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/pull/1304). Apologies if I failed to find out it's in the works already.

title: nest/unnest pipeline breaks for empty tibbles
description:
When using a nest / unnest pipeline as follows with an non-empty tibble everything works as expected:
``` r
library(tidyr, warn.conflicts = F)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = F)

tibble(x=c(2,3), y=4) %>%
nest(data = x) %>%
# usually perform additional calculations here
unnest(data) %>%
select(x, y)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     4
#> 2     3     4
```

<sup>Created on 2022-09-12 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

``` r
filter(1 == 2) %>%    # to simulate an empty tibble
```

title: hoist(): should get a `.default` argument and error for missing elements if no default is set
description:
In `purrr` one can choose `chuck()` to error if an element is missing. If one uses `pluck()` instead there is a `.default` argument that allows one to specify the value used if the target is empty or absent. It would make a lot of sense to have this kind of control with `hoist()`.


``` r
library(tidyr)
df <- tibble(
  list_col = list(
    list(age = 1L),
    list(),
    list(age = NULL)
  )
)

# should error because `age` is missing in the second element
df %>% 
  hoist(list_col,
    "age"
  )

# doesn't error but uses the specified default value
df %>% 
  hoist(list_col,
    "age",
    .default = list(age = 0)
  )
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>     age
#>   <dbl>
#> 1     1
#> 2    0
#> 3    0

# use a one element vector to set a default value for all columns
df %>% 
  hoist(list_col,
    "age",
    .default = NA
  )
```

title: Odd behaviour with `extract()` when some elements are absent
description:
When the pattern is not always respected, `extract()` does not behave smoothly.
 All new columns without a full match become `NA`. 
I think it would be better to at least have a warning for that.

---
I wonder if it would be possible to have similar arguments to `fill` and `extra` to extract(), similar to separate()

I know it is easy to solve with dplyr and a couple more steps, but I think that `extract()` provides a clean way to perform this task.
``` r
dat <- tibble::tibble(
  x = c("foo (1)", "foo1", "foo2 (2)", "foo3 (3)")
)
dat |> 
    tidyr::extract(
        x, 
        into = c("x1", "x2"),
        regex = "(.+) \\((\\d+)\\)",
        convert = TRUE
    )
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   x1       x2
#>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 foo       1
#> 2 <NA>     NA
#> 3 foo2      2
#> 4 foo3      3

# Using separate and its extra arguments can work for that.
dat |> 
  tidyr::separate(
    x, 
    into = c("x1", "x2"),
    sep = " "
  )
#> Warning: Expected 2 pieces. Missing pieces filled with `NA` in 1 rows [2].
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   x1    x2   
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 foo   (1)  
#> 2 foo1  <NA> 
#> 3 foo2  (2)  
#> 4 foo3  (3)
#  
```
<sup>Created on 2022-06-29 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>

You can silent the `separate()` warning by specifying `fill = "right"`. Maybe a similar argument could be useful in `extract()`

## Expected output
``` r
# With a warning
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   x1    x2   
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 foo   1    
#> 2 foo1  <NA> 
#> 3 foo2  2    
#> 4 foo3  3
# with a code that would look like that.
dat |> 
    tidyr::extract(
        x, 
        into = c("x1", "x2"),
        regex = "(.+) \\((\\d+)\\)",
        convert = TRUE, 
        fill = "right"
    )
```

title: Is an is_nest function  necessary?
description:
Hi, I was working with nesting tables and I had a need to know if a table has nest data or not. Looking in the repository and the tidyr source code, I didn't find a function that validates it. However I know that nesting tables have list class columns, then we can check if a table is nesting if any columns are a list, without using a "native" function. We don't need is_nest function.

But when we want to know if a table is tibble, we only need to check if inheritance from tbl_df, and there is a function that does this little validation.

Do you think that is necessary to make a function that validates if an object is nesting?

This is the code that i propose:
```R
#' Test if the object was nesting
#'
#' This function returns `TRUE` for if a nestable object is nesting
#'
#' @param x An object
#' @return `TRUE` if the object inherits from the `tbl_df` class and any columns are a list.
#' @export
is_nest <- function(x) {
  # check if x is nestable
  if (!inherits(x, "tbl_df")) {
    return(FALSE)
  }
  # get class by columns
  class_by_col <- purrr::map_chr(x, class)
  return(any(class_by_col == "list"))
}
```
The test:
```r
# is_nest ---------------------------------------------------------------

test_that("is_nest", {
  expect_false(is_nest(iris))
  expect_true(is_nest(nest(iris,data = everything())))
  expect_false(is_nest(NULL))
  expect_true(is_nest(nest(dplyr::group_by(iris,Species))))
})
```

title: Feature request: `"single"` direction argument for `fill()`
description:
This is related to sfirke/janitor#428

I often work with datasets where I need to combine information for subjects in clinical trials. For that, I need to ensure that I have the same information from each of the different sources. For example, I may have multiple sources for the age of a subject when they start the study.

When I combine those data sets, I need to end up with the age as the same across all data. A paradigm I often use is below . Would that be of interest?

An alternate name may be `"unique"` instead of `"single"`.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
single_value <- function (x, missing = NA, info = NULL) {
  mask_found <- !(x %in% missing)
  found_values <- unique(x[mask_found])
  if (length(found_values) == 0) {
    missing[1]
  }
  else if (length(found_values) == 1) {
    found_values
  }
  else {
    if (!is.null(info)) {
      info <- paste(":", info)
    }
    stop("More than one (", length(found_values), ") value found (", 
         paste(found_values, collapse = ", "), ")", 
         info)
  }
}

my_data_good <-
  tibble(
    Subject=rep(1:2, each=2),
    Age=c(1, NA, 2, NA)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Subject) %>%
  mutate(
    Age=single_value(Age)
  )
my_data_good
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#> # Groups:   Subject [2]
#>   Subject   Age
#>     <int> <dbl>
#> 1       1     1
#> 2       1     1
#> 3       2     2
#> 4       2     2

my_data_bad <-
  tibble(
    Subject=rep(1:2, each=2),
    Age=c(1, NA, 2, 3)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Subject) %>%
  mutate(
    Age=single_value(Age)
  )
#> Error in `mutate()`:
#> ! Problem while computing `Age = single_value(Age)`.
#> i The error occurred in group 2: Subject = 2.
#> Caused by error in `single_value()`:
#> ! More than one (2) value found (2, 3)

# Proposed interface (does not work now)

my_data_interface <-
  tibble(
    Subject=rep(1:2, each=2),
    Age=c(1, NA, 2, 3)
  ) %>%
  group_by(Subject) %>%
  fill(Age, .direction="single")
#> Error in `fill()`:
#> ! `.direction` must be one of "down", "up", "downup", or "updown", not
#>   "single".
```

title: pivot_longer changes unpivoted date-integer to date-double
description:
I learned today that dates in R can sometimes be represented as integers, not just as doubles. This can occur like in the example below with `seq`, which changes the date-double into a date-integer. It seems like an unorthodox data type and might be thought of as a bug of `seq` that it came to be at all. Unexpectedly, `pivot_longer` converts these date-integers into the typical date-double, and I couldn't figure out a way to undo that.

I'm not sure where this would cause problems for someone, but I was surprised to see one of my answers on SO did not exactly match the original data because of this subtle change. https://stackoverflow.com/questions/71972396/how-to-reduce-processing-time-of-a-code-in-r


```r
set.seed(42)
df <- data.frame(date_dbl = as.Date( "2022-04-23"),  
                 date_int = seq(as.Date("2022-04-23"), length.out=2, by=1),
                 a = 1:2,
                 b = 3:4)
df
typeof(df$date_dbl)
# [1] "double"
typeof(df$date_int)
# [1] "integer"

df_piv <- tidyr::pivot_longer(df, -(1:2))
typeof(df_piv$date_dbl)
# [1] "double"
typeof(df_piv$date_int)
# [1] "double"
```

title: `pivot_longer()` should allow for varying the columns slower than the rows
description:
I was somewhat surprised at the `pivot_longer()` results below. It seems to attempt to keep the _row_ values close together (i.e. the original row 1 values became the new row 1 and 2 values), when really I wanted to keep the _column_ values together (i.e. the original column 1 values became the new row 1 and row 2 values).

This seems very related to `names_vary` in `pivot_wider()`, but I don't quite think the name is exactly right here.

I think a good name might actually be `cols_vary = "fastest"` (i.e. it iterates through all the columns before moving on to the next row). This goes nicely with the `cols` argument.

``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(
  start = as.Date(c("2019-01-01", "2019-01-02")),
  end = as.Date(c("2019-01-03", "2019-01-04"))
)
df
#> # A tibble: 2 × 2
#>   start      end       
#>   <date>     <date>    
#> 1 2019-01-01 2019-01-03
#> 2 2019-01-02 2019-01-04

pivot_longer(df, c(start, end))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   name  value     
#>   <chr> <date>    
#> 1 start 2019-01-01
#> 2 end   2019-01-03
#> 3 start 2019-01-02
#> 4 end   2019-01-04

# I sort of expected this here:
pivot_longer(df, c(start, end)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(desc(name))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   name  value     
#>   <chr> <date>    
#> 1 start 2019-01-01
#> 2 start 2019-01-02
#> 3 end   2019-01-03
#> 4 end   2019-01-04

# This is what we get from gather
gather(df, "name", "value", start, end)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 2
#>   name  value     
#>   <chr> <date>    
#> 1 start 2019-01-01
#> 2 start 2019-01-02
#> 3 end   2019-01-03
#> 4 end   2019-01-04


df <- tibble(
  id = c(1L, 1L, 2L, 2L),
  start = as.Date(c("2019-01-01")) + 0:3,
  end = as.Date(c("2019-01-03")) + 0:3
)
df
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>      id start      end       
#>   <int> <date>     <date>    
#> 1     1 2019-01-01 2019-01-03
#> 2     1 2019-01-02 2019-01-04
#> 3     2 2019-01-03 2019-01-05
#> 4     2 2019-01-04 2019-01-06

# Not this:
pivot_longer(df, c(start, end))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>      id name  value     
#>   <int> <chr> <date>    
#> 1     1 start 2019-01-01
#> 2     1 end   2019-01-03
#> 3     1 start 2019-01-02
#> 4     1 end   2019-01-04
#> 5     2 start 2019-01-03
#> 6     2 end   2019-01-05
#> 7     2 start 2019-01-04
#> 8     2 end   2019-01-06

# I actually dont want this either because i think all of `id == 1` should
# be kept together
gather(df, "name", "value", start, end)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>      id name  value     
#>   <int> <chr> <date>    
#> 1     1 start 2019-01-01
#> 2     1 start 2019-01-02
#> 3     2 start 2019-01-03
#> 4     2 start 2019-01-04
#> 5     1 end   2019-01-03
#> 6     1 end   2019-01-04
#> 7     2 end   2019-01-05
#> 8     2 end   2019-01-06

# This is what I really wanted, and is what `cols_vary = "slowest"` would give
pivot_longer(df, c(start, end)) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(id, desc(name))
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#>      id name  value     
#>   <int> <chr> <date>    
#> 1     1 start 2019-01-01
#> 2     1 start 2019-01-02
#> 3     1 end   2019-01-03
#> 4     1 end   2019-01-04
#> 5     2 start 2019-01-03
#> 6     2 start 2019-01-04
#> 7     2 end   2019-01-05
#> 8     2 end   2019-01-06
```

Implementation wise, I think we need to _not_ interleave here:
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/48ba23db97ebeb78101a7542564d573106a7f682/R/pivot-long.R#L259-L265

And then maybe use `vec_rep_each()` here instead of `vec_rep()` (that feels very similar to how `names_vary` works)
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/48ba23db97ebeb78101a7542564d573106a7f682/R/pivot-long.R#L274

title: Add RStudio as funder
Should the `.value` placeholder be `.variable?
description:
Take this example:

```R
family <- tribble(
  ~family,  ~dob_child1,  ~dob_child2, ~name_child1, ~name_child2,
        1, "1998-11-26", "2000-01-29",      "Susan",       "Jose",
        2, "1996-06-22",           NA,       "Mark",           NA,
        3, "2002-07-11", "2004-04-05",        "Sam",       "Seth",
        4, "2004-10-10", "2009-08-27",      "Craig",       "Khai",
        5, "2000-12-05", "2005-02-28",     "Parker",     "Gracie",
)
family <- family %>% 
  mutate(across(starts_with("dob"), parse_date))
family
```

I think it's natural to say something like: This problem is hard because the column names contain both a variable name (`dob`, `name`) and a variable value (`child1`, `child2`).  But the specification is:

```R
family %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !family, 
    names_to = c(".value", "child"), 
    names_sep = "_", 
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
```

Would it be easier to understand if it was:

```R
family %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !family, 
    names_to = c(".variable", "child"), 
    names_sep = "_", 
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
```

?

(We'd still keep `.value` for backward compatibility)

title: `drop_na` is slower than equivalent `filter(!is.na)`
description:
Even though I'd expect to at least be the same, it seems that `drop_na` is consistently slower than the equivalent `dplyr` call using `filter. This may add further support to #939, but may also suggest a rewrite of the underlying function.

The biggest difference is when using `everything()`, but `drop_na` is slower even when calling specific columns.

Note that `drop_na` also removes empty vectors, whereas `filter(!is.na)` does not (see #1308).

``` r
library(tidyverse)

large_data_set <- slice(starwars, rep(1:nrow(starwars), 1000)) %>% 
  select(-vehicles, -starships)  # Remove columns with empty vectors which are treated differently by `drop_na` and `filter(!is.na)`

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  tidyr = drop_na(large_data_set),
  dplyr = filter(large_data_set, across(everything(), ~!is.na(.x))),
  check = "equal"
)
#> Unit: milliseconds
#>   expr      min       lq     mean   median       uq       max neval
#>  tidyr 56.05687 65.86542 71.92696 69.59035 75.00460 139.38936   100
#>  dplyr 10.23244 12.95009 17.74474 14.30317 16.10918  92.31145   100

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  tidyr = drop_na(large_data_set, hair_color),
  dplyr = filter(large_data_set, across(hair_color, ~!is.na(.x))),
  check = "equal"
)
#> Unit: milliseconds
#>   expr      min       lq     mean    median       uq      max neval
#>  tidyr 6.993897 9.019461 13.16170 10.127768 13.44942 81.56772   100
#>  dplyr 6.658303 8.750342 10.55285  9.901146 13.25528 18.40949   100

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  tidyr = drop_na(large_data_set, matches(c("hair_color", "birth_year"), ignore.case=T)),
  dplyr = filter(large_data_set, across(matches(c("hair_color", "birth_year"), ignore.case=T), ~!is.na(.x))),
  check = "equal"
)
#> Unit: milliseconds
#>   expr      min       lq     mean   median       uq      max neval
#>  tidyr 6.215764 7.307484 9.285488 7.528882 9.515669 76.95144   100
#>  dplyr 5.991358 7.514976 8.435270 7.726216 8.749177 15.98149   100
```

title: `drop_na` removes empty vectors where `filter(!is.na)` does not
description:
In #939, `filter(across(everything(), ~is.na(.x)))` is referenced as a `dplyr` replacement to `drop_na`.

However, `drop_na` removes empty vectors where `filter(!is.na)` does not:


``` r
library(tidyverse)

all_equal(drop_na(starwars),filter(starwars, across(everything(), ~!is.na(.x))))
#> [1] "Different number of rows"

starwars_without_empty_vectors <- filter(starwars, across(everything(), ~lengths(.x) > 0))
all_equal(drop_na(starwars_without_empty_vectors),filter(starwars_without_empty_vectors, across(everything(), ~!is.na(.x))))
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: Wrong SQL query generated for left_join() in sparklyr when column names same but case
description:
I encountered a bug when two tables have same joining column names that differ only in case (e.g. "x" and "X").
When they are the same the query is correct:
```
library(tidyverse)
library(sparklyr)

sc <- spark_connect(method = "databricks")

temp_tibble1 <- tibble(x = 1:5, y = 11:15) %>% copy_to(sc, ., name = "temp_tibble1", overwrite = TRUE)
temp_tibble2 <- tibble(x = 1:5, z = 111:115) %>% copy_to(sc, ., "temp_tibble2", overwrite = TRUE)

temp_tibble1 %>%
  left_join(temp_tibble2, by = c("x" = "x")) %>% show_query()
```
giving
```
<SQL>
SELECT `LHS`.`x` AS `x`, `y`, `z`
FROM `temp_tibble1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `temp_tibble2` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`x`)
```
but
```
temp_tibble1 <- tibble(x = 1:5, y = 11:15) %>% copy_to(sc, ., name = "temp_tibble1", overwrite = TRUE)
temp_tibble2 <- tibble(X = 1:5, z = 111:115) %>% copy_to(sc, ., "temp_tibble2", overwrite = TRUE)

temp_tibble1 %>%
  left_join(temp_tibble2, by = c("x" = "X")) %>% show_query()
```
gives
```
<SQL>
SELECT `x`, `y`, `z`
FROM `temp_tibble1` AS `LHS`
LEFT JOIN `temp_tibble2` AS `RHS`
ON (`LHS`.`x` = `RHS`.`X`)
```
which fails with

> Error : org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: Reference 'x' is ambiguous, could be: LHS.x, RHS.x.; line 1 pos 7

*I originally reported that issue to the sparklyr team but I suppose it belongs here.*

title: Feature request: separate over multiple columns
description:
Hi,

`separate()` is an awesome tool, but it is currently limited to one single column, hence the internal use of `tidyselect::vars_pull()`.

There are a whole lot of questions online on how to use it on several columns (for instance [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/47055033/splitting-several-columns-of-a-dataframe-with-separate-tidyr-in-r), [here](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48688747/split-multiple-columns-into-multiple-columns-using-r), or [here](https://groups.google.com/g/davis-rug/c/JTT-jYaBews?pli=1)), but there is no satisfying, elegant answer yet.

Here is an example use case:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
N_COL = 2
df = tibble(col_keys = c("X=1 & Y=1", "X=1 & Y=2", "X=2 & Y=1", "X=2 & Y=2")) %>% 
    separate(col_keys, into=paste0(".col_", seq(N_COL )), 
             sep=" & ", remove=FALSE)
df
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   col_keys  .col_1 .col_2
#>   <chr>     <chr>  <chr> 
#> 1 X=1 & Y=1 X=1    Y=1   
#> 2 X=1 & Y=2 X=1    Y=2   
#> 3 X=2 & Y=1 X=2    Y=1   
#> 4 X=2 & Y=2 X=2    Y=2
df %>% 
    separate(.col_1, into=paste0(".col_1", c("_key", "_value")), 
                sep="=", remove=TRUE) %>% #repeated `N_COL` times
    separate(.col_2, into=paste0(".col_2", c("_key", "_value")), 
                sep="=", remove=TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   col_keys  .col_1_key .col_1_value .col_2_key .col_2_value
#>   <chr>     <chr>      <chr>        <chr>      <chr>       
#> 1 X=1 & Y=1 X          1            Y          1           
#> 2 X=1 & Y=2 X          1            Y          2           
#> 3 X=2 & Y=1 X          2            Y          1           
#> 4 X=2 & Y=2 X          2            Y          2
```

<sup>Created on 2022-01-23 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v2.0.1)</sup>


I think it would be a very nice feature to add to `separate()`. For instance, I would expect a syntax such as:

```r
df %>% 
   separate(starts_with(".col_"), into=c("{.name}_key", "{.name}_value"), 
            sep="=", remove=FALSE)`
```

Here is how I would do it for now, using `dplyr` and some clever hack from Romain François:

``` r
#' @source https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/5563#issuecomment-721769342
across_unpack = function(...) {
    out = across(...)
    tidyr::unpack(out, names(out), names_sep = "_")
}

df %>% 
    mutate(across_unpack(starts_with(".col_"), ~{
        .name = cur_column()
        tibble(.x) %>% set_names(.name) %>% 
            separate(.name, into=c("key", "value"), 
                     sep="=", remove=TRUE)
    }))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 7
#>   col_keys  .col_1 .col_2 .col_1_key .col_1_value .col_2_key .col_2_value
#>   <chr>     <chr>  <chr>  <chr>      <chr>        <chr>      <chr>       
#> 1 X=1 & Y=1 X=1    Y=1    X          1            Y          1           
#> 2 X=1 & Y=2 X=1    Y=2    X          1            Y          2           
#> 3 X=2 & Y=1 X=2    Y=1    X          2            Y          1           
#> 4 X=2 & Y=2 X=2    Y=2    X          2            Y          2
```

title: 'AND' logic when specifying columns with drop_na()
description:
Using drop_na, I frequently want to drop NAs within multiple columns using AND logic instead of the default OR. 

For example, consider the `penguins` dataset from {palmerpenguins}. There are two rows where BOTH body_mass_g and sex are NA:

``` r
library(hacksaw)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins %>% 
  keep_na(body_mass_g, sex)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 8
#>   species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_… body_mass_g sex  
#>   <fct>   <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>            <int>       <int> <fct>
#> 1 Adelie  Torge…             NA            NA               NA          NA <NA> 
#> 2 Gentoo  Biscoe             NA            NA               NA          NA <NA> 
#> # … with 1 more variable: year <int>
```

<sup>Created on 2020-10-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

The following, however, removes *all* the NAs from sex, some of which I want to preserve:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins %>% 
  drop_na(body_mass_g, sex)
#> # A tibble: 333 x 8
#>    species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_… body_mass_g
#>    <fct>   <fct>           <dbl>         <dbl>            <int>       <int>
#>  1 Adelie  Torge…           39.1          18.7              181        3750
#>  2 Adelie  Torge…           39.5          17.4              186        3800
#>  3 Adelie  Torge…           40.3          18                195        3250
#>  4 Adelie  Torge…           36.7          19.3              193        3450
#>  5 Adelie  Torge…           39.3          20.6              190        3650
#>  6 Adelie  Torge…           38.9          17.8              181        3625
#>  7 Adelie  Torge…           39.2          19.6              195        4675
#>  8 Adelie  Torge…           41.1          17.6              182        3200
#>  9 Adelie  Torge…           38.6          21.2              191        3800
#> 10 Adelie  Torge…           34.6          21.1              198        4400
#> # … with 323 more rows, and 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>
```

<sup>Created on 2020-10-20 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

My workaround is to sum the NAs via mutate and then filter. But my dream syntax 😊  would be something like:

```
penguins %>% 
  drop_na(body_mass_g, sex, .logic = "AND")
```
 Does this sound reasonable? Or perhaps a fringe case?

title: Many, if not all tidyr functions coerce data frame input to tibbles
description:
Hi, first of all thanks for the great package.

The problem is that whenever you use tidyr, it takes your data frame and turns it into a tibble.
My expectation is that the I get the same object out, as I passed in (Like in `reshape2::melt()` for example).
At the very least, give us an argument or global option to set the return type.

If this is the desired behaviour, I don't agree with it, but that's okay. However, it should be documented.

title: pivot_wider() inconsistent column naming rule : no prefix if values_from corresponds to 1 column
description: By default, when _values_from_ correspond to several columns, each column name serves as prefix for the columns names of the widened dataset, while there is no prefix if values_from correspond to a single column. It would be more user friendly to have a consistent default behaviour, let alone that column names such as "1", "2", etc. with loss of the original column name represent a loss in meaningfulness.

title: Provide Wilkinson-Rogers formula interface to complete
description:
* `~ x / y` -> `nesting(x, y)`
* `~ x * y` -> `crossing(x, y)`
* `~ x * (y / z)` -> `crossing(x, nesting(y, z))`
* `~ x / (y * z)` -> `nesting(x, crossing(y, z))`

title: Should `complete()` and `expand()` disallow accessing the group columns?
description:
With #1289 we added a grouped-df method for `complete()`. Originally I made the decision to pass `cur_data_all()` through to each ungrouped call to `complete()` because it seemed like people were (nonsensically) completing on grouping variables. This actually causes issues!

https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/c73cf216434ca5edb1b560000d5e5aeca3bf39ef/R/complete.R#L99-L108

I am thinking we should just pass `cur_data()` through instead, which would avoid the issue seen below.

This would result in a __breaking change__ that people would no longer be able to complete on a grouping variable (You'd get an error saying that the grouping variable isn't found). But I think that completing on a grouping variable is a bit useless, as the whole point is to complete _within_ that variable, so you shouldn't have access to it.

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

df <- tibble(
  item_id = c(1:2, 2, 3),
  value1 = c(1, NA, 3, 4),
  item_name = c("a", "a", "b", "b"),
  value2 = 4:7,
  group = c(1:2, 1, 2)
)
gdf <- group_by(df, group)
gdf
#> # A tibble: 4 × 5
#> # Groups:   group [2]
#>   item_id value1 item_name value2 group
#>     <dbl>  <dbl> <chr>      <int> <dbl>
#> 1       1      1 a              4     1
#> 2       2     NA a              5     2
#> 3       2      3 b              6     1
#> 4       3      4 b              7     2

# expand "within" each group. so the group value should be repeated.
expand(gdf, item_id, item_name)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 3
#> # Groups:   group [2]
#>   group item_id item_name
#>   <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1     1       1 a        
#> 2     1       1 b        
#> 3     1       2 a        
#> 4     1       2 b        
#> 5     2       2 a        
#> 6     2       2 b        
#> 7     2       3 a        
#> 8     2       3 b

# (the NAs in the 1 `group` should be 1, and should be 2 in the 2 `group`)
# we don't get that here because we passed the "full" data including grouping
# cols through to `complete.data.frame()`, which did a full-join resulting in
# missing values for those columns. So then `summarize()` thought it didn't
# need to add the grouping columns back on.
complete(gdf, item_id, item_name)
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#> # Groups:   group [3]
#>   group item_id item_name value1 value2
#>   <dbl>   <dbl> <chr>      <dbl>  <int>
#> 1     1       1 a              1      4
#> 2    NA       1 b             NA     NA
#> 3    NA       2 a             NA     NA
#> 4     1       2 b              3      6
#> 5     2       2 a             NA      5
#> 6    NA       2 b             NA     NA
#> 7    NA       3 a             NA     NA
#> 8     2       3 b              4      7
```

title: FR: Rectangling a list according to a specification
description:
Some time ago I have written a function for rectangling a nested list according to a given specification. I basically like `hoist()` but I think that something like my list parser could also be a nice addition.

A specification basically has the following form:

``` r
lcols(
  `col_name = lcol_*(pluck_specification)`,
  `col_name = lcol_*(pluck_specification)`,
  ...
)
```

(I'm not that keen on the name but didn't think of anything better yet). The functions `lcol_*` are like follows

* `lcol_lgl(path)`: creates a logical column.
* similarly `lcol_int/dbl/chr/fct`, `dat` for date, `dtt` for datetime, `hms`, `guess`.
* `lcol_lst_of`(path, .ptype): creates a list-of-<ptype> column.
* `lcol_df(path, ...)` creates a dataframe column where `...` are `lcol_*` functions again.
* `lcol_df_lst` similar to `lcol_df` but creates a list of dataframe column.

These functions all have the arguments:
* `.req`: if it is `TRUE` and the path is missing an error is thrown (basically `chuck` is used instead of `pluck`).
* `.parser` can be used for a custom conversion function. This can be especially useful for date or datetime columns

For example to parse the `discog` data from `repurrrsive` this could like below:

``` r
recordlist <- repurrrsive::discog

col_specs <- lcols(
  lcol_int("id"),
  first_artist_name = lcol_chr(list("basic_information", "artists", 1, "name")),
  artists_df_lst = lcol_df_lst(
    c("basic_information", "artists"),
    lcol_chr("join"),
    lcol_chr("name"),
    lcol_chr("role"),
    lcol_int("id")
  ),
  rating_list = lcol_lst_of("rating", .ptype = ""),
  info = lcol_df(
    "basic_information",
    lcol_int("id"),
    lcol_chr("title")
  ),
)

list_parse(recordlist, col_specs)
#> # A tibble: 155 x 5
#>         id first_artist_name   artists_df_lst rating_list info$id $title        
#>      <int> <chr>               <list<df[,4]>> <list<chr>>   <int> <chr>         
#>  1  7.50e6 Mollot                     [1 × 4]         [1]  7.50e6 Demo          
#>  2  4.49e6 Una Bèstia Incontr…        [1 × 4]         [1]  4.49e6 Observant Com…
#>  3  9.83e6 S.H.I.T. (3)               [1 × 4]         [1]  9.83e6 I             
#>  4  9.77e6 Rata Negra                 [1 × 4]         [1]  9.77e6 Oído Absoluto 
#>  5  7.24e6 Ivy (18)                   [1 × 4]         [1]  7.24e6 A Cat's Cause…
#>  6  1.31e7 Tashme                     [1 × 4]         [1]  1.31e7 Tashme        
#>  7  7.11e6 Desgraciados               [1 × 4]         [1]  7.11e6 Demo          
#>  8  1.05e7 Phantom Head               [1 × 4]         [1]  1.05e7 Let The Mirac…
#>  9  1.13e7 Sub Space (2)              [1 × 4]         [1]  1.13e7 Sub Space     
#> 10  1.17e7 Small Man (2)              [1 × 4]         [1]  1.17e7 Demo          
#> # … with 145 more rows
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-13 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

I think this approach has the following perks:
* the specification is concise and readable
* one can create dataframe columns and list of dataframe columns. I find them useful (especially the list of dataframe columns are sometimes basically required) and I didn't find an easy way to do this with `hoist()` and `unnest_*()`.
* in spirit of `jsonlite:::simplify()` and `readr::read_csv()` one could have an auto parser and print a copy-pastable specification (this is one of my favourite features of this approach!).
* one can have things like an argument `.default = "guess"` in `lcols` to auto parse all new unspecified fields.
* parsing of nested lists still works even when the nested field is missing.
* knowing the specification beforehand can make this quite fast.


Things missing:
* parameters to control unnesting in `lcol_df`.
* how to handle names of list elements.

title: unnest no longer works for AsIs columns?
description:
Hi, I'm trying to update from `tidyr` 1.1.3 to 1.1.4 and noticed it broke some tests. It looks like this is an MRE:

```
DF = data.frame(a = 1:2, b = I(list(3:4, 5:6)))
tidyr::unnest(DF, "b")
```

output in tidyr:1.1.3
```
# A tibble: 4 x 2
      a     b
  <int> <int>
1     1     3
2     1     4
3     2     5
4     2     6
```

vs in tidyr:1.1.4
```
# A tibble: 2 x 2
      a b        
  <int> <I<list>>
1     1 <int [2]>
2     2 <int [2]>
```

We can solve this by doing `class(DF$b) = NULL`, but I don't see this mentioned in the NEWS, so I'm wondering if it's an unintended regression / bug.

title: `pivot_longer()` ptype arg updates and S3 extensions
description:
In https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/pull/1287 we updated `names_ptypes = list()` and `values_ptypes = list()` to instead have default values of `NULL` and accept a single empty ptype as the ptype that would be applied to all columns while pivoting longer. This was part of the larger unification of this idea in #1284.

The ptype arguments in particular are a little special because `list()` now has a different meaning than before. Previously it meant "no columns to apply a ptype for". Now it means "apply a list ptype on all the columns".

This is fine for tidyr itself, because the new default it `NULL`. But extension packages like dbplyr and sparklyr, which eventually call tidyr tools, will still be using the old default value of `list()`, which causes them to break.

What should we do here? Temporarily force `list()` to be equal to `NULL` for these two ptype related arguments with a warning? In the meantime we can open PRs for dbplyr and sparklyr to update them to the new defaults, and then remove this in the next version of tidyr.

Packages with the issue:
- dbplyr
- sparklyr
- sf
- tidyseurat
