description:
Wondering if the speed problem I'm observing between: `tidyr::pivot_longer`  and `tidyr::gather` or `data.table::melt.data.table` is a problem or not. 

Below is a reproducible example:

# generate the test dataset: genomic data
```r
require(tidyverse)
require(data.table)
data.test <- matrix(
  data = sample(
    x = c(0L, 1L, 2L, NA_integer_),#the genotypes
    size = 2e+07,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(0.8, 0.10, 0.05, 0.05)
    ),
  nrow = 20000,#number of SNPs/markers
  ncol = 1000,#number of samples
  dimnames = list(rownames = seq(1, 20000, 1), colnames = seq(1, 1000, 1))
  ) %>%
  tibble::as_tibble(x = ., rownames = "MARKERS")
```

# test1: `data.table::melt.data.table`
```r
system.time(
test1 <- data.table::as.data.table(data.test) %>%
  data.table::melt.data.table(
    data = .,
    id.vars = "MARKERS",
    variable.name = "INDIVIDUALS",
    value.name = "GENOTYPES",
    variable.factor = FALSE) %>%
  tibble::as_tibble(.)
)
#~0.41sec
```

# test2: `tidyr::gather`
```r
system.time(
test2 <- tidyr::gather(
  data = data.test,
  key = "INDIVIDUALS",
  value = "GENOTYPES",
  -MARKERS)
)
#~0.39sec
```

# test3: latest `tidyr::pivot_longer`
```r
system.time(
test3 <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  df = data.test,
  cols = -MARKERS,
  names_to = "INDIVIDUALS",
  values_to = "GENOTYPES")
)
#~90sec !!!
```

Is this normal or not ?
Thanks
Thierry

title: extract () function to separate a column
description:
Hello:)
I hope you might help.

My cdr3s_aa column in df looks like this: TRA:CILRGVYNNNDMRF;TRA:CAFMYNNDMRF;TRB:CATGGGRTSNEQFF;TRB:CASSLGGAYEQYF

I was thinking to use extract () to devide this column into two called alpha and beta. Alpha column would then have only TRA sequences where beta only TRB.

I got stuck on the regex, so could you please suggest how it could look like? This is how my code looks like now:

aa_frequency <- reactive_tcr1 %>% extract (cdr3s_aa, into = c("alpha", "beta"), regex = "([^TRA;])-([^TRB;])", remove = FALSE)

However, this doesn't find any groups. 

Thanks!

title: tidyr 1.1.1 cannot be installed on centOS 7
description:
`tidyr` `1.1.1` cannot be installed on `centOS 7`

---

Starting from a `centOS 7` docker image, install dependencies of `tidyr`

Installing `1.1.0` from archive works
```
Rscript -e 'install.packages("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/tidyr/tidyr_1.1.0.tar.gz")'
```

Installing `1.1.1` does not.
```

title: `crossing()` a zero-row data frame
description:
I believe it used to be that `tidyr::crossing(x=1:3, data.frame())` would return a value equivalent to `data.frame(x=1:3)`, but now it seems that `tidyr` returns a zero-row data frame with the column `x`.

I personally find the idea that crossing something with an empty data frame and returning the original value (in data frame format) to be more intuitive and much more useful.  It also would parallel behavior with a `NULL` argument.  Unless there's a principled decision behind this that I'm now aware of?

title: reciprocate of `hoist()` ?
description:
I find it odd that this function doesn't have a reciprocate, it's also quite hard to achieve it by other ways : 

``` r
library(tidyr)
df <- tibble(x=1:2, listcol = list(list(a=3, b =4, c=5), list(a=6, b =7, c=8)))
print.data.frame(df) # as.data.frame just for printing
#>   x listcol
#> 1 1 3, 4, 5
#> 2 2 6, 7, 8
x <- hoist(df, listcol, "b")
print.data.frame(x)
#>   x b listcol
#> 1 1 4    3, 5
#> 2 2 7    6, 8
```

Say from here I want to modify the `b` column and put it back to its place, wouldn't it be handy to have something like : 

    unhoist(df, listcol, "b", .after = 1) # or `.after = "a"`, or `.before = "c"`

title: melt data.frames with non-atomic 'measure' columns
description:
Is it possible to `gather()` a data frame when it contains list elements?

``` r
library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("purrr")

data <- data_frame(
    name = c("Alex", "Alex", "Alex", "Tim", "Tim", "Tim"),
    year = c(1990, 1991, 1992, 1990, 1991, 1992),
    height = c(160, 165, 170, 120, 134, 150),
    weight = c(50, 52, 53, 48, 48, 52)
)

models <- data %>%
    group_by(name) %>%
    nest() %>%
    mutate(
        lm = map(data, ~lm(year ~ height, data = .)),
        lm2 = map(data, ~lm(year ~ height + weight, data = .))
    )

models
```

This produces the following output:

```
   name           data      lm     lm2
  (chr)          (chr)   (chr)   (chr)
1  Alex <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm>
2   Tim <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm>
```

Now I would want to `gather()` this into a long format:

``` r
models %>% gather(variabe, value, -name, -data)
```

But I get:

```
Error: Can't melt data.frames with non-atomic 'measure' columns
```

I would like to end up with final data frame like this:

```
   name            data  variable    value
  (chr)           (chr)     (chr)    (chr)
1  Alex  <tbl_df [3,3]>        lm  <S3:lm>
2  Alex  <tbl_df [3,3]>       lm2  <S3:lm>
3   Tim  <tbl_df [3,3]>        lm  <S3:lm>
4   Tim  <tbl_df [3,3]>       lm2  <S3:lm>
```

title: pivot_longer: "lossy cast" when names_ptypes includes double
description:
When asking pivot_longer to parse doubles out of column names, round-number values fail with a "lossy cast" error:

```r
ok <- tribble(~X1.1cm, ~X1.2cm, 1, 2)
fail <- tribble(~X1.0cm, ~X1.5cm, 1, 2)

pivot_longer(
    data = ok,
    cols = starts_with("X"),
    names_pattern = "X([\\d.]+)cm",
    names_ptypes = list(name = double()))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#    name value
#   <dbl> <dbl>
# 1   1.1     1
# 2   1.2     2

pivot_longer(
    data = fail,
    cols = starts_with("X"),
    names_pattern = "X([\\d.]+)cm",
    names_ptypes = list(name = double()))
# Error: Lossy cast from `x` <character> to `to` <double>.
# Locations: 1
# Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.

# workaround: pivot as character, then coerce
pivot_longer(
    data = fail,
    cols = starts_with("X"),
    names_pattern = "X([\\d.]+)cm") %>%
mutate(name = parse_number(name))
# # A tibble: 2 x 2
#    name value
#   <dbl> <dbl>
# 1   1       1
# 2   1.5     2
```

Looks like the complaint originates from a `!=` comparison inside `vctrs:::vec_cast.double.character`. I realize the cast technically *is* lossy (in the sense that `c("1.0", "1.1") != c(1.0, 1.1)` evaluates to `c(TRUE, FALSE)`), which is why I'm opening the issue here instead of in vctrs -- whether or not this is the intended behavior from `vec_cast.double.character`, I'd hope that `pivot_longer` would account for float precision when I give it an explicit float prototype.

title: Passing values to pivot_longer's repair argument when passing ".value" to names_to causes unused argument error
description:
When passing `".value"` to the `names_to` argument in `pivot_longer()`, passing a value to the `names_repair` argument produces an "unused arguments" error. This is likely because of special functionality of `".value"` but is inconsistent with how `names_repair` is supposed to behave, i.e. it should resolve the bad names problem by appending numeric suffixes.

```r
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

# Create example data
dat <- data.frame(
  foo_1a = rnorm(20),
  foo_1b = rnorm(20),
  foo_2a = rnorm(20),
  foo_2b = rnorm(20),
  bar_1a = rnorm(20),
  bar_1b = rnorm(20),
  bar_2a = rnorm(20),
  bar_2b = rnorm(20),
  cat = runif(20),
  dog = 1:20
)

# No error
dat %>% tidyr::pivot_longer(
  cols = ends_with(c("1a", "1b", "2a", "2b")),
  names_to = c(".value", "profile"),
  names_sep = "_"
)

# Add another variable that causes duplicate names
# when pivoted due to column name prefix
dat_fail <- dat %>% mutate(foo = rnorm(20))

# "Error: Failed to Create output due to bad names"
# because the function tries to create foo when it's
# already in the data.
dat_fail %>% tidyr::pivot_longer(
  cols = ends_with(c("1a", "1b", "2a", "2b")),
  names_to = c(".value", "profile"),
  names_sep = "_"
)

# Attempt to fix: try passing "unique" to
# repair argument leads to unused argument
# error in pivot_longer_spec.
dat_fail %>% tidyr::pivot_longer_spec(
  cols = ends_with(c("1a", "1b", "2a", "2b")),
  names_to = c(".value", "profile"),
  names_sep = "_",
  names_repair = "unique"
)

```
The error was simply a typo in using `pivot_longer_spec()` instead of `pivot_longer`.

title: `replace_na` fails on a tibble when a variable is named `0`
description:
---

When using `tidyr::replace_na`, if a you're using the `replace` parameter for a list with multiple variables, if one of those variables in the named list is `0` then the function fails. It seems to interpret the variable name of `0` as an index rather than a variable name, despite properly recognizing the other numeric variable names (called using back ticks) as explicit variable names. 

I'm actually unsure if this is an issue with `tidyr` or `tibble` - because this issue didn't exist in `tibble_2.1.3` but was introduced when I updated to `tibble_3.0.1`. 

``` r
dat <- tibble::tibble(
  `2` = c(1, NA, 2), 
  `1` = c('a', NA, 'b'), 
  `0` = c(1, NA, 2)
)

tidyr::replace_na(dat, replace=list(
  `2` = 0,
  `1` = ''
  )
)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>     `2` `1`     `0`
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dbl>
#> 1     1 "a"       1
#> 2     0 ""       NA
#> 3     2 "b"       2

tidyr::replace_na(dat, replace=list(
  `2` = 0,
  `1` = '',
  `0` = 0
  )
)
#> Error: Must extract column with a single valid subscript.

title: Unnest functions fail with lists of exprs
description:
Hi,

I have some code which uses a fair bit of meta programming (so a table of audit measures basically - where we have lists of the audit measure function being applied). I spotted a neat-looking optimisation to use tidyr to unnest the list.

Unfortunately, when using unnest where the list elements are functions, we get errors within the function (and presumably unpredictable behaviour). Ironically it's presumably because internally tidyr is doing exactly what my code is trying to do with the results of the function!

To demonstrate this, I used the tidyr example and converted the 'films' list-column to have functions rather than film titles (imagine we're going to pluck those functions and insert them into a later dplyr query on a table).

<details>

---

Brief description of the problem

```r
df <- tibble(
   character = c("Toothless", "Dory"),
   metadata = list(
     list(
       species = "dragon",
       color = "black",
       films = c(
         rlang::expr(.data[["title"]] == "How to Train Your Dragon"),
         rlang::expr(.data[["title"]] == "How to Train Your Dragon 2"),
         rlang::expr(.data[["title"]] == "How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World")
        )
     ),
     list(
       species = "clownfish",
       color = "blue",
       films = c(rlang::expr(.data[["title"]] == "Finding Nemo"),
         rlang::expr(.data[["title"]] == "Finding Dory"))
     )
   )
 )

tidyr::unnest_wider(df, metadata)

tidyr::unnest_longer(df, films)
```

The last command to unnest films results in:

Error in eval_tidy(enquo(var), var_env) : object 'films' not found

title: pivot_wider fails with unintuitive error message when values_fill is not a list
description:
The error message given when the `values_fill` argument to `pivot_wider` is not a list is currently somewhat unintuitive:
``` r
library(tidyr)
example_df <- tibble(x = c(1, 1, 2),
                     y = c("a", "b", "a"),
                     z = c(100, 100, 100))
pivot_wider(example_df, names_from = y, values_from = z)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>       x     a     b
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1   100   100
#> 2     2   100    NA

pivot_wider(example_df, names_from = y, values_from = z, values_fill = list(z = 0))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>       x     a     b
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1   100   100
#> 2     2   100     0

pivot_wider(example_df, names_from = y, values_from = z, values_fill = 0)
#> Error in values_fill[[value]]: subscript out of bounds
```

<sup>Created on 2020-05-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

It seems to me that in this particular case, where `values_from` is length 1, it would be fine to accept an unnamed scalar to `values_fill`, making the function call a little less verbose without any real loss of expressiveness. 

The same error occurs when providing a named vector instead of a list when using multiple `vaules_from` arguments:
``` r
library(tidyr)
example_df <- tibble(x = c(1, 1, 2),
                     y = c("a", "b", "a"),
                     z = c(100, 100, 100),
                     a = c(200, 200, 200))

pivot_wider(example_df, names_from = y, values_from = c(z, a), values_fill = c(z = 0))
#> Error in values_fill[[value]]: subscript out of bounds
```

<sup>Created on 2020-05-17 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The documentation does specify that the argument to `values_fill` should be a named list, but I think it would be helpful to have the error message here say so explicitly as well.

title: Using unite(na.rm = TRUE) on all NA rows results in ""
description:
Using `tidyr::unite()` with `na.rm = TRUE` on entirely `NA` rows results in "" rather than `NA`, which seems more expected.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
packageVersion("tidyr")
#> [1] '1.0.2'
dat <- tribble(
  ~a, ~b, ~c,
  "a", "b", "c",
  NA, NA, NA,
  "a", NA, "c",
)

(dat <- unite(
  data = dat,
  col = abc,
  a, b, c,
  na.rm = TRUE
))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   abc    
#>   <chr>  
#> 1 "a_b_c"
#> 2 ""     
#> 3 "a_c"
```

The easiest solution is to use `dplyr::na_if()`, but this doesn't work if there are any date type columns. Then you need to use a scoped `dplyr::mutate()`, which is a hassle.

```r
na_if(dat, "")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   abc  
#>   <chr>
#> 1 a_b_c
#> 2 <NA> 
#> 3 a_c

dat %>% 
  mutate(d = Sys.Date()) %>% 
  na_if("")
#> Error in charToDate(x): character string is not in a standard unambiguous format
```

title: Regrettable error message
description:
This is what happens when `unnest_wider()` is going to produce a column name collision.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)

(df <- tibble(
  id = 1:2,
  stuff = list(
    list(id = "one", foo = "a"),
    list(id = "two", foo = "b")
  )
))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>      id stuff           
#>   <int> <list>          
#> 1     1 <named list [2]>
#> 2     2 <named list [2]>

df %>%
  unnest_wider(stuff)
#> Column name `id` must not be duplicated.
#> Use .name_repair to specify repair.
```

This error comes from tibble and refers to `.name_repair`. But tidyr uses `names_repair`. So doing what the error message says also fails.

``` r
df %>%
  unnest_wider(stuff, .name_repair = "unique")
#> Error in unnest_wider(., stuff, .name_repair = "unique"): unused argument (.name_repair = "unique")
```

This succeeds, which requires reading the docs for `unnest_wider()`.

``` r
df %>%
  unnest_wider(stuff, names_repair = "unique")
#> New names:
#> * id -> id...1
#> * id -> id...2
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   id...1 id...2 foo  
#>    <int> <chr>  <chr>
#> 1      1 one    a    
#> 2      2 two    b
```

title: document difference between unnest_longer and unchop ?
description:
The conceptual difference between them is not obvious to me and they don't refer to each other in their help pages, which I feel would be helpful.

> unchop() makes df longer by expanding list-columns so that each element of the list-column gets its own row in the output.

> unnest_longer() preserves the columns, but changes the rows, Or if you unnest_longer() a list of data frame, the number of columns must be preserved so it creates a packed column.

Contrasting examples would help too, as of now all examples of `unnest_longer()` can be done with `unchop()`, except for 1, and the latter contradicts the principle above as it adds a column.

My own fuzzy understanding is that I will have generally more flexibility with `unnest_longer()` thanks to the additional arguments, as long as my column elements are of the same type, if they're not, or if I want to strongly enforce that I won't create columns, or if I want to remove rows containing a zero length element in a given column, I should use `unchop()`.

**unnest_longer() example 1**

``` r
library(tidyr)
df <- tibble(
  character = c("Toothless", "Dory"),
  metadata = list(
    list(
      species = "dragon",
      color = "black",
      films = c(
        "How to Train Your Dragon",
        "How to Train Your Dragon 2",
        "How to Train Your Dragon: The Hidden World"
      )
    ),
    list(
      species = "clownfish",
      color = "blue",
      films = c("Finding Nemo", "Finding Dory")
    )
  )
)

identical(
  df %>%
  unnest_wider(metadata) %>%
  unnest_longer(films),
  df %>%
  unnest_wider(metadata) %>%
  unchop(films))
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


**unnest_longer() example 2**

``` r
library(tidyr)
df <- tibble(
  x = 1:3,
  y = list(NULL, 1:3, 4:5)
)
identical(
  df %>% unnest_longer(y),
  df %>% unchop(y,keep_empty = T))
#> [1] TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


**unnest_longer() example 3**

In this one `unnest_longer()` and  `unchop()` work differently, but `unnest_longer()` creates a new column, which goes against the bit quoted above  : 

``` r
library(tidyr)
df <- tibble(
  x = 1:2,
  y = list(c(a = 1, b = 2), c(a = 10, b = 11, c = 12))
)
df %>% unnest_longer(y)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>       x     y y_id 
#>   <int> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1     1     1 a    
#> 2     1     2 b    
#> 3     2    10 a    
#> 4     2    11 b    
#> 5     2    12 c
df %>% unchop(y)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <int> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     1     2
#> 3     2    10
#> 4     2    11
#> 5     2    12
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

**`unchop()` examples**

Examples 1 and 3 of `unchop()` are also equivalent or similar using `unnest_longer()`, 2nd example shows however that `unchop()` is tolerant to having different data types in a list column while `unnest_longer()` is not but it's not very clear why, and the error message is not very helpful (and I think there's a few words missing in the comment :) ) : 

``` r
library(tidyr)
# Incompatible types -------------------------------------------------
# If the list-col contains types that can not be natively              <<<-------- unfinished sentence
df <- tibble(x = 1:2, y = list("1", 1:3))
try(df %>% unchop(y))
#> Error : No common type for `..1$y` <character> and `..2$y` <integer>.
try(df %>% unnest_longer(y))
#> Error : No common type for `..1$y$y` <character> and `..2$y$y` <integer>.
df %>% unchop(y, ptype = tibble(y = integer()))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>       x     y
#>   <int> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     2     1
#> 3     2     2
#> 4     2     3
df %>% unnest_longer(y, ptype = tibble(y = integer()))
#> Error: No common type for `..1$y$y` <character> and `..2$y$y` <integer>.

```

title: `separate_rows()` error with dev vctrs, dev tidyr, cran dplyr
description:
Dev vctrs now implements `vctrs:::vec_restore.grouped_df()` which calls `grouped_df()`. In CRAN dplyr, this function validates if any grouping vars are lists, and errors if so.

A tidyr test tries to do this, which errors on dev vctrs + cran dplyr for me.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

df <- tibble(x = 1, y = "a:b") %>% group_by(x, y)
out <- df %>% separate_rows(y)
#> Error: Column `y` can't be used as a grouping variable because it's a list
```

`separate_rows()` uses `stringi::stri_split_regex()` on the grouping variable, which returns a list. It then runs through `unchop()` which eventually calls `vec_slice()` on this grouped-df that has a grouping variable that is a list. The restore method is called in `vec_slice()` and we get an error

Maybe `separate_rows()` should ungroup its input?

title: automatically name unnamed pluckers in hoist

Often one wants to name the columns produced by `hoist()` the same as the element in the list. So to make `hoist()` less verbose and more comfortable for interactive use I propose automatically naming the column as follows for unnamed arguments:

* if the last part of the pluck specification is a number paste the number to the last character part of the spec, e.g. `list("film", 1)` would produce the column name `film_1`.

title: Proposal to change arguments order of pivot_wider()
description:
I imagine the (great!) new functions `pivot_wider()` and `pivot_longer()` have had a lot of thought, which is awesome. However, for the arguments order of `pivot_wider()`, I think some extra user-friendliness would improve convenience a lot.

For `pivot_wider()`, I would suggest to move the argument `id_cols` to a 5th place, after `data`, `names_from`, `values_from` and `values_fill`:
```r
# current
pivot_wider(data, id_cols = NULL, names_from = name,
  names_prefix = "", names_sep = "_", names_repair = "check_unique",
  values_from = value, values_fill = NULL, values_fn = NULL)

# suggested
pivot_wider(data, names_from = name, values_from = value, 
  values_fill = NULL, id_cols = NULL, names_prefix = "",
  names_sep = "_", names_repair = "check_unique", values_fn = NULL)
```

I have two arguments for this:

1. Since you softly force users to migrate from `spread()` as this function [is now retired](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/spread.html) which [will lead to future removal](https://www.tidyverse.org/lifecycle/), I guess most users expect the use of `pivot_wider()` to be somewhat as fast and easy as `spread()`. But `pivot_wider()` often requires manual and cumbersome definition of arguments, which in my experience is needed in almost all use cases. This means it is quite far from a drop-in replacement of `spread()`. With the suggested order, this would be solved immediately:
    ```r
    # old
    storms %>%
      count(year, status) %>%
      spread(status, n, 0)

    # current
    storms %>%
      count(year, status) %>%
      pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = n, values_fill = list(n = 0))

    # suggested
    storms %>%
      count(year, status) %>%
      pivot_wider(status, n, list(n = 0))
    ```

    For `values_fill`, I would additionally suggest to make it work more intelligently by picking `values_from` as a new list name at default so e.g. `pivot_wider(status, n, 0)` works, but that's another discussion.

2. You [added 4 use cases](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/pivot_wider.html#examples) to the documentation, that (as users can reasonably expect) shows best practises. Not a single one of them works with `id_cols`, which is now the second argument. Instead, all examples at least contain the manually set (and consequently typed!) `names_from` and `values_from`:
    ```r
    # (pasted from: https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/pivot_wider.html#examples)

    fish_encounters %>%
      pivot_wider(names_from = station, values_from = seen)
    # Fill in missing values
    fish_encounters %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from = station,
        values_from = seen,
        values_fill = list(seen = 0)
      )

    # Generate column names from multiple variables
    us_rent_income %>%
      pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe))

    # Can perform aggregation with values_fn
    warpbreaks <- as_tibble(warpbreaks[c("wool", "tension", "breaks")])
    warpbreaks
    warpbreaks %>%
      pivot_wider(
        names_from = wool,
        values_from = breaks,
        values_fn = list(breaks = mean)
      )
    ```

    At best, this makes users even wonder how `id_cols` works. But in my honest opinion, it strongly suggests that a reordering of arguments would improve convenience, decrease typing, fasten analysis and, most importantly, help users adapt to `pivot_wider()` in a most user-friendly way.

title: FR: list of dataframe columns in hoist
description:
List of dataframe columns are sometimes basically required, e.g. in the `discog` data of the `repurrrsive` package one might be interested in the labels and artists but unnesting doesn't really make sense as they are unrelated and have unequal length. Using `tidyr` my approach would currently be the following:

``` r

title: FR: Implement names_glue on pivot_wider
description:
Currently, names produced by `pivot_wider` can partly be controlled via `names_sep`.
Further controls require additional renaming by `dplyr::rename`.
I suggest to add `names_glue` option which glues names in the manner of glue package.
In the example below, `.value` is a special key word like that of `names_pattern` of `pivot_longer`

``` r
data.frame(
  x = c('a' , 'b'),
  y = 1:2,
  foo = 1:2,
  bar = 1:2
) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = c(x, y),
    values_from = c(foo, bar),
    names_glue = '{x}{y}_{.value}'
  )
```

| a1_foo| a1_bar| b1_foo| b2_bar|
|------:|------:|------:|------:|
|      1|      2|      1|      2|

title: Dataset patching tools
description:
Formerly filed in dpylr repo.

I'm doing an analysis that requires a lot of manual corrections to the original dataset. I keep tables of changes that mirror the original (see example in code) and then I use the code below to impute the original values. Probably niche, but who am I to decide. Here's my code:

``` R
library(dplyr)
library(lazyeval)

update_with = function(data, update, by) {

  # columns to be updated
  # (data intersect cols) -- by

  orig_order = colnames(data)
  update_cols =
    setdiff(intersect(colnames(data), colnames(update)), by)

  # left join update
  data = data %>% left_join(update, by=by)

  # transmutate one by one
  for(col in update_cols) {
    col.x = paste(col, "x", sep=".")
    col.y = paste(col, "y", sep=".")

    myifelse = function(x, y) {
      x[!is.na(y)] <- y[!is.na(y)]
      x
    }
    update = interp( ~myifelse(x, y)
                   , x=as.name(col.x)
                   , y=as.name(col.y)
                   )

    data = data %>%
      mutate_( .dots = setNames(list(update), col) ) %>%
      select( -one_of(c(col.x,col.y)) )
  }

  # deletes extra columns too
  data[,orig_order]
}



a = data.frame(x = 1:100,y = 5, z = 1:50)
b = data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 0)

# sets y to 0 when x  is in range 1:10, otherwise a remains the same 
a %>% update_with(b, by="x")
```

After using this method for awhile I keep my patches in this format, which assigns `value` to the cell described by `Row` and `Column`.

| Row | Column | Value | Data to help fill in value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | x | 123 | hint: it's as easy as... |
| 2 | y | xyz | link to pathology report |

and I remove the rightmost column use `spread` on the column `Column` and feed the subsequent dataframe into `update_with`. This probably has some unintended side effects when mixing integers and factors together in the `value` column. This has been surprisingly robust and I've been able to keep a single patch file for each table. 

thanks,
Marcus

title: pivot_longer() takes longer... and too much memory than gather()
description:
Possibly related to #897

The following command takes all the memory and stops with the error "cannot allocate vector of size X":

```r
test <- data.frame(s = rep(1:32, 3587928),
                   var1 = rep(c(NA, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), 28703424),
                   var2 = rep(c(NA, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), 28703424),
                   var3 = rep(c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L), 28703424),
                   var4 = rep(c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L), 28703424), 
                   var5 = rep(c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L), 28703424),
                   var6 = rep(c(NA, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), 28703424))
test <- test %>% pivot_longer(-s, names_to = "period_type", values_to = "duration")
```

Gather do this fast and no memory  issues:

```r
test <- data.frame(s = rep(1:32, 3587928),
                   var1 = rep(c(NA, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), 28703424),
                   var2 = rep(c(NA, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), 28703424),
                   var3 = rep(c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L), 28703424),
                   var4 = rep(c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L), 28703424), 
                   var5 = rep(c(NA, 1L, 2L, 3L), 28703424),
                   var6 = rep(c(NA, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0), 28703424))
test  <- test  %>% gather(period_type, duration, -s)
```

PS: I have 32GB memory on my computer.

title: pivot_longer throws error with haven_labelled columns
description:
---

In a similar instance as below but for a bigger dataset imported with `haven`, `haven_labelled` variables do not seem to work quite right with `pivot_longer` . But `pivot_longer` does work if  `haven` attributes are removed prior to using `pivot_longer`.  The below reprex is from the `pivot_longer` vignette but I added some haven labels. 
Thank you for the great package!!! 
```r
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)

family <- tribble(
  ~family,  ~dob_child1,  ~dob_child2, ~gender_child1, ~gender_child2,
  1L, "1998-11-26", "2000-01-29",             1L,             2L,
  2L, "1996-06-22",           NA,             2L,             NA,
  3L, "2002-07-11", "2004-04-05",             2L,             2L,
  4L, "2004-10-10", "2009-08-27",             1L,             1L,
  5L, "2000-12-05", "2005-02-28",             2L,             1L,
  )


family$dob_child1<-labelled(family$dob_child1,NULL, label = "test_label") 
family$dob_child2<-labelled(family$dob_child2,NULL, label = "test_label2") 


family %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    -family, 
    names_to = c(".value", "child"),

title: NA handling in unite

title: unnest 1.0.2 fails if dataframe doesn't contain list-cols
description:
In tidyr versions < 1.0, issuing MYDATA %>% unnest() would simply return MYDATA if there were no list-cols present.  This made constructing generic functions very easy and transparent because one may not know whether the input function is nested or not.  For example, the data frame may have been unnested in a previous analysis step.

Now, if we use a simple unnest() on a previously unnested dataframe we get the warning to use "cols = c(data)" since cols is now required.  However it still returns the original input dataframe that will permit a workflow to continue.

If we heed the warning and try using unnest(cols = c(data)) we are instead presented with a fatal error that halts the workflow.


```r
library(tidyverse)
nestcars <- mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% nest()
nestcars

nestcars %>% unnest(cols = c(data)) # works fine

mtcars %>% unnest() # sends warning, but still works
mtcars %>% unnest(cols = c(data)) # fails with error
```

title: Comparison of `unnest` behaviour for nested tibbles and named lists
description:
# Motivation and Discussion

This issue is not reporting a bug, but rather a discussion on the interface of the new `pivot_` functions. Given, that `tibble` and `data.frame` are built on top of lists, I initially expected the `pivot` functions to work the same, regardless of whether they where dealing with a list of tibbles or a list of lists. There is a point to be made, that people tend to think of `tibbles` as being horizontal (the header row of a spreadsheet) and of lists as being vertical (like a ToDo list), so the behavior in the code examples below could be justified. However, this makes it non-trivial to actually reach the 
tidy end result of `unnest(nestedTibble, data)` when starting from `nestedNamedList`.

---

# Code Examples

```r
library(tidyverse)

nestedNamedList <- tibble(
  category = c("A", "B"),
  data = list(
    list(x = rnorm(5),
         y = rnorm(5))
  )
)

nestedTibble <- tibble(
  category = c("A", "B"),
  data = list(
    tibble(x = rnorm(5),
         y = rnorm(5))
  )
)

unnest_wider(nestedTibble, data)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   category x         y        
#>   <chr>    <list>    <list>   
#> 1 A        <dbl [5]> <dbl [5]>
#> 2 B        <dbl [5]> <dbl [5]>
unnest_wider(nestedNamedList, data)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   category x         y        
#>   <chr>    <list>    <list>   
#> 1 A        <dbl [5]> <dbl [5]>
#> 2 B        <dbl [5]> <dbl [5]>

unnest(nestedTibble, data)
#> # A tibble: 10 x 3
#>    category       x      y
#>    <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 A         0.0107  3.07 
#>  2 A        -1.96   -0.434
#>  3 A         0.906   0.825
#>  4 A        -0.883   0.188
#>  5 A        -0.103   0.310
#>  6 B         0.0107  3.07 
#>  7 B        -1.96   -0.434
#>  8 B         0.906   0.825
#>  9 B        -0.883   0.188
#> 10 B        -0.103   0.310
unnest(nestedNamedList, data)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   category data     
#>   <chr>    <list>   
#> 1 A        <dbl [5]>
#> 2 A        <dbl [5]>
#> 3 B        <dbl [5]>
#> 4 B        <dbl [5]>

unnest_longer(nestedTibble, data)
#> # A tibble: 10 x 2
#>    category  data$x     $y
#>    <chr>      <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 A         0.0107  3.07 
#>  2 A        -1.96   -0.434
#>  3 A         0.906   0.825
#>  4 A        -0.883   0.188
#>  5 A        -0.103   0.310
#>  6 B         0.0107  3.07 
#>  7 B        -1.96   -0.434
#>  8 B         0.906   0.825
#>  9 B        -0.883   0.188
#> 10 B        -0.103   0.310
unnest_longer(nestedNamedList, data)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   category data      data_id
#>   <chr>    <list>    <chr>  
#> 1 A        <dbl [5]> x      
#> 2 A        <dbl [5]> y      
#> 3 B        <dbl [5]> x      
#> 4 B        <dbl [5]> y
```

title: Document c(col1, col2) tidyselect specification for pivot_longer()
description:
I couldn't find out from any documentation how to name multiple columns in the `cols` argument of `pivot_longer()`.  This would be equivalent to the `...` argument of `gather()`.

Eventually I guessed that `c(col_name_1, col_name_2)` works.

The four statements below all do the same thing, and could be given in the documentation for `pivot_longer()` and `vignette("pivot")`.

```r
# Including more than one column in `cols` by name
smiths %>%
  gather("key", "value", age, weight, height)

smiths %>%
  pivot_longer(c(age, weight, height), names_to = "metric")

# Excluding more than one column in `cols` by name
smiths %>%
  gather("key", "value", -subject, -time)

smiths %>%
  pivot_longer(c(-subject, -time), names_to = "metric")
```

title: Why is the replace argument of replace_na() so strict?
description:
`replace`	    If `data` is a data frame, a named list giving the value to replace NA with for each column. If data is a vector, a single value used for replacement.

I believe that if the users puts a single value to replace NAs and inputs a data frame, the same replacement value should be applied across all columns. If however the user wants a more elaborate replacement pattern, a named list can be provided. I think the case where you replace NAs across the board is quite common.

title: `pivot_wider` not working with class <Period>
description:
*Brief description of the problem:*
`pivot_wider` throws a strange error when used with a value_from column of type `<Period>` (as output from lubridate).
I am using R-3.6.3, lubridate_1.7.4, dbplyr_1.4.2.

*Reprex:*
```r
df_0 <- tibble(period_name   = c("a", "b", "c"), 
               period_value  = c("1:1:1", 
                                 "2:2:2", 
                                 "4:4:4")) %>% 
         mutate(period_value = lubridate::hms(period_value))

df_0
## A tibble: 3 x 2
#  period_name period_value
#  <chr>       <Period>
#1 a           1H 1M 1S
#2 b           2H 2M 2S
#3 c           4H 4M 4S
```
Now, let's try widening the data frame
```r
df_0 %>% pivot_wider(names_from = period_name, values_from = period_value)
#Error: No common type for `value` <Period> and `x` <Period>.
```
This error does not make sense to me.
BTW, at least it throws an error, whereas `spread` silently messed it up (see [Stackoverflow question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/60751518/lubridate-periods-get-messed-up-after-using-dplyr-spread)).

It works fine, though, with date_time type:
```r
df_1 <- tibble(dttm_name   = c("a", "b", "c"), 
               dttm_value  = c("2020-01-01 1:1:1", 
                               "2020-02-03 2:2:2", 
                               "2020-05-10 4:4:4")) %>% 
         mutate(dttm_value = lubridate::as_datetime(dttm_value))

df_1
## A tibble: 3 x 2
#  dttm_name dttm_value
#  <chr>     <dttm>
#1 a         2020-01-01 01:01:01
#2 b         2020-02-03 02:02:02
#3 c         2020-05-10 04:04:04

df_1 %>% pivot_wider(names_from = dttm_name, values_from = dttm_value)
## A tibble: 1 x 3
#  a                   b                   c
#  <dttm>              <dttm>              <dttm>
#1 2020-01-01 01:01:01 2020-02-03 02:02:02 2020-05-10 04:04:04
```
Is that something wrong with `pivot_wider` (and `spread`) or with lubridate's `Period` class?

title: Provide rbind solution that can add list element names as a variable in the output
description:
Problem: you have a list of data.frames and the element names convey information. You want to row bind them together and, in the new data.frame, you want a variable for the list element each observation originated in.

![2014-08-22_rbind-and-store-as var](https://cloud.githubusercontent.com/assets/599454/4014866/0ed7df14-2a25-11e4-9a31-b086f3cc37b9.png)

Demo: fragment subset of iris into separate data.frames, stored as list.
Note: Species info carried _only_ via list names

``` r
my_list <- lapply(split(subset(iris, select = -Species),
                        iris$Species), "[", 1:2, )
```

Simple rbind-y calls cannot recover Species:

``` r
do.call("rbind", my_list) # rownames have never looked so good ...
```

```
##               Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
## setosa.1               5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2
## setosa.2               4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2
## versicolor.51          7.0         3.2          4.7         1.4
## versicolor.52          6.4         3.2          4.5         1.5
## virginica.101          6.3         3.3          6.0         2.5
## virginica.102          5.8         2.7          5.1         1.9
```

``` r
dplyr::rbind_all(my_list)
```

```
##   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width
## 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2
## 2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2
## 3          7.0         3.2          4.7         1.4
## 4          6.4         3.2          4.5         1.5
## 5          6.3         3.3          6.0         2.5
## 6          5.8         2.7          5.1         1.9
```

Current workaround: prep with mapply() to restore Species, then rbind (thanks @kara_woo for this snippet)

``` r
my_list2 <-
  mapply(`[<-`, my_list, 'Species', value = names(my_list), SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
dplyr::rbind_all(my_list2)
```

```
##   Sepal.Length Sepal.Width Petal.Length Petal.Width    Species
## 1          5.1         3.5          1.4         0.2     setosa
## 2          4.9         3.0          1.4         0.2     setosa
## 3          7.0         3.2          4.7         1.4 versicolor
## 4          6.4         3.2          4.5         1.5 versicolor
## 5          6.3         3.3          6.0         2.5  virginica
## 6          5.8         2.7          5.1         1.9  virginica
```

title: Enhance pivot_longer/wider with names_mutate
description:
I have a dataset that has character dates as some (but not all) of the column names. I can use pivot_longer to pivot to the shape I want, but this leaves the dates as characters. This is ok, but inhibits some kinds of analysis. To remedy this, I can then mutate those values in a post-processing step to get them as real dates. However, I presume this requires looping through the entire dataset. So if there are T of these columns, and N rows, then it requires NT mutations, rather than just T conversions normally. Ideally, there could be an option to pivot_longer/wider that would allow one to mutate/format the names before the final output.



``` r
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

temp <- tibble(id = 1:5, 
               "12/31/2019" = runif(5), 
               "01/31/2020" = runif(5))

temp2 <- temp %>% 
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -id,
        names_to = "strdate",
        names_pattern = "(.*)",
        values_to = "value",
    ) %>% 
    mutate(Date = as.Date(strdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

temp2

title: pivot_wider and pivot_longer need to document "tidyselect specification"
description:
The help files for `pivot_longer()` and `pivot_wider()`, which replace tidyr's core functions `gather()` and `spread()`, state that the main argument, `cols`, "takes a tidyselect specification." Nowhere is this "tidyselect specification" defined within the help files for these functions, no links are provided to such documentation, and no examples are offered.

The functions are unusable without a full understanding of the "tidyselect specification." This is a serious oversight in the current tidyr package.

title: `separate_rows()` fails if list columns are of unequal length.
description:
---

The separate_rows function behaves oddly when collapsed columns are of unequal length.

In some instances, the function throws an error, such as:
```
Error: No common size for `colX`, size 4, and `colY`, size 5.
```
and in other instances, it return just the first and last element as shown here:
```r
df <- tibble(id = c("a", "b", "c"), col1 = list(1:2, 1:5, NA), col2 = list(1:4, 1:2, 1))
separate_rows(df, -id)
``` 

It might just be my opinion, but the `separate_rows` function should have a `fill` argument, which I see was also mentioned in #413 , thereby always returning a tibble of the expected size, while allowing the user to define what should happen when columns are of unequal length. 

Maybe I just misunderstood the usecase of the `separate_rows` function. Please let me know, if that is the case.

title: `unchop()` and `NULL` elements
description:
`unchop()` currently handles `NULL` elements unconsistently depending on whether one column or multiple columns are unchopped:

```r
df <- tibble(x = 1:4, y = list(NULL, 1:2, 4, NULL), z = list(NULL, 1:2, NULL, 5))
df
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>       x y         z
#>   <int> <list>    <list>
#> 1     1 <NULL>    <NULL>
#> 2     2 <int [2]> <int [2]>
#> 3     3 <dbl [1]> <NULL>
#> 4     4 <NULL>    <dbl [1]>

df %>% unchop(y)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>       x     y z
#>   <int> <dbl> <list>
#> 1     2     1 <int [2]>
#> 2     2     2 <int [2]>
#> 3     3     4 <NULL>

df %>% unchop(c(y, z))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>       x     y     z
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     2     1     1
#> 2     2     2     2
#> 3     3     4    NA
#> 4     4    NA     5
```

It also seems that the promotion of `NULL` to `NA` in the second case is not consistent, when a row has all `NULL` they are ignored.

Proposed behaviour is to coerce `NULL` to `NA` in all cases:

```r
df %>% unchop(y)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>       x     y z
#>   <int> <dbl> <list>
#> 1     1    NA <NULL>
#> 2     2     1 <int [2]>
#> 3     2     2 <int [2]>
#> 4     3     4 <NULL>
#> 5     4    NA <dbl [1]>

df %>% unchop(c(y, z))
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>       x     y     z
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1    NA    NA
#> 2     2     1     1
#> 3     2     2     2
#> 4     3     4    NA
#> 5     4    NA     5
```

title: pivot_wider generates incorrect values when values_from is a integer64 column
description:
The DBI interface generates data frames that have integer64 columns, for example when counting the number of records.

pivot_wider generates incorrect & repeated output when the values_from is a integer64 column. The resulting data frame has the following value repeated many times:  `9218868437227407266`.

A less than satisfying fix is:

  `mutate(n = as.numeric(n))`

or 

  `bigint = "integer"` in 

```
con <- dbConnect(
  # prefer `connection_open` when running interactively...
  RPostgres::Postgres(),
  # without the following (and preceding) lines, 
  # bigint become int64 which is a problem for ggplot
  bigint = "integer",  
  host = "localhost",
  port = 5432 ...
```

title: names_repair in pivot_[wider|longer] does not accept function
description:
The `names_repair` argument in `pivot_wider()`/`pivot_longer()` does not accept a function. This is contrary to the documentation, which points to `vctrs::vec_as_names()` for more options. It says there a function can be provided, which will receive a vector of minimal names and output the minimal names transformed. To be clear, I think this is a tidyr documentation issue, and not a vctrs issue. Looking at many vctrs functions, they explicitly only support the character argument options for  name repair.

It seems like the correct course of action is to document the remaining character argument to names_repair in `pivot_wider()`/`pivot_longer()`, since 3 of the 4 are documented there. Additionally, add a helpful error message when a function is provided.  If you agree, let me know and I would be happy to provide a PR. 
```
library(tidyr)
#> Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 3.6.2
packageVersion("tidyr")
#> [1] '1.0.2'
packageVersion("vctrs")
#> [1] '0.2.2'
df <- tibble::tibble(name = c("first", "second"), a = c("hello", "hello"), b = c("there", "you"))
pivot_wider(df, names_from = name, values_from = c(a, b), names_repair = toupper)
#> Error in vec_cbind(rows, !!!value_out, .name_repair = names_repair): STRING_ELT() can only be applied to a 'character vector', not a 'closure'
pivot_longer(df, cols = c(a, b), names_repair = toupper)
#> Error in vec_cbind(vec_slice(df_out, rows$df_id), vec_slice(keys, rows$key_id), : STRING_ELT() can only be applied to a 'character vector', not a 'closure'

# But vec_as_names works
vctrs::vec_as_names(c(df$a, df$b), repair = toupper)
#> New names:
#> * hello -> HELLO
#> * hello -> HELLO
#> * there -> THERE
#> * you -> YOU
#> [1] "HELLO" "HELLO" "THERE" "YOU"
```

f <- function(df, groupname, nbtch = 3000){

title: Allow pivot_longer() names_to to be list
description:
In `pivot_longer` there are only indirect ways of specifying the columns in wide form
that correspond to each column in long form.  Often one has to change the column names of the wide form input as an extra step since such specification is done indirectly via names.  It would be convenient if this could optionally be provided explicitly by allowing `names_to` to be a list whose names are the column names in long form output and whose components are vectors of corresponding column names or numbers in the wide form input.

For example, due to the naming of the columns we can create x and y columns in the long form output in the following example.
```
anscombe %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c(".value", "set"), names_pattern = "(.)(.)")
```
However, if the names were V1, V2, etc. then one would have the extra step of changing the names even though we know that the first 4 and last 4 columns of `anscombe` are known to be the two groups of input columns that are to correspond to `x` and `y` output columns.

Using this proposal we could write it like this without changing the names on the input:

```
anscombe %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = list(x = 1:4, y = 5:8))
```

This is the same as the `varying` argument in base `reshape` except that `varying` ignores the list names.

```
reshape(anscombe, dir = "long", varying = list(1:4, 5:8), v.names = c("x", "y"))
```

title: crossing and nesting no longer supports lazy evaluation
description:
On tidyr 0.8.3, `tidyr::crossing` and `tidyr::nesting` used `tibble::lst` to capture dots, and supported lazy evaluation of arguments.
On tidyr 1.0.0, they use `tidyr:::dots_cols`, and no more support lazy evaluation.
Is this intended or unexpected?

# tidyr 1.0.0

title: `unnest()` fails to unnest empty list, `unnest_wider()` works
description:
## Summary
I can reproduce here that #650 still persists with `tidyr_1.0.0.9000`.

On a side note, `tidyr_1.0.0.9000` fixes the behaviour of `unnest_wider()`:
When unnesting a list, `unnest_wider()` in versions before 1.0.0.9000 seems to have trouble if a nested list in the first record is empty, but subsequent records have data in those nested list elements. I'm struggling a bit with a reproducible example here but have provided what I can below.

## `tidyr` version 1.0.0.9000 (current master) 
The example from https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/650#issuecomment-514683131 doesn't work as expected:
``` r
library(magrittr)
library(tidyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'tidyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:magrittr':
#> 
#>     extract
df <- tibble(x = list(), y = integer())
df %>% unnest(y)
#> Error: Input must be list of vectors
df %>% unnest(y) %>% names()
#> Error: Input must be list of vectors
df %>% unnest_wider(y)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 1
#> # … with 1 variable: x <list>
df %>% unnest_wider(y) %>% names()
#> [1] "x"
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-04 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

However, `tidyr_1.0.0.9000` **fixes** my issue https://github.com/dbca-wa/ruODK/issues/46.
* List of lists, parsed from OData/XML, then using `tidyr::unnest_wider()` to rectangle list of lists.
* First record has empty nested list, subsequent records have data in that list element.

## `tidyr` version 1.0.0 (current CRAN)

title: nest strips off the class to `data.frame` if input is not a tibble
description:
For example with a *data.table* : 

``` r
library(tidyverse, warn.conflicts = F)
library(data.table, warn.conflicts = F)
df  <- tibble(x = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3), y = 1:6, z = 6:1)
dt <- as.data.table(df)
df %>% nest(data = c(y, z)) %>% class()
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
dt %>% nest(data = c(y, z)) %>% class()
#> [1] "data.frame"
```

<sup>Created on 2019-12-01 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Some *tidyverse* functions don't modify the input's class and some coerce to `tbl_df`, I think it would be more intuitive to pick one of those 2 behaviors for `nest`.

  exdata$data,

description:

Hello,

I have identified a possible bug in using the `unnest` function after `mutate`.
I thought it would be the bug reported in #483  , but then I realized that they are different. The bug only appears when I run the mutate function before unnest.

With bug: `mutate` function before` unnest`:

library(magrittr)

df_a <- tibble::tribble(~x, ~z,
                            "a", 10,

df_b <- df_a %>% 
        dplyr::filter(!z %in% c(10, 20)) %>%

title: Allow unpack() to work with vctrs_rcrd
description:
Original/motivating issue: https://github.com/tidyverts/fabletools/issues/122

The current application of `separate()` and `extract()` is limited to character columns, however there are other vector classes that you may want to `separate()` or `extract()` information from.

For my particular use-case this is the `fabletools` `hilo` class. As a vector (specifically a *record*), it stores a confidence interval for some prediction, consisting of the lower and upper bounds with their confidence level. Stylistically, `[lower, upper]level` e.g. `[-3, 3]95`. Some other examples of composite objects can be dreamt up, such as the `latlon` example class in [*Extending tibble*](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/dev/articles/extending.html).

Gaining access to the underlying elements of these classes within a data context is difficult, and I think the `separate()` and `extract()` verbs could be the appropriate interface for simplifying this.

To achieve this, `separate()` and `extract()` would now call some generic to separate or extract things from a vector (say `separate_col()` and `extract_col()`). Existing functionality would be preserved via `separate_col.character(x, into, sep = "[^[:alnum:]]+", remove = TRUE, convert = FALSE, extra = "warn", fill = "warn", ...)` and new functionality could be added with `separate_col.class(x, ...)`.

For the hilo class, this would look like `separate_col.hilo(x, into = c("lower", "upper", "level"), ...)` allowing this workflow:

``` r
library(fabletools)
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(hilo = new_hilo(rnorm(5), rnorm(5, 3), 95))
df
#> # A tibble: 5 x 1
#>                       hilo
#>                     <hilo>
#> 1 [ 0.7348065, 3.369723]95
#> 2 [-0.9783929, 2.784432]95
#> 3 [-0.7608599, 4.152290]95
#> 4 [ 0.4115154, 2.760376]95
#> 5 [-1.4132969, 2.969952]95
df %>% separate(hilo)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>    lower upper level
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  0.735  3.37    95
#> 2 -0.978  2.78    95
#> 3 -0.761  4.15    95
#> 4  0.412  2.76    95
#> 5 -1.41   2.97    95
```

Similarly `extract_col.hilo(x, into, what = into, ...)` could be used to pull out elements of interest from the `hilo`.

``` r
df %>% extract(hilo, c("lower", "upper"))
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>    lower upper
#>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  0.735  3.37
#> 2 -0.978  2.78
#> 3 -0.761  4.15
#> 4  0.412  2.76
#> 5 -1.41   2.97
```

---

I don't think this would introduce breaking changes, although to do so the `separate_col.default()` must coerce to character instead of erroring (perhaps a warning/message would be useful here?).

Adding this support may make it harder for users to find the right place for documentation of each separation/extraction methods. Using `generics` style method linking and plenty examples in the docs would be helpful for this.

The alternative (if `separate()` and `extract()` shouldn't be generalised) would be to create `separate_hilo(data, col, ...)` and `extract_hilo(data, col, ...)`. Keeping the status quo would naturally also have some advantages (such as familiarity and not requiring as much knowledge of dispatch methods).

Which approach is preferable? Would generalising `separate()` and `extract()` to dispatch on the column type be a useful contribution to `tidyr`?

title: Better naming options for pack()
description:
I like the idea of pack and unpack, especially as they sometimes come quite natural when working with JSON data from APIs. In such a case I might want to unpack a tibble column, manipulate it and pack it afterwards again. E.g.

``` r
library(tidyr)
api_data <- tibble(
  Sepal = tibble(
    Length = c(5.1, 4.7),
    Width = c(3.5, 3.2)
  ),
  Petal = tibble(
    Length = c(1.4, 1.3),
    Width = c(0.2, 0.2)
  )
)

data_to_work_with <- api_data %>% 
  unpack(c(Sepal, Petal), names_sep = ".")

# some data manipulation

data_to_work_with %>% 
  pack(Sepal = starts_with("Sepal"))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   Petal.Length Petal.Width Sepal$Sepal.Length $Sepal.Width
#>          <dbl>       <dbl>              <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1          1.4         0.2                5.1          3.5
#> 2          1.3         0.2                4.7          3.2
```

<sup>Created on 2019-10-30 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Unfortunately, this repacking step isn't supported very nicely as I cannot change the names in the step of packing. I would imagine something along the following lines to be possible:

```r
data_to_work_with %>% 
  pack(Sepal = c(Length = Sepal.Length, Width = Sepal.Width))

data_to_work_with %>% 
  pack(Sepal = c(Sepal.Length, Width = Width), .prefix = "Sepal.")
```

The first case is especially confusing as the names are simply ignored without a warning.

title: unnest errors when df contains a column with subclass or custom class
description:
When a dataframe contains a list-column with a subclass, `unnest()` throws an error, when trying to unnest a regular list of dataframes column.

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

df <-
  tibble(
    x = 1:2,
    y = list(
      tibble(a = 1, b = 2),
      tibble(a = 1:3, b = 3:1)
    ),
    z = list(
      c(2, 5),
      c(3, 6)
    )
  )

class(df$z) <- c("custom_subclass", "list")

unnest(df, y)
#> Error: Can't slice a scalar
```

This used to work with tidyr \< v1.0 (and still does with `unnest_legacy()`) and I don't understand why it shouldn't anymore:

``` r
unnest_legacy(df, y, .drop = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>       x z             a     b
#>   <int> <list>    <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1 <dbl [2]>     1     2
#> 2     2 <dbl [2]>     1     3
#> 3     2 <dbl [2]>     2     2
#> 4     2 <dbl [2]>     3     1
```

Is this intentional (and if it is, what am I missing?) or is it a bug?

As far as I can tell this is due to `vctrs::vec_slice()` refusing to slice a dataframe with said custom subclass list column.

``` r
vctrs::vec_slice(df, 1)
#> Error: Can't slice a scalar
```

FWIW, the same problem occurs when z has a custom class (which is still of type list)

``` r
class(df$z) <- c("custom_class")

typeof(df$z)
#> [1] "list"

unnest(df, y)
#> Error: Can't slice a scalar
```

title: Unexpected Column production via hoist() and unnest_wider() on tibble()
description:
An empty `tibble()` behaves unexpectedly when subject to `under_wider()`. Specifically a new `..1` column is produced:

``` r
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tidyr)
```

This makes sense:

``` r
tibble(
    x = c("ok", "empty"), 
    y = list(
        tibble(ix = 1, iy = 2), 
        tibble()
    )
) %>%

title: Building new column names in pivot_wider()
description:
#586 introduced multiple `values_from` columns in `pivot_wide()` by appending the value column names to the new column names in the output.

It would be nice to have a more general interface to control how the new column names are built: there are many examples of cases where the value names are prepended rather than appended to the column names (e.g. all [examples in the vignette](https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/3268807babf9a545cad1560003cab0160d939004/vignettes/pivot.Rmd#L144-L200)), but both methods can be useful.

One possible solution could be to mirror the use of a `.value` sentinel introduced to `pivot_longer()`'s `names_to` in `names_from` for a neat additional symmetry between the pivoting functions:

```r
# for names like: income_estimate, income_moe, ...
us_rent_income %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    values_from = c(estimate, moe),
    names_from = c(variable, .value)
  )

# for names like: estimate_income, estimate_rent, ...
us_rent_income %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    values_from = c(estimate, moe),
    names_from = c(.value, variable)
  )
```

title: Allow single values_fill in pivot_wider()
description:
This is a feature suggestion inspired by how the `fill` argument was used in `spread`. 

Currently, in `pivot_wider`, when you want to "fill" non-existing values, you need to provide a named list for each original column (what fill value should be used). It is common to use the same fill value for all column (and sometimes, its just a single column we're widening). 

I suggest that if the user provides a value instead of a named list, the function will apply this value on all cases (as if it was specified with a named list containing all the value columns).

By example:

```
to_wider <- tribble(
  ~id, ~names_from_here, ~values_from_here,
  1, "col_a", 10,
  1, "col_b", 20,
  2, "col_b", 30
)

# this works fine:
pivot_wider(to_wider, 
   names_from = names_from_here, values_from = values_from_here, 
   values_fill = list(values_from_here = -99))

# A tibble: 2 x 3
#     id col_a col_b
#  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#1     1    10    20
#2     2   -99    30


# this yields an error (but I expected it to work and yield the same output as the previous call)
pivot_wider(to_wider, 
   names_from = names_from_here, values_from = values_from_here, 
   values_fill = -99)

# Error in values_fill[[value]] : subscript out of bounds

```

This suggestion slightly resembles issue #739  (which suggests a similar behavior for the `values_fn` argument).

title: Allow single values_fn in pivot_wider()
description:
See https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/737 for full example

``` r
library(tidyverse)
df1 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~type, ~name, ~var1, ~var2, ~var3,
  10L, "Country",   "Norway", 169L,         14L, 164L,
  10L,   "Sport",     "Skii", 169L,         14L, 164L,
  10L,  "Format",    "Video", 169L,         14L, 164L,
  11L, "Country",    "Spain", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,  "Format",    "Photo", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,   "Sport",     "Bike", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,   "Sport",   "Soccer", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,   "Sport",   "Basket", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  12L, "Country",      "USA",   0L,          0L,   0L,
  12L,  "Format",    "Video",   0L,          0L,   0L,
  12L,   "Sport", "Baseball",   0L,          0L,   0L
)

################################################################
# This default behavior is nice but to get rid of the default  #
# message requires to be explicit, which can be annoying       #
################################################################

pivot_wider(df1, names_from = "type", values_from = "name")
#> Warning: Values in `name` are not uniquely identified; output will contain list-cols.
#> * Use `values_fn = list(name = list)` to suppress this warning.
#> * Use `values_fn = list(name = length)` to identify where the duplicates arise
#> * Use `values_fn = list(name = summary_fun)` to summarise duplicates
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>      id  var1  var2  var3     Country       Sport      Format
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <list<chr>> <list<chr>> <list<chr>>
#> 1    10   169    14   164         [1]         [1]         [1]
#> 2    11   150    16   178         [1]         [3]         [1]
#> 3    12     0     0     0         [1]         [1]         [1]

pivot_wider(df1, names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>      id  var1  var2  var3     Country       Sport      Format
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <list<chr>> <list<chr>> <list<chr>>
#> 1    10   169    14   164         [1]         [1]         [1]
#> 2    11   150    16   178         [1]         [3]         [1]
#> 3    12     0     0     0         [1]         [1]         [1]

################################################################
# It becomes a lot of work if we have several "values_from"    #
################################################################

df2 <- df1 %>% mutate(name2 = substr(name,1,1)) %>%
  filter(type != "Format")

pivot_wider(df2, names_from = "type", values_from = c("name","name2"),
            values_fn = list(name=list, name2 = list))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 8
#>      id  var1  var2  var3 name_Country name_Sport name2_Country name2_Sport
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int>  <list<chr>> <list<chr>   <list<chr>> <list<chr>>
#> 1    10   169    14   164          [1]        [1]           [1]         [1]
#> 2    11   150    16   178          [1]        [3]           [1]         [3]
#> 3    12     0     0     0          [1]        [1]           [1]         [1]
```

Why couldn't we just do : 

    pivot_wider(df2, names_from = "type", values_from = c("name","name2"), values_fn = list)

In `mutate_at` / `summarize_at` we can feed either a function or a list of functions, this would feel natural here as well.

title: Let `pivot_wider` column name order be the same as the `name_from` column factor order
description:
Look at the following example, it is clear that the `pivot_wider` will not preserve the order of column names as the factor order even if `value_fill` is provided. In this way, the behavior of `spread` is more desired.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
test <- tibble(
  id = c(1, 2, 2),
  name = factor(c("B", "A", "B"), levels = c("A", "B")),
  value = c(5, 1, 1)
)
pivot_wider(
  test,
  names_from = "name", values_from = "value",
  values_fill = list(value = 0)
)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id     B     A
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     5     0
#> 2     2     1     1
spread(test, name, value, fill = 0)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id     A     B
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     0     5
#> 2     2     1     1
```

title: unite(na.rm = TRUE) only removes character NAs
description:
The NA values from all-NA columns get concatenated in as `"NA"` strings, as if `na.rm = FALSE`. If this is intended, then that's not documented.

``` r
library(tidyverse)

data <- tribble(
  ~Name,    ~Postalcode, ~Parent,  ~Parent2, ~Parent3, 
  "Paul",   "4732",      "Mother", NA,       NA,       
  "Edward", "9045",      NA,       NA,       NA, 
  "Mary",   "3476",      "Mother", NA,       NA,       
  NA,       NA,          NA,       NA,       NA,      
  NA,       "2468",      NA,       NA,       NA
)

# The NAs from both Parent2 and Parent3 are pasted in as strings, while the NAs
# from Parent1 are properly removed
data %>% unite(Parent_full, Parent:Parent3, sep = "|", na.rm = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   Name   Postalcode Parent_full 
#>   <chr>  <chr>      <chr>       
#> 1 Paul   4732       Mother|NA|NA
#> 2 Edward 9045       NA|NA       
#> 3 Mary   3476       Mother|NA|NA
#> 4 <NA>   <NA>       NA|NA       
#> 5 <NA>   2468       NA|NA

# Add a value anywhere in Parent3, and all its NAs get removed, but Parent2 is
# still getting pasted in in the middle
data[[2, "Parent3"]] <- "Uncle"
data %>% unite(Parent_full, Parent:Parent3, sep = "|", na.rm = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3
#>   Name   Postalcode Parent_full
#>   <chr>  <chr>      <chr>      
#> 1 Paul   4732       Mother|NA  
#> 2 Edward 9045       NA|Uncle   
#> 3 Mary   3476       Mother|NA  
#> 4 <NA>   <NA>       NA         
#> 5 <NA>   2468       NA

# Add a value to Parent3, and now there's no columns with all NAs, so no NAs are

title: Duplicate identifiers for rows in `spread`
description:
This may be a duplicate of #296, but there's a community [discussion ](https://community.rstudio.com/t/spread-why-errors/2076/7) about duplicate identifiers in `spread`.  I find it very difficult to explain to newcomers why `spread` has sometimes difficulties spreading what `gather` has just gathered.

Lets take example from [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/45898614/how-to-spread-columns-with-duplicate-identifiers/45898919#45898919):

```
 library(tidyverse)
 df <- structure(list(age = c("21", "17", "32", "29", "15"), 
                        gender = structure(c(2L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("Female", "Male"), class = "factor")), 
                   row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"), .Names = c("age", "gender"))
 df
#> # A tibble: 5 x 2
#>   age   gender
#>   <chr> <fct> 
#> 1 21    Male  
#> 2 17    Female
#> 3 32    Female
#> 4 29    Male  
#> 5 15    Male  

df %>% 
  spread(key=gender, value=age)
#> Error: Duplicate identifiers for rows (2, 3), (1, 4, 5)
```
Ok, so for some strange reason `tidyr` needs another index to do the `spread`. Fine! Why can't it intercept the call and do something along the lines of:

```
df %>% 
  group_by_at(vars(-age)) %>%  # group by everything other than the value column. 
  mutate(row_id=1:n()) %>% ungroup() %>%  # build group index
  spread(key=gender, value=age) %>%    # spread
  select(-row_id)  # drop the index

#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   Female Male 
#>   <chr>  <chr>
#> 1 17     21   
#> 2 32     29   
#> 3 NA     15   
```
Is there any reason why doing it on behalf of user might be against his/her interest?

)

###########################################################################

title: Poor performance of `pivot_wider`
description: The new `pivot_wider` is roughly twice as slow as the old `spread` (and `reshape2::dcast`) were. ``` r library(tidyr) library(dplyr) #> #> Attaching package: 'dplyr' #> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats': #> #> filter, lag #> The following objects are masked from 'package:base': #> #> intersect, setdiff, setequal, union mydf <- expand_grid( case = sprintf("%03d", seq(1, 4000)), year = seq(1900, 2000), name = c("x", "y", "z") ) %>% mutate(value = rnorm(nrow(.))) bench::mark( pivot = pivot_wider(mydf, names_from = "name", values_from = "value"), spread = spread(mydf, name, value), dcast = reshape2::dcast(mydf, case + year ~ name) ) #> Warning: Some expressions had a GC in every iteration; so filtering is #> disabled. #> # A tibble: 3 x 6 #> expression min median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` #> #> 1 pivot 1.02s 1.02s 0.984 125MB 1.97 #> 2 spread 457.02ms 461.95ms 2.16 430MB 15.2 #> 3 dcast 449.15ms 472.34ms 2.12 457MB 11.6 ``` Created on 2019-10-10 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0) This performance penalty is prohibitively severe for some even larger datasets I'm working with. description:

I use nest() a lot for creating JSONs from dataframes to interact with an API. Here's an example:

```
require(tidyverse)

title: pivot_longer is quadratic in number of input columns to reshape
description:
Hi @lionel-  @hadley first of all thanks for your great package, it is really fascinating and inspiring!

I have been performance testing `tidyr::pivot_longer`, which seems to be quadratic in the number of input columns to reshape, when `names_to` contains `".value"` and several output columns are generated. but I expected the timings to be linear in the input size! Here is a figure that shows significant slowdowns after about 10,000 input columns:

![figure-iris-cols](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/932850/67725382-6d470d00-f99f-11e9-907f-d93a2ade2e14.png)

- script to compute timings: https://github.com/tdhock/nc-article/blob/master/figure-iris-cols-data.R
- script to make figures: https://github.com/tdhock/nc-article/blob/master/figure-iris-cols.R

a simplified version of the timings script which only has tidyr code is:
```r
N.rep <- 10000
i.vec <- 1:N.rep
L <- lapply(i.vec, function(i)iris[, 1:4])
names(L) <- i.vec
L[["0"]] <- iris
some.iris <- do.call(data.frame, L)
pattern <- "X(.*)[.](.*)[.](.*)"
system.time({
  result <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
    some.iris,
    grep(pattern, names(some.iris)),
    names_to=c("before", ".value", "dim"),
    names_pattern=pattern)
})
```
I expected that computation time should be linear in `N.rep` but it appears to be quadratic. To fix that issue you may check into how `data.table` is doing it, because they seem to have implemented a linear time algorithm.

I also checked `pivot_longer` without `.value` in `names_to` and that seems to be linear:
![figure-who-cols-minimal](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/932850/67726607-a6817c00-f9a3-11e9-99ac-9f55c2f93429.png)

title: Pivot wider fails when the class of variable is a vector longer than one.
description:
When running `pivot_wider` over data where one of the character variables is labelled using the `Hmisc::label` function, I get the warning message `Error: Only bare vectors have shapes.` 

The `Hmisc::label` function not only adds a `label` attribute to the variable, but it changes the variable class to `c("labelled", "character")`.

I found that I could reproduce this error by adding to the `class` of any variable prior to using `pivot_wider`. Interestingly, this doesn't occur for factors - so I'm guessing factor variables are treated differently?

I'm not sure if editing the class of a variable is peculiar to `Hmisc` (and should be corrected there), or whether it should be considered acceptable in general and thus catered for?

```r

## This works
data("fish_encounters")
fish_encounters$fish <- as.character(fish_encounters$fish)
fish_encounters %>% pivot_wider(names_from = station, values_from = seen)

## So does this
data("fish_encounters")
class(fish_encounters$fish) <- c("factor", "extra")
fish_encounters %>% pivot_wider(names_from = station, values_from = seen)

## But these all fail
data("fish_encounters")
fish_encounters$fish <- as.character(fish_encounters$fish)
class(fish_encounters$fish) <- c("character", "extra")
fish_encounters %>% pivot_wider(names_from = station, values_from = seen)

data("fish_encounters")
fish_encounters$station<- as.character(fish_encounters$station)
class(fish_encounters$station) <- c("character", "extra")
fish_encounters %>% pivot_wider(names_from = station, values_from = seen)

data("fish_encounters")
class(fish_encounters$seen) <- c("integer", "extra")
fish_encounters %>% pivot_wider(names_from = station, values_from = seen)

```

title: No variable new column name in nest()?
Nested list-column is not a list and doesn't act like one
description:
The list-column created by `nest` is not actually a `list`, it is a `vctrs_list_of`. This changes the behavior of the column. Specifically, it used to be possible to mutate values of the list-column in place by adding new columns; that no longer works.

I encountered this when adding columns to a very wide data frame; in that case the error message was truncated and un-helpful.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

df = tibble(x=rep(c('a', 'b'), each=10), y=rnorm(20), z=1:20)
df_data = df %>% nest(data=-x) %>% pull(data) %>% setNames(c('a', 'b'))
class(df_data)
#> [1] "vctrs_list_of" "vctrs_vctr"

# Doesn't work
df_data$a = df_data$a %>% mutate(w=1:10)
#> Lossy cast from <tbl_df<
#>   y: double
#>   z: integer
#>   w: integer
#> >> to <tbl_df<
#>   y: double
#>   z: integer
#> >>.
#> Dropped variables: `w`

# Works
df_data = as.list(df_data)
df_data$a = df_data$a %>% mutate(w=1:10)
```

title: Does pivot_wider allow build different number of columns depending on variables?
description:
Assume we have the next data frame:
```
structure(list(id = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4), id_cases = c("1", 
"2", "3", "1", "2", "3", "1", "2", "3", "1", "2", "3"), x = structure(c(1L, 
2L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L), .Label = c("a", 
"b"), class = "factor"), y = c(1, 1, NA, 1, 0, NA, 0, 1, NA, 
1, 1, NA)), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"), row.names = c(NA, 
-12L))
# A tibble: 12 x 4
      id id_cases x         y
   <dbl> <chr>    <fct> <dbl>
 1     1 1        a         1
 2     1 2        b         1
 3     1 3        a        NA
 4     2 1        a         1
 5     2 2        b         0
 6     2 3        b        NA
 7     3 1        b         0
 8     3 2        b         1
 9     3 3        a        NA
10     4 1        a         1
11     4 2        a         1
12     4 3        b        NA
```
If I apply `pivot_wider` as follows I get
```
> df %>% pivot_wider(id_cols = "id", names_from = "id_cases", values_from = c("x","y"))
# A tibble: 4 x 7
     id x_1   x_2   x_3     y_1   y_2   y_3

2     2 a     b     b         1     0    NA
3     3 b     b     a         0     1    NA
4     4 a     a     b         1     1    NA

My question is if it is possible (maybe with some kind of specifications in `names_from` and `values_from` or using `pivot_wider_spec` instead of `pivot_wider`) to get simultaneously 3 columns for `x` but just 2 columns to `y`, since it has no information for `id_cases == 3`, so the output would be

1     1 a     b     a         1     1

title: `nest(.data, ...)` unquoting support of left hand side in name-variable pairs of `...`
description:
I find `tidyr::nest()` very useful and use it quite heavily in my modeling workflows. I mostly do so using wrappers and quasiquotation/tidyeval. 

As of tidyr 1.0.0 the `.key` argument is depreciated and issues friendly warning. However, I couldn't figure out an equivalent solution to capture user input for the resulting nest list-column name without `.key`.

It seems that omitting `.key` would involve unquoting the left hand side provided in the new `...` interface, for example unquoting `data` in `c(data  = c(x, y, z)`. The reprex is provided below the text.

It would be neat if `nest()` supported this in the near future. Are there any plans to realize this, in a similar way as `:=` in `dplyr::mutate()`? Or is there a workaround that allows wrapping `!!!cols` into the equivalent of `c(data  = c(x, y, z)`?

Thanks a lot in advance for some hints.
Cheers, 
Philipp

```r
``` r
library("tidyr")
library("tibble")

df <- tibble(
  a = 1:10,
  b = 1:10,
  c = 1:10, 
  d = list(rep(1:10, 10))
)

nest_wrapper <- function(.data, ..., .key = "data") {
  cols <- rlang::enquos(...)
  .key <- rlang::enquo(.key)
  
  tidyr::nest(.data = .data, !!!cols, .key = !!.key)
}

title: `extract` doesn't work properly when text contains `\n`
description:
`tidyr::extract()` doesn't extract values correctly when text in column contains `\n`. In the example below, `a` and `d` are ignored.

```r
data.frame(x="a\nb-c\d") %>% 
    tidyr::extract(x,into = c("ab","cd"),regex = "(.+)-(.+)")
```

returns 

```r
  ab cd
1 b c
```

instead of 

```
    ab  cd
1 a\nb c\nd
```

title: better error message for missing parameter?
