title: several issues with pivot_wider and unnest_wider
description:
On SO I ran into an[ example](https://stackoverflow.com/a/57943359/2270475) where `pivot_wider()`, `unnest_wider()` could unleash its powers but it didn't make my life easy because of several details, see below. 

**Input**

```
+----+---------+----------+------+------+------+
| id |  type   |   name   | var1 | var2 | var3 |
+----+---------+----------+------+------+------+
| 10 | Country | Norway   |  169 | 14   |  164 |
| 10 | Sport   | Skii     |  169 | 14   |  164 |
| 10 | Format  | Video    |  169 | 14   |  164 |
| 11 | Country | Spain    |  150 | 16   |  178 |
| 11 | Format  | Photo    |  150 | 16   |  178 |
| 11 | Sport   | Bike     |  150 | 16   |  178 |
| 11 | Sport   | Soccer   |  150 | 16   |  178 |
| 11 | Sport   | Basket   |  150 | 16   |  178 |
| 12 | Country | USA      |    0 | 0    |    0 |
| 12 | Format  | Video    |    0 | NA   |    0 |
| 12 | Sport   | Baseball |    0 | 0    |    0 |
+----+---------+----------+------+------+------+
```

**Expected output**

```
+----+------+------+------+---------+--------+----------+---------+---------+
| id | var1 | var2 | var3 | Country | Format | Sport_1  | Sport_2 | Sport_3 |
+----+------+------+------+---------+--------+----------+---------+---------+
| 10 |  169 |   14 |  164 | Norway  | Video  | Skii     | NA      | NA      |
| 11 |  150 |   16 |  178 | Spain   | Photo  | Bike     | Soccer  | Basket  |
| 12 |    0 |    0 |    0 | USA     | Video  | Baseball | NA      | NA      |
+----+------+------+------+---------+--------+----------+---------+---------+
```

**data** 

```
df1 <- structure(list(id = c(10L, 10L, 10L, 11L, 11L, 11L, 11L, 11L, 
12L, 12L, 12L), type = c("Country", "Sport", "Format", "Country", 
"Format", "Sport", "Sport", "Sport", "Country", "Format", "Sport"
), name = c("Norway", "Skii", "Video", "Spain", "Photo", "Bike", 
"Soccer", "Basket", "USA", "Video", "Baseball"), var1 = c(169L, 
169L, 169L, 150L, 150L, 150L, 150L, 150L, 0L, 0L, 0L), var2 = c(14L, 
14L, 14L, 16L, 16L, 16L, 16L, 16L, 0L, NA, 0L), var3 = c(164L, 
164L, 164L, 178L, 178L, 178L, 178L, 178L, 0L, 0L, 0L)),
class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, 
-11L))
```

## *1st issue : value_fn is applied even when not needed*

It comes from the fact its behavior is ruled by the source column and not the destination, here I need it only for `Sport` but I get values of `Format` and `Country` as well : 

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>      id  var1  var2  var3     Country       Sport      Format
#>   <int> <int> <dbl> <int> <list<chr>> <list<chr>> <list<chr>>
#> 1    10   169    14   164         [1]         [1]         [1]
#> 2    11   150    16   178         [1]         [3]         [1]
#> 3    12     0     0     0         [1]         [1]         [1]
```

Shouldn't the aggregation happen only when the destination column has elements with length !=1 ?

By the way, typing `list(name=list)` is a bit annoying here, why not just `values_fn = list` ? dplyr's `_at` functions allow either functions or list of functions, I've already made the mistake several times, and in some cases, typing `values_fn = list(foo = list, bar = list, baz = list)` just not to get the verbose message is a bit frustrating.

## *2nd issue : I can only unnest_wider one column at a time*

I first think that the fact that Country and Sport are lists is not a problem because I will `unnest_wider()` everything. But as far as I can tell I can't `unnest_wider` several columns at the same time, this strikes me as odd given the otherwise extreme flexibility of the new functions.

So I try those but they fail with an unhelpful error, forcing me to (gasp), read the doc : 

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  unnest_wider(5:7)
#> Error in .subset2(x, i) : no such index at level 2

df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  unnest_wider(one_of("Country","Sport","Format"))
#> Error in .subset2(x, i) : no such index at level 2
```

## *3rd issue : I can't convert vctrs objects intuitively*

I'm thinking OK, though it can be annoying in the general case, here I can just convert `Format` and `Country` to character as anyway I really to `unnest_wider()` the `Sport` column only, but I end up with weird values "<chr>" in my `Format` and `Country` columns : 

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Country, Format), as.character)
  
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>        id  var1  var2  var3 Country       Sport Format
#>     <int> <int> <dbl> <int> <chr>   <list<chr>> <chr> 
#>   1    10   169    14   164 <chr>           [1] <chr> 
#>   2    11   150    16   178 <chr>           [3] <chr> 
#>   3    12     0     0     0 <chr>           [1] <chr> 
```

I then realise this is a `vctrs` issue (a bug possibly ?), so I use `unlist()` instead and it works fine (using inserting a `mutate_all(., unclass)` step to get rid of the *vctrs* classes worked too).

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Country, Format), unlist)
  
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>      id  var1  var2  var3 Country       Sport Format
#>   <int> <int> <dbl> <int> <chr>   <list<chr>> <chr> 
#> 1    10   169    14   164 Norway          [1] Video 
#> 2    11   150    16   178 Spain           [3] Photo 
#> 3    12     0     0     0 USA             [1] Video 
```

## *4th issue : I can't `unnest_wider()` a vctrs list column*

and I get a cryptic error :  

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Country, Format), unlist) %>%
  unnest_wider(Sport, names_sep = "_")
# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# * `` -> ...2
# * `` -> ...3
# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# Error: No common type for `x` <tbl_df<...1:character>> and `y` <character>.
```

I understand that it is again a vctrs error so I decide to unclass it, but `unnest_wider()` seems to accept only symbols, so the following fails : 

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Country, Format,), unlist) %>%
  unnest_wider(unclass(Sport), names_sep = "_")
#> Error in .f(.x[[i]], ...) : object 'Sport' not found
```

So I add another step and finally get : 

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Country, Format,), unlist) %>%
  mutate_at("Sport", unclass) %>%
  unnest_wider(Sport, names_sep = "_")

# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# * `` -> ...2
# * `` -> ...3
# New names:
#   * `` -> ...1
# # A tibble: 3 x 9
#      id  var1  var2  var3 Country Sport_...1 Sport_...2 Sport_...3
#   <int> <int> <dbl> <int> <chr>   <chr>      <chr>      <chr>     
# 1    10   169    14   164 Norway  Skii       NA         NA        
# 2    11   150    16   178 Spain   Bike       Soccer     Basket    
# 3    12     0     0     0 USA     Baseball   NA         NA        
# # ... with 1 more variable: Format <chr>
```

## *5th issue : the "repaired names" look bad*

names are repaired when they don't need to, so I have to design my own (not very robust) repairing function and get my expected output: 

```
df1 %>%
  replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list)) %>%
  mutate_at(vars(Country, Format), unlist) %>%
  mutate_at("Sport", unclass) %>%
  unnest_wider(Sport, names_sep = "_", names_repair = ~sub("..." , "", ., fixed=TRUE))

# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# * `` -> ...2
# * `` -> ...3
# New names:
# * `` -> ...1
# # A tibble: 3 x 9
#      id  var1  var2  var3 Country Sport_1  Sport_2 Sport_3 Format
#   <int> <int> <dbl> <int> <chr>   <chr>    <chr>   <chr>   <chr> 
# 1    10   169    14   164 Norway  Skii     NA      NA      Video 
# 2    11   150    16   178 Spain   Bike     Soccer  Basket  Photo 
# 3    12     0     0     0 USA     Baseball NA      NA      Video
```

This is a trick that I had to use [there ](https://stackoverflow.com/a/57935520/2270475)as well.


## *6th issue : I cannot get rid of verbose message*

Unless I use a `SuppressMessages()` call, or `purrr::quietly()` etc, I have to keep this red ink and don't have a parameter to turn it off.

This is not specific to this issue as I encountered it already in : 

* https://stackoverflow.com/a/57935520/2270475
* https://stackoverflow.com/a/57932001/2270475

So I had this issue in 3 questions out of 3 that I've answered so far using `unnest_wider()`

 
*conclusion : what I would have liked to work silently*

```
df1 %>%
 replace_na(list(var2=0)) %>%
 # just mention list in the values_fn function, or have a global option to turn verbosity off 
  pivot_wider(names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn =list) %>%
  # not convert columns, not repair names
  unnest_wider(Sport, names_sep = "_")

# 2    11   150    16   178 Spain   Bike     Soccer  Basket  Photo 
# 3    12     0     0     0 USA     Baseball NA      NA      Video
```

The functions are great and fun to play with and I believe the code I came up with is still better than what I could come up with alternatives, but I also believe there was unnecessary friction to get there in that case.

title: value_fn is applied even when not needed
description:
See https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/737 for full example

``` r

library(tidyverse)

df1 <- tibble::tribble(
  ~id, ~type, ~name, ~var1, ~var2, ~var3,
  10L, "Country",   "Norway", 169L,         14L, 164L,
  10L,   "Sport",     "Skii", 169L,         14L, 164L,
  10L,  "Format",    "Video", 169L,         14L, 164L,
  11L, "Country",    "Spain", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,  "Format",    "Photo", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,   "Sport",     "Bike", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,   "Sport",   "Soccer", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  11L,   "Sport",   "Basket", 150L,         16L, 178L,
  12L, "Country",      "USA",   0L,          0L,   0L,
  12L,  "Format",    "Video",   0L,          0L,   0L,
  12L,   "Sport", "Baseball",   0L,          0L,   0L
)

pivot_wider(df1, names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>      id  var1  var2  var3     Country       Sport      Format
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <list<chr>> <list<chr>> <list<chr>>
#> 1    10   169    14   164         [1]         [1]         [1]
#> 2    11   150    16   178         [1]         [3]         [1]
#> 3    12     0     0     0         [1]         [1]         [1]
```

The behavior of `value_fn()` is ruled by the source column and not the destination, here I need it only for Sport but I get values of Format and Country as well,  I think it would be more intuitive to apply value_fn only when the columns has elements of length different than 1.

Expected: 

```
pivot_wider(df1, names_from = "type", values_from = "name", values_fn = list(name=list))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 7
#>      id  var1  var2  var3 Country       Sport Format
#>   <int> <int> <int> <int> <chr>   <list<chr>> <chr> 
#> 1    10   169    14   164 Norway          [1] Video 
#> 2    11   150    16   178 Spain           [3] Photo 
#> 3    12     0     0     0 USA             [1] Video
```

title: feature request: extract() adapted for list-column of atomic vectors
description:
tidyr::extract() transfers regex capture groups "into" new columns in a dataframe, what an awesome feature.

I often need to "extract" the elements of atomic vectors in a list-column into new columns. Below I show my workaround implemented in the extract_list() function using a combination of unnest()+spread():

For efficiency, my feature request is that extract_list() below be built into tidyr:

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
df <- data_frame(y=c("a","b","c"), x=list(c(1,2,3), c(4,5,6,-1), c(7,8,9)))
df
```
y, x // [chr,list]
"a", c(1,2,3)
"b", c(4,5,6,-1)
"c", c(7,8,9)

```{r}
extract_list <- function(df,col) {
  col <- enquo(col)
  df %>% 
    mutate(.l=map(!!col,~str_c("X",1:length(.x)))) %>% 
    unnest(!!col,.l) %>%
    spread(.l,!!col)
}
```

```{r}
extract_list(df,x)
```
y,X1,X2,X3,X4 // [chr,int,int,int,int]
"a",1,2,3,NA
"b",4,5,6,-1
"c",7,8,9,NA

title: Zero-row list-column tibble names are not propogated through unnest()
description:
I don't know if this is is a problem per se, but is a change in behaviour from tidyr 0.8.3, where all column names from a list-column are included in the output, even if all of them have zero rows. rclimateca actively uses this behaviour (paleolimbot/rclimateca#17) but could be rewritten not to.

Using the development version of tidyr:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

df <- tibble(x = "string", data = list(tibble(y = character(0))))
colnames(unnest(df, data))
#> [1] "x"
```

Using the CRAN version:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

df <- tibble(x = "string", data = list(tibble(y = character(0))))
colnames(unnest(df, data))
#> [1] "x" "y"
```

title: If names_to contains multiple values with missing levels pivot_longer fails.
description:
If there are multiple values in `names_to`, but they don't define a full grid, then `pivot_longer()` fails correctly impute NAs for the missing levels.

``` r
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
df <- tribble(
  ~id, ~x_1, ~x_2, ~y_2,
  "A",    1,    2,  "a",
  "B",    3,    4,  "b",
)
pv <- pivot_longer(df, -id, names_to = c(".value", "n"), names_sep = "_")
#> `nm` must be `NULL` or a character vector the same length as `x`
```

<sup>Created on 2019-08-14 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


Expect outcome would be this:

``` r
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)
df <- tribble(
  ~id, ~x_1, ~x_2, ~y_2,
  "A",    1,    2,  "a",
  "B",    3,    4,  "b",
)
pv <- pivot_longer(df, -id, names_to = c(".value", "n"), names_sep = "_")
pv
#> # A tibble: 4 x 4
#>   id    n         x y    
#>   <chr> <chr> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 A     1         1 <NA> 
#> 2 A     2         2 a    
#> 3 B     1         3 <NA> 
#> 4 B     2         4 b
```

It's going wrong in lines 162 and 166 of pivot_long.R, please see my attempt to fix it here:
https://github.com/banfai/tidyr/commit/3a55be89e7ebace60e8fb29347f02c110bc9af86

Also tried to add a test for it (passes with my version, fails with the current):
https://github.com/banfai/tidyr/commit/c909e180155af20f0cf35e32d8451023f8125b69

Let me know if I should submit a PR or if you want to review this issue in more detail.

title: Dealing with 'structural' missings in pivot_longer?
description:
I am dealing with some wide data where not all variables were collected at all times/waves. I can't use `pivot_longer` in a straightforward way because the long versions of the variables have different lengths. Is there some way to indicate that we should generate `NA`'s for variables that are missing one of the `time`s? I thought I might be able to add a row to the spec like:

```
# A tibble: 1 x 3
  .name .value time 
  <lgl> <chr>  <chr>
1 NA    score  2    
```
but that doesn't seem to work. Is there any other way to allow for the missing times, either with an option in `pivot_longer` or by manipulating the spec?

``` r
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(tidyr)

df = tibble(
    id = 1:5,
    score_t1 = sample(1:10, 5),
    score_t3 = sample(1:10, 5),
    rating_t1 = sample(1:100, 5),
    rating_t2 = sample(1:100, 5),
    rating_t3 = sample(1:100, 5)
)

df %>%
    pivot_longer_spec(
        cols = -id,
        names_to = c(".value", "time"),
        names_pattern = c("([a-z]+)_t(\\d)")
    )
#> # A tibble: 5 x 3

#> 2 score_t3  score  3    
#> 3 rating_t1 rating 1    
#> 4 rating_t2 rating 2    
#> 5 rating_t3 rating 3
    
df %>%
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -id,
        names_to = c(".value", "time"),
        names_pattern = c("([a-z]+)_t(\\d)")
    )
#> Tibble columns must have consistent lengths, only values of length one are recycled:
#> * Length 10: Column `score`
#> * Length 15: Column `rating`
```

<sup>Created on 2019-07-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

The desired output could be created with:

```r
df %>%
    mutate(score_t2 = NA) %>%
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -id,
        names_to = c(".value", "time"),
        names_pattern = c("([a-z]+)_t(\\d)")
    )
```

but I don't want to have to create the missing columns for every variable I'm trying to pivot.

title: drop_na drops attributes
description:
I expect drop_na to work basically the same way as an equivalent `filter(is.na(x))`. However, it drops attributes such as the label attribute and other custom attributes that I use. This prevents me from using it, although I like the idiom.

Here you can see that dplyr preserves the attribute `label`, but drop_na does not.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(x = 1:10)
attributes(df$x)$label <- "Not y"
attributes(df$x)$label
#> [1] "Not y"
df <- filter(df, is.na(x))
attributes(df$x)$label
#> [1] "Not y"
df <- drop_na(df, x)
attributes(df$x)$label
#> NULL
```

title: Expand data frame for all combinations of values for all variables without explicitly specifying variables names
description:
Hi,

I posted the following question on Twitter:

> I can’t seem to figure out how to use expand to get all combinations of values for all variables in df without specifying each var name explicitly? It’s easy with expand.grid. tibble(x=1:3, y=1:3) %>% expand.grid(). Can I tell expand() to use all vars?

@hadley asked if I would file an issue so he could think about it some more.

I suppose the Tweet is self-explanatory, I want to be able to expand a data frame for all possible combinations of values for every variable, without having to specify variable names explicitly.

This works:
```
tibble(x = 1:3, y = 1:3) %>% expand.grid()
```

This doesn't:
```
tibble(x = 1:3, y = 1:3) %>% expand()
```
Of course, in the two variable setting, explicitly typing `tibble(x = 1:3, y = 1:3) %>% expand(x, y)` is not a problem, but it doesn't scale well.

Something like this might be a possible solution:
```
tibble(x = 1:3, y = 1:3) %>% expand(vars(everything()))
```

title: Issue with unnest() and NextMethod() black magic
description:
This is a painful issue (but hopefully an easy fix!). Notice that when:

- We have a method for `nest()`
- We then call `nest.grouped_df` from that method
- We have supplied _something_ in the `...`

Then we trigger the `.key is deprecated` warning _no matter what_.

I think this is an insane case where `NextMethod()` isn't resetting the value of `.key` like it it supposed to:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

mtcars <- as_tibble(mtcars)

mtcars_special <- structure(mtcars, class = c("special_df", class(mtcars)))

nest.special_df <- function(.data, ..., .key = "DEPRECATED") {
  class(.data) <- setdiff(class(.data), "special_df")
  .data <- group_by(.data, vs)
  # run the grouped df version of nest()
  nest(.data, ..., .key = .key)
}

# WAT
mtcars_special %>%
  nest(data = am)
#> Warning: `.key` is deprecated
#> # A tibble: 32 x 11
#> # Groups:   vs [2]
#>      mpg   cyl  disp    hp  drat    wt  qsec    vs  gear  carb         data
#>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <list<df[,1>
#>  1  21       6  160    110  3.9   2.62  16.5     0     4     4      [1 × 1]
#>  2  21       6  160    110  3.9   2.88  17.0     0     4     4      [1 × 1]
#>  3  22.8     4  108     93  3.85  2.32  18.6     1     4     1      [1 × 1]
#>  4  21.4     6  258    110  3.08  3.22  19.4     1     3     1      [1 × 1]
#>  5  18.7     8  360    175  3.15  3.44  17.0     0     3     2      [1 × 1]
#>  6  18.1     6  225    105  2.76  3.46  20.2     1     3     1      [1 × 1]
#>  7  14.3     8  360    245  3.21  3.57  15.8     0     3     4      [1 × 1]
#>  8  24.4     4  147.    62  3.69  3.19  20       1     4     2      [1 × 1]
#>  9  22.8     4  141.    95  3.92  3.15  22.9     1     4     2      [1 × 1]
#> 10  19.2     6  168.   123  3.92  3.44  18.3     1     4     4      [1 × 1]
#> # … with 22 more rows

mtcars_special %>%
  nest()
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#> # Groups:   vs [2]
#>      vs            data
#>   <dbl> <list<df[,10]>>
#> 1     0       [18 × 10]
#> 2     1       [14 × 10]
```

<sup>Created on 2019-08-05 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

I think what _normally_ happens is that on this line `.key` is normally set to `"data"`
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/56116de14492679727ef941b0d9ebd8982fe15c4/R/nest.R#L140

But then when `NextMethod()` is called here, it gets reset to `"DEPRECATED"`
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/56116de14492679727ef941b0d9ebd8982fe15c4/R/nest.R#L146

So that this check in `nest.tbl_df` passes cleanly:
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/56116de14492679727ef941b0d9ebd8982fe15c4/R/nest.R#L120

BUT for whatever reason when it is called in this way the `.key` is not reset to `"DEPRECATED"` when `NextMethod()` is called. So `check_key("data")` is run from `nest.tbl_df` and we get the warning.

I think the fix is to just move this check into the `if(missing(...))` branch, but man this is a weird one.
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/56116de14492679727ef941b0d9ebd8982fe15c4/R/nest.R#L140

title: `unpack()` doesn't completely respect minimal name repair

description:
Hi 

I think it would be nice if `separate_rows()` could have better handling of NA column values. 

Currently, it only gives the error that _"All nested columns must have the same number of elements_". Instead, I thought it could just cycle the NA of a column for every row added. 

The following code gives an example.

title: full_seq only checks for tolerance in one direction
description:
`full_seq()` has a `tol` parameter that is the tolerance for checking periodicity. However, the implementation of the check, which uses the `%%` operator only checks for tolerances in one direction:

``` r
tidyr::full_seq(c(0, 10, 20), 11, tol = 2)
#> Error: `x` is not a regular sequence.
```

<sup>Created on 2019-06-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

Here's an updated `full_seq.numeric()` that I think solves the issue, and also pads the range if the last element falls short of being k*period more than the first element:

``` r
full_seq.numeric.patched <- function(x, period, tol = 1e-6) {
    rng <- range(x, na.rm = TRUE)
    if (any((x - rng[1]) %% period > tol & 
            period - (x - rng[1]) %% period > tol)) {
        stop("`x` is not a regular sequence.", call. = FALSE)
    }
    
    if (period - ((rng[2] - rng[1]) %% period) <= tol)
        rng[2] <- rng[2] + tol
            
    seq(rng[1], rng[2], by = period)
}

full_seq.numeric.patched(c(0, 10, 20), 11, tol = 2)
#> [1]  0 11 22
full_seq.numeric.patched(c(0, 10, 20), 11, tol = 1.8)
#> Error: `x` is not a regular sequence.
full_seq.numeric.patched(c(0, 10, 17), 11, tol = 5)
#> [1]  0 11 22
full_seq.numeric.patched(c(0, 10, 16), 11, tol = 5)
#> [1]  0 11
```

title: performance testing on hoist and unnest_wider
description:
I am testing out the new functions `unnest_wider()` and `hoist` to parse large JSON arrays of objects (e.g. from a REST API response). I'm loving the functionality, but I'm seeing a performance hit compared to my previous method, which was converting each object to a tibble and combining them with `purrr::map_dfr()`. 

Below is a reprex using the `repurrrsive` `got_chars` dataset. I replicated the `got_chars` data to make larger lists of objects and recorded run-time for different parsing methods. In my case, JSON array fields are always consistent in the response object, so I enforced that on the `got_chars` data as a pre-processing step.

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(repurrrsive)
library(tibble)
library(tidyr)

# enforce json schema ====
# convert array fields to lists for all items
array_fields <- c("titles", "aliases", "allegiances", "books", 
                  "povBooks", "tvSeries", "playedBy")
got_chars2 <- map(got_chars, 
                  ~map_at(.x, array_fields, ~as.list(.x)))

# tibble to track run times ====
times <- tibble(
  method = character(),
  rows = integer(),
  time = numeric()
)

# time different methods for increasing item count ====
# (this takes a while)
rows <- c(100, 1000, 5000, 10000)
for (n_rows in rows) {
  data <- rep(got_chars2, length.out = n_rows)
  
  # unnest_wider:
  t <- system.time(
    tibble(data = data) %>% 
      unnest_wider(data, simplify = TRUE)
  )
  times <- times %>% 
    add_row(method = "unnest_wider", 
            rows = n_rows,  
            time = t["elapsed"])
  
  # hoist (.remove=TRUE)
  t <- system.time(
    tibble(data = data) %>% 
      hoist(data, .remove = TRUE,
            url = "url",
            id = "id",
            name = "name",
            gender = "gender",
            culture = "culture",
            born = "born",
            died = "died",
            alive = "alive",
            titles = "titles",
            aliases = "aliases",
            father = "father",
            mother = "mother",
            spouse = "spouse",
            allegiances = "allegiances",
            books = "books",
            povBooks = "povBooks",
            tvSeries = "tvSeries",
            playedBy = "playedBy")
  )
  times <- times %>% 
    add_row(method = "hoist (.remove=TRUE)", 
            rows = n_rows,  
            time = t["elapsed"])
  
  # hoist (.remove=FALSE)
  t <- system.time(
    tibble(data = data) %>% 
      hoist(data, .remove = FALSE,
            url = "url",
            id = "id",
            name = "name",
            gender = "gender",
            culture = "culture",
            born = "born",
            died = "died",
            alive = "alive",
            titles = "titles",
            aliases = "aliases",
            father = "father",
            mother = "mother",
            spouse = "spouse",
            allegiances = "allegiances",
            books = "books",
            povBooks = "povBooks",
            tvSeries = "tvSeries",
            playedBy = "playedBy")
  )
  times <- times %>% 
    add_row(method = "hoist (.remove=FALSE)", 
            rows = n_rows,  
            time = t["elapsed"])
  
  
  # purrr::map_dfr:
  obj_to_tibble <- function(x) {
    # remove NULL items
    x <- purrr::compact(x)
    # wrap length >1 items into list
    x <- purrr::map_if(x, is.list, ~list(.x))
    tibble::as_tibble(x)
  }
  t <- system.time(
    purrr::map_dfr(data, obj_to_tibble)
  )
  times <- times %>% 
    add_row(method = "purrr::map_dfr", 
            rows = n_rows,  
            time = t["elapsed"])
  
}
times
#> # A tibble: 16 x 3
#>    method                 rows     time
#>    <chr>                 <dbl>    <dbl>
#>  1 unnest_wider            100   0.23  
#>  2 hoist (.remove=TRUE)    100   0.124 
#>  3 hoist (.remove=FALSE)   100   0.04  
#>  4 purrr::map_dfr          100   0.0730
#>  5 unnest_wider           1000   2.65  
#>  6 hoist (.remove=TRUE)   1000   1.19  
#>  7 hoist (.remove=FALSE)  1000   0.415 
#>  8 purrr::map_dfr         1000   0.719 
#>  9 unnest_wider           5000  34.7   
#> 10 hoist (.remove=TRUE)   5000   8.59  
#> 11 hoist (.remove=FALSE)  5000   5.00  
#> 12 purrr::map_dfr         5000   3.27  
#> 13 unnest_wider          10000 131.    
#> 14 hoist (.remove=TRUE)  10000  24.4   
#> 15 hoist (.remove=FALSE) 10000  14.8   
#> 16 purrr::map_dfr        10000   6.09

# plot times ====
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(times, aes(rows, time)) +
  geom_line(aes(color = method)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = method)) +
  labs(x = "number of list items", 
       y = "time [sec]") +
  ggtitle("List-to-Tibble processing time")
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/91FPi0v.png)

<sup>Created on 2019-05-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>


When I profiled `unnest_wider()`, it looks like most of the time is taken on the `unchop()` step. I'm not sure if there are cases when unchoping is needed to expand the rows, but in my case parsing a list of JSON objects, this seems unnecessary. The function below reworks `unnest_wider()` without chop (using `purrr::map_dfr` instead) -- this makes it about as fast as `hoist()` is, which is a big improvement for larger JSON arrays.

```r
unnest_wider2 <- function(data, col,
                          names_sep = NULL,
                          simplify = TRUE,
                          names_repair = "check_unique",
                          ptype = list()) {
  col <- tidyselect::vars_select(names(data), !!enquo(col))
  
  data[[col]] <- purrr::map_dfr(data[[col]], tidyr:::vec_to_wide, col = col)
  inner_cols <- names(data[[col]])
  
  data[[col]][] <- map2(
    data[[col]], ptype[inner_cols],
    tidyr:::simplify_col,
    keep_empty = TRUE,
    simplify = simplify
  )
  
  unpack(data, !!col, names_sep = names_sep, names_repair = names_repair)
}
```

The method below is even faster (~3s for 5k items instead of ~8s using unnest_wider2), though it relies on list columns being explicitly and consistently identified in the JSON objects. For my use, I can typically rely on API JSON schemas to be consistent (e.g. arrays are always arrays), so this doesn't seem too dangerous. Maybe this could be an option to use for speed when schemas are more reliable? 

```r
obj_to_tibble <- function(x) {
  # remove NULL items
  x <- purrr::compact(x)
  # wrap length >1 items into list
  x <- purrr::map_if(x, is.list, ~list(.x))
  tibble::as_tibble(x)
}

unnest_wider3 <- function(data, col) {
  col <- tidyselect::vars_select(names(data), !!enquo(col))
  purrr::map_dfr(data[[col]], obj_to_tibble)
}
```

title: Should gathering operation preserve groups?
description:
`tidyr::gather()` is the only verb in dplyr/tidyr that does not maintain groups in the output tibble. Perhaps its successor should keep them, here are some considerations:

- Duality of behaviour between grouped and non-grouped tibbles increases the usefulness of a single verb.

- Grouping variables often act as identifiers which are useful for further data manipulation.

- Consistently maintaining groups in all verbs makes the result more predictable.

- In general, it seems that consistently maintaining groups in reshaping functions, and excluding them in transformative functions (with implicit selections, erroring out otherwise) makes the components more easily composable for grouped tibbles (see for instance the rstudio::conf talk about passing dots to tidyverse components).

title: pivot_longer() should accept single names_pattern
description:
While `names_prefix` is a handy option, we sometimes need to use a regex to extract values from column names with more complex frills. But, `pivot_longer()` seems to ignore `names_pattern` when the length of `names_to` is 1. For example, 

``` r
library(tidyr)

billboard %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"), 
    names_to =  "week", 
    names_pattern = "wk(\\d+)",
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
```

I expected the result would be the same as this:

title: Error when pivoting with glue strings
description:
When using a variable that is a glue string in a pivot function,  I came across the error “Only bare vectors have shapes.” I'm not exactly sure what this error means, and it seems like something someone who is not expected to interact with vctrs might come across.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)

df <- tibble(
  a = rep(1:2, 2), 
  b = LETTERS[1:4], 
  c = letters[1:4],
  d = c("X", "X", "Y", "Y")
  )

# works with paste -------------------------------------------------------------
df2 <- df %>%
  mutate(info = paste(b, c, sep = " - ")) %>%
  select(-b, -c) 

class(df2$info)
#> [1] "character"

df2 %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = d, values_from = info)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>       a X     Y    
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>
#> 1     1 A - a C - c
#> 2     2 B - b D - d

# doesn't work with glue -------------------------------------------------------
df3 <- df %>%
  mutate(info = glue("{b} - {c}")) %>%
  select(-b, -c)

class(df3$info)
#> [1] "glue"      "character"

df3 %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = d, values_from = info)
#> Only bare vectors have shapes.

# works with glue after converting to character --------------------------------
df4 <- df %>%
  mutate(info = as.character(glue("{b} - {c}"))) %>%
  select(-b, -c)

class(df4$info)
#> [1] "character"

df4 %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = d, values_from = info)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
```

``` r
library(tidyr)
```

title: Inconsistent class dropping with unnest()
description:
Hi all,
I am pleased to see that `purrr::pmap()` no longer drop classes. Nonetheless, for non trivial classes, the output of `pmap()` must be a `list`, which then need to be unnested (or flattened?). My issue is that it seems that the unnesting sometimes still looses the class (but not always):

``` r

library(magrittr)

## consistent output (list of correct class):
  
tibble::tibble(date = as.Date("2000/01/01"), duration = 1) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(new = purrr::pmap(list(duration, date), ~ ..2 + lubridate::duration(..1))) -> foo

foo
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   date       duration new       
#>   <date>        <dbl> <list>    
#> 1 2000-01-01        1 <dttm [1]>

tibble::tibble(date = as.Date("2000/01/01"), duration = 1) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(new = purrr::pmap(list(duration), ~ lubridate::duration(..1))) -> bar

bar
#> # A tibble: 1 x 3
#>   date       duration new       
#>   <date>        <dbl> <list>    
#> 1 2000-01-01        1 <Duration>

#> Warning in combine_all(args[[1]]): Vectorizing 'Duration' elements may not
```

Best,
Alex

title: More intuitive example for "Wider" section of "Manual Spec" in pivoting vignette
description:
In the "Wider" section of "Manual Spec" in "Pivoting" vignette, customized manual spec is created by a combination of `expand` and `mutate`.
The order of rows and columns of the customized spec are different from that of the basic custom spec.
It is hard to compare them.

I suggest mutating the result of `pivot_wider_spec` is much easier and safer.

By mutating, the order of columns and rows in customized manual spec and basic spec are identical.
This is significantly easy to compare.

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
  
# Base spec
us_rent_income %>% 
  pivot_wider_spec(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe))
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   .name           .value   variable
#>   <chr>           <chr>    <chr>   
#> 1 estimate_income estimate income  
#> 2 estimate_rent   estimate rent    
#> 3 moe_income      moe      income  
#> 4 moe_rent        moe      rent

# Customized manual spec by Hadley
spec <- us_rent_income %>% 
  expand(variable, .value = c("estimate", "moe")) %>% 
  mutate(
    .name = paste0(variable, ifelse(.value == "moe", "_moe", ""))
  )
spec
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   variable .value   .name     
#>   <chr>    <chr>    <chr>     
#> 1 income   estimate income    
#> 2 income   moe      income_moe
#> 3 rent     estimate rent      
#> 4 rent     moe      rent_moe

# Customized manual spec by Atusy
spec2 <- us_rent_income %>%
  pivot_wider_spec(names_from = variable, values_from = c(estimate, moe)) %>%
  mutate(.name = paste0(variable, ifelse(.value == "moe", "_moe", "")))
spec2
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   .name      .value   variable
#>   <chr>      <chr>    <chr>   
#> 1 income     estimate income  
#> 2 rent       estimate rent    
#> 3 income_moe moe      income  
#> 4 rent_moe   moe      rent

# Check results
hadley <- us_rent_income %>% pivot_wider(spec = spec)
atusy <- us_rent_income %>% pivot_wider(spec = spec2)
identical(hadley, atusy[names(hadley)])
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: `unnest` sometimes removes rows
description:
I encountered this when disentangling JSON data. `NULL` elements are converted by `tibble` into *0x0* tibbles. When unnesting these zero dimensional tibbles the row is removed and we lose data, and I didn't expect `unnest` to be able to remove data.

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse, warn.conflicts = FALSE, quiet = TRUE))
df1 <- tibble(id = 1:3, data = list(list(a=1,b=2), NULL , list(a=3,b=4)))
df1
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      id data      
#>   <int> <list>    
#> 1     1 <list [2]>
#> 2     2 <NULL>    
#> 3     3 <list [2]>

df2  <- df1 %>% mutate(data = map(data, as_tibble))
df2
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      id data            
#>   <int> <list>          
#> 1     1 <tibble [1 x 2]>
#> 2     2 <tibble [0 x 0]>
#> 3     3 <tibble [1 x 2]>

unnest(df2, data)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id     a     b
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1     2
#> 2     3     3     4
```

<sup>Created on 2019-06-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

<details>
I can see how it makes sense and `n` rows in the data to `unnest` give `n` rows in the output data, but on the other hand I believe you rarely wants to remove rows by using unnest (you'd typically use `filter` in a previous step).

In my case I'm using `unnest` to expand the table horizontally and I expect the number of rows to stay constant. This is my workaround, which is not obvious : 

``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse, warn.conflicts = FALSE, quiet = TRUE))
df1 <- tibble(id = 1:3, data = list(list(a=1,b=2), NULL , list(a=3,b=4)))
df1
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      id data      
#>   <int> <list>    
#> 1     1 <list [2]>
#> 2     2 <NULL>    
#> 3     3 <list [2]>

df2  <- df1 %>% mutate(data = map_if(data, is.null, ~tibble(.rows = 1), .else = as_tibble))
df2
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>      id data                
#>   <int> <list>              
#> 1     1 <tibble [1 x 2]>    
#> 2     2 <tibble [1 x 0]>
#> 3     3 <tibble [1 x 2]>

unnest(df2, data)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#>      id     a     b
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1     2
#> 2     2    NA    NA
#> 3     3     3     4
```

<sup>Created on 2019-06-03 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>


I don't know if the default behavior should change or it would justify an extra parameter, but maybe a warning when `unnest` destroys data ? possibly with a pointer to a workaround. It wasn't so obvious to debug.

EDIT : 

A new verb dedicated to `unnest` horizontally only, working directly from `lists` or atomic vectors might be a good alternative, I use a lot this conversion from `list` to `tibble` and it's somewhat awkward. 

it might help provide more elegant solutions to use cases such as:

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/51813445/how-to-spread-a-list-column/51823029#51823029
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/46251040/flatten-column-as-argument/46346344#46346344
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/50919060/use-merge-with-one-data-frame-in-r/50919280#50919280
</details>

title: unnest fails on data.frame: can't slice scalar
description:
Thanks so much for all your work on tidyr! I'm very excited for the new `pivot_` functions. 

I've been using the development version (commit hash: 56fb136), and when I try to unnest a data.frame with a list-column, `unnest` throws the error: `Error: Can't slice a scalar`. 

If I create a tibble with a list-column rather than a data.frame, I am able to unnest. If I convert the list-col tibble back to a data.frame, I'm also able to unnest.

Here is a quick example:
```
library(tibble)

# create data.frame and corresponding tibble
df_1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = I(list(1:2)))
tb_1 <- tibble(a = 1, b = list(1:2))

# fails
tidyr::unnest(df_1, cols = c(b))
#> Error: Can't slice a scalar

tidyr::unnest(as_tibble(df_1), cols = c(b))
#> Error: Can't slice a scalar

# succeeds
tidyr::unnest(tb_1, cols = c(b))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       a     b
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     1     2

tidyr::unnest(as.data.frame(tb_1), cols = c(b))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       a     b
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1
#> 2     1     2
```

title: Support using `fill = NaN` in `spread()`
description:
Currently, calling `spread()` with `fill = NaN` instead fills with `NA`:
```r
library(tidyverse)
#> Registered S3 methods overwritten by 'ggplot2':
#>   method         from 
#>   [.quosures     rlang
#>   c.quosures     rlang
#>   print.quosures rlang
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'rvest':
#>   method            from
#>   read_xml.response xml2
tb <- tibble(Other = c("o1", "o1", "o2"), Key = c("k1", "k2", "k1"), 
    Val = c(5, 8, 10))
tb %>%
    spread(Key, Val, fill = Inf)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   Other    k1    k2
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 o1        5     8
#> 2 o2       10   Inf
tb %>%
    spread(Key, Val, fill = NaN)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   Other    k1    k2
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 o1        5     8
#> 2 o2       10    NA

Created on 2019-05-14 by the reprex package (v0.2.1)
```

@hadley 's reply to #274 for `fill()` seems relevant but I would argue is actually a reason for supporting a user's ability to fill with NaN's: Because NA and NaN are different, if a user wants to fill with NaNs for some application, they should be able to, since they can't just use NA as a substitute. E.g., the NaNs denote cases of 0/0, and not simply "missing".

Edit: A workaround is to use `complete()` first,
```r
tb %>%
    complete(Other, Key, fill = list(Val = NaN)) %>%
    spread(Key, Val)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   Other    k1    k2
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 o1        5     8
#> 2 o2       10   NaN
```
I do see an argument for forcing the user to do this, since `fill =NaN` in spread will convert existing NAs to NaN as well as filling them in for missing rows, which is somewhat dangerous---but this argument applies to `spread(..., fill = 0)` just as well as to `spread(..., fill = NaN)`.

title: Calling `nest()` on `grouped_df` grouped variable over-rides nesting variable
description:
If calling `nest()` on a `grouped_df`, the grouping variable, i.e. `group_vars(df)`, over-rides the user specified variable passed to `nest()`. 
In the reprex below, `df` is grouped by `cyl`, however when `nest(df, -gear)` is called, the `cyl` variable over-rides the deliberately specified nesting variable (`gear`). Further, `gear` is removed entirely from the nested tibbles themselves and disappears.

```r
reprex::reprex({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(tibble)

  #' Unexpected result calling `tidyr::nest(-gear)` if upstream `dplyr::group_by(cyl)`.
  df <- as_tibble(mtcars) %>%
    group_by(cyl)

  group_vars(df)

  #' The grouping variable (cyl) over-rides user-defined nesting variable (gear).
  #' Additionally, 'gear' is removed from the 'data' tibbles.
  ndf <- nest(df, -gear)
  ndf

  # gear disappears completely!
  "gear" %in% names(ndf)
  "gear" %in% names(ndf$data)

  #' Expected result (compare tibble dims to those above):
  df %>%
    ungroup(mtcars) %>%    # remove group_var: cyl
    nest(-gear)
})
```

This is a follow up to #551.

title: Unexpected result calling `nest()` on `grouped_df` object, variable dropped but not nested
description:
Unexpected result when calling `nest()` on a `grouped_df` object **AND** passing a _different_ variable from the one used to generate the `grouped_df` object. 

The variable passed in the `nest()` call (`gear`) is dropped from the data (expected), but it is **not** part of the nesting in the output (unexpected).  The `gear` variable is absent from `data[[1]]`, but it is also absent from the `df`. See the `reprex` below. This could be related to #463, but I don't think so.

Perhaps separate branch is could resolve this conflict via splitting out a new `nest.grouped_df()` method?

``` r
library(magrittr)
library(tibble)
suppressMessages(library(tidyr))
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))
```

Assume you used dplyr::group\_by() upstream, forgot to
ungroup and then wanted to tidyr::nest() on `gear`:

``` r

  as_tibble() %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
```

title: Linking between pivot_* docs and gather/spread docs
description:
The new `pivot_*` functions solve a clear need. Both in providing advanced features to `tidyr` and hopefully in simplifying folks' workflows. However, IMO it's important that users do not feel overwhelmed or that the existing functions will be deprecated. 

In particular, I think the following should be communicated to users:

- We acknowledge folks found `spread`/`gather` difficult to memorise and use, as mentioned in the vignette.
- We assure users that `spread`/`gather` are not going to be deprecated. They do not need to use the new `pivot_*`
- We tell users that new things are possible with the `pivot_*` functions
- We tell new users who meet `pivot_*` first that `spread`/`gather` exist, to reduce confusion when reading old SO answers etc.
- We provide more examples real dataset examples of how to switch between `spread`/`gather` and the `pivot_*` functions.

Here are places where I think that we need to add notes or examples, there might be more I've not considered.

- `spread`/`gather` docs pages
- `pivot_*` docs pages

title: Remove hint suggesting using tibble::rowid_to_column in s spread error
description:
This is in reference to the following line in the `spread()` function definition:

https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/c7c2ce6dc86d8edf04300cde85edda906c2b5d51/R/spread.R#L88

Below is a reprex that triggers the error in question:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))

df <- tribble(
  ~A, ~B,
  "x",  1,
  "x",  2,
  "y",  3,
  "y",  4
)

df
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   A         B
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 x         1
#> 2 x         2
#> 3 y         3
#> 4 y         4

df %>%
  spread(key = A, value = B)
#> Each row of output must be identified by a unique combination of keys.
#> Keys are shared for 4 rows:
#> * 1, 2
#> * 3, 4
#> Do you need to create unique ID with tibble::rowid_to_column()?
```

However applying this function would likely never give the desired result:

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)
suppressMessages(library(dplyr))

df <- tribble(
  ~A, ~B,
  "x",  1,
  "x",  2,
  "y",  3,
  "y",  4
)

df
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   A         B
#>   <chr> <dbl>
#> 1 x         1
#> 2 x         2
#> 3 y         3
#> 4 y         4

df %>%
  rowid_to_column() %>%
  spread(key = A, value = B)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   rowid     x     y
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1    NA
#> 2     2     2    NA
#> 3     3    NA     3
#> 4     4    NA     4
```

Instead we would want an identifier for each `x`,`y` pair:

``` r
df %>%
  mutate(rowid = rep(1:2, 2)) %>%
  spread(key = A, value = B)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   rowid     x     y
#>   <int> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1     1     3
#> 2     2     2     4
```

title: nest with a grouped data frame Gives Unexpected Results
description:
When using `nest` with a `group_df`, the grouping columns are kept outside the nested results silently.  I would either expect for the columns to be moved inside the nested data.frame or to have a warning and for them to be kept outside.  Also, if grouping columns are maintained outside of the nested structure, I would expect the result to be a `group_df` rather than losing the `group_df` class.

Specifically, I would expect a warning when creating `d3` below that not all grouping columns were requested in the nesting and the additional grouping columns were added.  (I think that this is more consistent.)

Or

I would expect the results to be like `d4` (without having the `ungroup` call) and for the the class of `d4$data[[1]]` to be a `group_df` with only column `B` as the grouping column for `d4$data[[1]]`.

``` r
library(tidyr)                     
#> Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 3.4.4
library(dplyr)                     
#> Warning: package 'dplyr' was built under R version 3.4.4
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
                                   
d <- data.frame(A=rep(1:2, each=4),
B=rep(1:4, each=2),                
C=1:8)                             
d2 <-                              
d %>%                              
group_by(A, B)                     
class(d2)                          
#> [1] "grouped_df" "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
names(d2)                          
#> [1] "A" "B" "C"
                                   
d3 <-                              
d2 %>%                             
nest(-A)                           
#> Warning: package 'bindrcpp' was built under R version 3.4.4
class(d3)                          
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
names(d3)                          
#> [1] "A"    "B"    "data"
names(d3$data[[1]])                
#> [1] "C"
                                   
d4 <-                              
d2 %>%                             
ungroup() %>%                      
nest(-A)                           
class(d4)                          
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
names(d4)                          
#> [1] "A"    "data"
names(d4$data[[1]])                
#> [1] "B" "C"
```

Since this seems to be a `nest` issue, I'm reporting it here rather than in `dplyr`.  If preferred, please move it to `dplyr`.

title: FR: promote() to create new variable from a list column
description:
Putting on the radar here at @hadley's suggestion.

What about a function `promote()` that can create a simplified variable from info extracted from a list column?

Example:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
x <- tibble(
  character = c("Toothless", "Dory"),
  metadata = list(
    list(species = "dragon", color = "black",
         films = c("How to Train Your Dragon", "How to Train Your Dragon 2")),
    list(species = "clownfish", color = "blue",
         films = c("Finding Nemo", "Finding Dory"))
  )
)

## hypothetical call to promote()
## x %>% promote(metadata, species)
## indicative result
x %>%
  mutate(species = simplify(map(metadata, "species"))) %>% 
  select(character, species, everything())
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>   character   species   metadata
#>       <chr>     <chr>     <list>
#> 1 Toothless    dragon <list [3]>
#> 2      Dory clownfish <list [3]>
```

What friction would `promote()` remove? The auto-simplification and "putting the new variable in front of the old instead of at the end where I can never see it".

Related to https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/336. The new capability of `purrr::pluck()` also seems interesting in this context.

In my real life, both issues are motivated by dealing with tibblized JSON from an API, where I have one row per item and I'm dragging around a list-column of metadata.

title: Apply universal renaming after unnest()
description:
Otherwise, duplicate column names may lead to hard-to-detect failures.

In the example below, an early `mutate()` that adds a column that exists in the sub-tibble breaks code that worked previously in a way that may go unnoticed. With universal names, the failure is detected immediately.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
data <- tibble(x = 1, b = list(tibble(a = 2:3)))
data
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       x b               
#>   <dbl> <list>          
#> 1     1 <tibble [2 × 1]>

old_data <-
  data %>%
  unnest()

old_data
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>       x     a
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     2
#> 2     1     3
old_data %>% filter(a == 2)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>       x     a
#>   <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     2

new_data <-
  data %>%
  mutate(a = 1) %>% # This breaks existing code!
  unnest()

new_data
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>       x     a    a1
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <int>
#> 1     1     1     2
#> 2     1     1     3
new_data %>% filter(a == 2)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 3
#> # ... with 3 variables: x <dbl>, a <dbl>, a1 <int>

# Suggested fix: Safe failure

new_data <-
  new_data %>%
  rename(a..2 = a, a..3 = a1) %>%
  filter(a == 2)
#> Error: Evaluation error: object 'a' not found.
```

title: Directional unnesting
description:
Copying notes from lingering file on my desktop:

```R
# Some intersting challenges from Jenny
# https://github.com/tidyverse/googledrive/blob/519452fc4d3257354079324e4afede777604848f/data-raw/discovery-doc-prep.R#L118-L124

library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(
  g = c("a", "a", "b"),
  x = c(1, 3, 5),
  y = c("x", "y", "z")
)
df

# One missing case z = list(1, 2, 3)
# There you just want to simplify the list col to a vector


# rows and cols change; current nest behaviour
# df %>% nest(x, y, .key = "data")
nest_both <- tribble(
  ~g,  ~data,
  "a", tibble(x = c(1, 3), y = c("x", "y")),
  "b", tibble(x = 5, y = "z")
)
nest_both

# rows change; cols don't
# get list of vectors
# df %>% nest_rows(x, y)
nest_rows <- tribble(
  ~g, ~x,       ~y,
  "a", c(1, 3), c("x", "y"),
  "b", 5,       "z"
)

# cols change; rows don't
# use lists, not tibbles to convey intent.
# df %>% nest_cols(x, y, .key = "data")
nest_cols <- tribble(
  ~g,  ~data,
  "a", list(x = 1, y = "x"),
  "a", list(x = 3, y = "y"),
  "b", list(x = 5, y = "z")
)
nest_cols

# unnest ------------------------------------------------------------------

# All of these should be able to automatically determine the
# unnested direction: data frame = both; named vector = col;
# unnamed vector = row; anything else or mix = error.

unnest(nest_both, data)
unnest(nest_cols, data)
unnest(nest_rows, x, y)

# Lengths must be consistent (otherwise would have to cross?)
# nest_row %>% unnest_row()
nest_rows %>% unnest(x, y)

# bind_rows() handles name/type consistency
# nest_col %>% unnest_col()
nest_cols %>%
  mutate(data = data %>% map(as_tibble)) %>%
  unnest(data)

# What happens if we try do to the "wrong" direction?
nest_rows %>% unnest_col()
nest_cols %>% unnest_row()

# needs column names
# can you supply multiple columns? (yes, but how to supply names? provide numbers by default?)
# can you provide maximum number? need to handle potential raggedness
# (this is starting to feel like separate)
nest_rows %>% unnest_col()

# needs option to capture names
# how to manage types of data col? here would be mix of character and integer
# use purrr::simplify? uses unlist() but guarantees length will be ok

nest_cols %>% unnest(data)
nest_cols %>% unnest(.id = "name") # not picking up name

# would simplify to integer or die trying?
nest_cols %>% unnest(.id = "name", .type = "integer")
```

title: pivot_wider sort order is different from spread sort order when not all combinations of grouping variables are present
description:
I don't think this has been raised as an issue already. `pivot_wider` does not seem to retain the sort order of the variables that are not spread (pivoted) in the way that `spread` does, when not all combinations of grouping variables are present.

I don't know if this is a problem or not, but to me it seems desirable to retain the sort order as `spread` does. See example below, in which the group2 variable sort order changes in `pivot_wider`.

```r
library("tidyverse")

# create a data frame with two groups
df <- expand_grid(group1=c("a", "b"),
                  group2=1:4) %>%
  mutate(value=row_number()) %>%
  # drop one of the combinations of grouping variables
  filter(!(group1=="a" & group2==3)) 

df
#> # A tibble: 7 x 3
#>   group1 group2 value
#>   <chr>   <int> <int>
#> 1 a           1     1
#> 2 a           2     2
#> 3 a           4     4
#> 4 b           1     5
#> 5 b           2     6
#> 6 b           3     7
#> 7 b           4     8

df %>%
  spread(group1, value)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   group2     a     b
#>    <int> <int> <int>
#> 1      1     1     5
#> 2      2     2     6
#> 3      3    NA     7
#> 4      4     4     8

df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from=group1, values_from=value)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>   group2     a     b
#>    <int> <int> <int>
#> 1      1     1     5
#> 2      2     2     6
#> 3      4     4     8
#> 4      3    NA     7
# note that group2 now is ordered differently

```

title: Parsing new columns from old column names in pivot_longer()
description:
https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/commit/3268807babf9a545cad1560003cab0160d939004 added a `names_sep` argument to `pivot_longer()` to make it easier to support `separate()` based spec construction (https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/586#issuecomment-475364183).

For even further added flexibility, it would be nice to have a `names_pattern`/`names_regex` argument to support `extract()` based spec construction:

```r
who %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = new_sp_m014:newrel_f65,
    names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"),
    names_pattern = "new_?(.*)_(.)(.*)",
    values_to = "count"
  )
```

An alternative (or additional?) improvement could be a vector `names_sep` that can specify splitting by both separators and positions (https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/586#issuecomment-475598589).

title: Adding aggregation parameter to spread() to manage multiple values for the same key
description:
The `tidyr` function `spread()` returns an error if the same key (here `a`) has multiple values:

```r
> df <- data.frame(key = c("a","a"), value = c(2,3))
> df
  key value
1   a     2
2   a     3
> spread(df, key, value)
Error: Duplicate identifiers for rows (1, 2)
```

In our project we needed to spread on multiple rows in order to get this:

```
  a
1 2
2 3
```

Spreading these duplicates to multiple rows can be seen as a special case of the more general problem of handling duplicate identifiers. For example in Python (in the `pandas` package) and in Microsoft Excel (under the name *pivot table*) duplicate identifiers are handled using an **aggregation function**, which is currently not supported in `tidyr`. 

With this in mind, we suggest an alternative implementation of `spread` which supports all current parameters, but adds the **`aggfunc` parameter** to define how any multiple rows for the same key should be aggregated (e.g. average, sum, …). The default value `NULL` does not aggregate, but keeps the multiple rows. An implementation of this is provided at [`spread_with_multiple_values()`](https://github.com/trias-project/trias/blob/master/R/spread_with_multiple_values.R). Examples:

## 1. Dataframe without multiple values for same key

```r
library(trias)
df_1 <- data.frame(
  col1 = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
  col2 = c("H", "H", "H", "H"),
  key = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  value = c("R", "S", "T", "X"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
spread_with_multiple_values(df_1, key, value)
```

Which produces the same result as `tidyr::spread(df_1, key, value)`:

```
  col1 col2 A B C D
1    1    H R S T X
```

## 2. Dataframe with multiple values for same key + no aggfunc provided

```r
library(trias)
df_2 <- data.frame(
  col1 = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
  col2 = c("H", "H", "H", "H"),
  key = c("A", "B", "C", "C"),
  value = c("R", "S", "T", "X"), # multiple values T, X for key C
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
spread_with_multiple_values(df_2, key, value) # no “aggfunc” parameter
```

Which results in multiple rows for multiple values for the same key:

```
  col1 col2 A B C
1    1    H R S T
2    1    H R S X
```

While `tidyr::spread(df_2, key, value)` would throw an error.

Alternative ways to get the same result:

```r
spread_with_multiple_values(df_2, 3, 4)
spread_with_multiple_values(df_2, -2, -1)
spread_with_multiple_values(df_2, "key", "value")
```

## 3. Dataframe with multiple values for same key + aggfunc provided

```r
library(trias)
df_3 <- data.frame(
  col1 = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
  col2 = c("H", "H", "H", "H"),
  key = c("A", "B", "C", "C"),
  value = c(2, 3, 1, 8), # multiple values 1, 8 for key C
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
spread_with_multiple_values(df_3, key, value, aggfunc = str_c, collapse = "-")
spread_with_multiple_values(df_3, key, value, aggfunc = min)
spread_with_multiple_values(df_3, key, value, aggfunc = mean)
```

Which results in:

```R
> spread_with_multiple_values(df_3, key, value, aggfunc = str_c, collapse = "-")
# A tibble: 1 x 5
   col1 col2  A     B     C    
  <dbl> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
1     1 H     2     3     1-8  
> spread_with_multiple_values(df_3, key, value, aggfunc = min)
# A tibble: 1 x 5
   col1 col2      A     B     C
  <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1 H         2     3     1
> spread_with_multiple_values(df_3, key, value, aggfunc = mean)
# A tibble: 1 x 5
   col1 col2      A     B     C
  <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1 H         2     3   4.5
```

---

`spread_with_multiple_values()` shows that it is possible to combine an aggregate function with the standard input parameters of `tidyr::spread()`. Would it be an option to extend the functionality of `spread` in this direction and support an `aggfunc` parameter? Any input is welcome, but I'm certainly willing to add a PR with this adaptation if it would provide added value.

Consider argument order in pivot_wide()
description:
Currently the `keys` argument to `pivot_wide()` takes up the "prime" argument spot as the first argument specified when the function is called after a pipe. As a result, `names_from` and `values_from` (which are virtually always needed) must always be explicitly named; this can be helpful for educational purposes but I suspect will quickly become a hindrance for an experienced user.

`keys` is currently not mentioned in [the vignette](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/dev/articles/pivot.html) (as noted in #566), and was not even present in the predecessor function `spread()`. Considering this, I would assume that it won't be commonly used, and as such placing it as the primary argument to `pivot_wide()` seems unwarranted.

Moving `keys` to come after `names_from` and `values_from` would place commonly used parameters at better positions, and for simple use cases make `pivot_wide()` a drop-in replacement for `spread()`:

```r
# I would like to be able to just write
fish_encounters %>% 
  pivot_wide(station, seen)

# ... and get the behaviour of
fish_encounters %>% 
  spread(station, seen)
```

title: Allow multiple value_from cols in pivot_wide()
description:
In the spirit of \#149, could `pivot_wide()`’s `values_from` support selecting multiple columns?

Specifically, if `values_from` has more than one column, the names given by the `names_from` columns could additionally be suffixed with the names of the `values_from` columns (similar to how scoped dplyr verbs suffix variable names with function names, if given multiple variables and functions simultaneously). This would allow behaviour similar to using data.table’s `dcast()` with multiple `value.var`’s.

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(data.table)

# a common use case would be to format summary statistics
long_table <- survival::transplant %>% 
  group_by(sex) %>% 
  count(abo) %>% 
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n) * 100) %>% 
  ungroup()

# hmm.. I'd like to have the stats by sex side-by-side
long_table
#> # A tibble: 8 x 4
#>   sex   abo       n   pct
#>   <fct> <fct> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 m     A       185 41.4 
#> 2 m     B        51 11.4 
#> 3 m     AB       24  5.37
#> 4 m     O       187 41.8 
#> 5 f     A       140 38.0 
#> 6 f     B        52 14.1 
#> 7 f     AB       17  4.62
#> 8 f     O       159 43.2

# can get the desired shape but suboptimal new column names with dcast
dcast(setDT(long_table), ... ~ sex, value.var = c("n", "pct"))
#>    abo n_m n_f     pct_m     pct_f
#> 1:   A 185 140 41.387025 38.043478
#> 2:   B  51  52 11.409396 14.130435
#> 3:  AB  24  17  5.369128  4.619565
#> 4:   O 187 159 41.834452 43.206522

# the same with `pivot_wide()` requires a manual spec
long_table %>% 
  expand(sex, .value = c("n", "pct")) %>% 
  mutate(.name = paste(sex, .value, sep = "_")) %>% 
  pivot_wide(long_table, spec = .)
#> # A tibble: 4 x 5
#>   abo     m_n m_pct   f_n f_pct
#>   <fct> <int> <dbl> <int> <dbl>
#> 1 A       185 41.4    140 38.0 
#> 2 B        51 11.4     52 14.1 
#> 3 AB       24  5.37    17  4.62
#> 4 O       187 41.8    159 43.2
```

While creating a manual spec for `pivot_wide()` to achieve this is not complicated (and is more flexible), when trying out different `names_from` columns, the extra lines of code and variable name duplication add up quickly; this shows especially when doing quick ad-hoc analyses and looking to just glance at the summary statistics in a neater format.

``` r
# if `values_from` could take multiple columns, the above would simplify to:
pivot_wide(long_table, names_from = sex, values_from = c(n, pct))

# and a different `names_from` only requires 1 more line
pivot_wide(long_table, names_from = abo, values_from = c(n, pct))
```

The fairly hefty downside with this approach would be that if using multiple `values_from` columns, the new column names would no longer only depend on the `names_from` argument. I would argue that the added flexibility outweighs this, though.

title: gather for matrix class
description:
is it possible to mimic `reshape2::melt.matrix` in `tidyr::gather`?

i wrote this function that does it, but wondered if it is already possible and I missed an obvious solution.

```
#' @export 
#' @importFrom dplyr as_data_frame bind_cols select
#' @importFrom tidyr gather
gather.matrix <- function(data){
  
  s <- dim(data)
  nm <- dimnames(data)
  
  if(is.null(nm)){
    new_list <- lapply(s,seq,from=1)
  }else{
    new_list <- mapply(function(x,s){
      if(is.null(x)){
        seq(1,s)
      }else{
        x
      }
    },x=nm,s=s,SIMPLIFY = FALSE)
  }
  
  data%>%
    dplyr::as_data_frame()%>%
    tidyr::gather()%>%
    dplyr::bind_cols(.,expand.grid(new_list,stringsAsFactors = FALSE))%>%
    dplyr::select(Var1,Var2,value)
}
```

title: Performance of fill() after group_by()
description:
The `fill()` function after a `group_by()`, especially if the number of groups is large, is more than 10x slower than `mutate()` with `na.locf()`, from the `zoo` package, yet gives identical results. Maybe I'm missing something and there is another way to peform this same operation?

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(zoo)
library(tibble)

n <- 1e6
df <- tibble(a = sample(paste("id", 1:(n/4)), n, replace = T),
             b = sample(c("2012", "2013", "2014"), n, replace = T),
             c = sample(c("NA", "A", "B", "C"), n, replace = T))


t1 <- system.time(df1 <-
                    df %>% 
                      arrange(a, b) %>% 
                      group_by(a) %>% 
                      mutate(c = na.locf(c, na.rm=F))
                  )

print(t1)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>   21.45    0.06   21.81

t2 <- system.time(df2 <-
                    df %>%
                      arrange(a, b) %>% 
                      group_by(a) %>%
                      fill(c)
                  )
print(t2)
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>  313.37    0.47  316.75
print(identical(df1, df2))
#> [1] TRUE
```

title: More fill() options - fill-down-then-up, and fill-up-then-down
description:
Currently for missing data within groups, I do quite a lot of `fill()`ing down and then back up to densely fill in the missing values.

Depending upon number of groups and number of variables to replace, this can take a noticeable amount of time. 

The current duplicate call to fill() could be avoided with additional options for `.direction`, i.e. `downup` and `updown`

An example of the new usage is shown below.

An implementation is included in this PR https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/pull/504


``` r
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
})

# Sample data
df <- data_frame(
  group = c( 1, 1,  1,  1,   2,  2,    2,  2),
  value = c(NA, 8, NA,  7,  NA, NA, 12.3, NA)
)

df
#> # A tibble: 8 x 2
#>   group value
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1  NA  
#> 2     1   8  
#> 3     1  NA  
#> 4     1   7  
#> 5     2  NA  
#> 6     2  NA  
#> 7     2  12.3
#> 8     2  NA

# Current call
df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  tidyr::fill(value, .direction = 'down') %>%
  tidyr::fill(value, .direction = 'up'  ) %>%
  ungroup()
#> # A tibble: 8 x 2
#>   group value
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1   8  
#> 2     1   8  
#> 3     1   8  
#> 4     1   7  
#> 5     2  12.3
#> 6     2  12.3
#> 7     2  12.3
#> 8     2  12.3

# Suggested call with new new 'fill()' options for '.direction'
df %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  tidyr::fill(value, .direction = 'downup') %>%
  ungroup()
#> # A tibble: 8 x 2
#>   group value
#>   <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1     1   8  
#> 2     1   8  
#> 3     1   8  
#> 4     1   7  
#> 5     2  12.3
#> 6     2  12.3
#> 7     2  12.3
#> 8     2  12.3
```

title: FR: Add function to tidy non-mutually exclusive factors surveyed over multiple inputs
description:
I'd like to see a function which would turn a ragged array to a sparse one, usually when a "factor" with non-mutually exclusive choices is tentatively recorded using a group of drop-downs.

For example, if you have such a "factor" with legal values `A`/`B`/`C`/`D` recorded over three variables `col1`, `col2` and `col3`.

|id|col1|col2|col3|
|--|----|----|----|
|1|A|B|C|
|2|B|C|NA|
|3|D|NA|NA|
|4|B|D|NA|

calling such a function, indicating that `col1`, `col2` and `col3` are encoding for the same information, would yield

|id|A|B|C|D|
|--|----|----|----|----|
|1|T|T|T|F|
|2|F|T|T|F|
|3|F|F|F|T|
|4|F|T|F|T|

Options would include the ability to set a prefix for the new variable names to avoid collisions, and to create the `NA` column.

I found this use case many times in medical surveys where disease history is badly recorded using multiple drop-down lists or sets of checkboxes. IIRC, google surveys also treats sets of checkboxes this way, with one column containing semi-colon separated values. This can be dealt with using a call to `separate` then a call to `binarize`.

Playing around a bit with `spread` and `gather` allows this behavior but this can be CPU/memory heavy on large dataframes.

There is a (pre-tidyeval) implementation in PR #288

title: Pivot with duplicate column names
description:
I'm more and more often confronted with messy spreadsheets with duplicate column names that need to be tidied up as for example in this [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48380122). 

`tidyr::gather` simply refuse to do it (error message) and `reshape::melt` pr `reshape2::melt` return the wrong numbers without any warning. The `data.table` version of `melt` works as intended.

<details>
Here is a minimal reprex : 

``` r

# Reprex
d <- data.frame(Group = c("A", "B"), 
                rbind(c(0, 0, 5, 5), 
                      c(0, 0, 10, 10)))
colnames(d) <- c("Group", "Var1", "Var2", "Var1", "Var2")

# Dataframe with duplicate column names --> quite frequent situation in messy spreadsheets...
d
#>   Group Var1 Var2 Var1 Var2
#> 1     A    0    0    5    5
#> 2     B    0    0   10   10

# With tidyr we have an error message : definitively better than to have the 
# wrong numbers...
tidyr::gather(d,,,-1)
#> Error: Can't bind data because some arguments have the same name

# with reshape and reshape2 : wrong results (0 everywhere, the 5 and 10 values have disapeared)
reshape::melt(d, id.vars = 1)
```

title: Spread does not preserve order
description:
When going from a wide dataset to long and then back, there seems to be an implicit sort that occurs on non key/value variables. This prevents the ability to recover an initial data set by undoing the `gather()` operation with `spread()`.

Consider the following example:

``` r
library("tidyr")
(init_data = tibble::tibble(
  Group = c("B", "C", "A"),
  `Cost Week 1` = c(1, 2, 3),
  `Cost Week 2` = c(4, 5, 6),
  `Cost Week 3` = c(7, 8, 9)
))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   Group `Cost Week 1` `Cost Week 2` `Cost Week 3`
#>   <chr>         <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 B                1.            4.            7.
#> 2 C                2.            5.            8.
#> 3 A                3.            6.            9.

long = init_data %>% 
  gather(key = "Week", value = "Cost", -Group)

long
#> # A tibble: 9 x 3
#>   Group Week         Cost
#>   <chr> <chr>       <dbl>
#> 1 B     Cost Week 1    1.
#> 2 C     Cost Week 1    2.
#> 3 A     Cost Week 1    3.
#> 4 B     Cost Week 2    4.
#> 5 C     Cost Week 2    5.
#> 6 A     Cost Week 2    6.
#> 7 B     Cost Week 3    7.
#> 8 C     Cost Week 3    8.
#> 9 A     Cost Week 3    9.

wide = long %>%
  spread(key = "Week", value = "Cost")

wide
#> # A tibble: 3 x 4
#>   Group `Cost Week 1` `Cost Week 2` `Cost Week 3`
#>   <chr>         <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>
#> 1 A                3.            6.            9.

init_data
```

title: spread with drop=FALSE and additional columns
description:
Let's say I have the following data.frame:

``` R
df <- data.frame(year=rep(1:5,3), blood=rep(c("A", "B", "0"), 5), count=1:15)
df$blood <- factor(df$blood, levels=c("A", "B", "AB", "0"))

df
       year blood count
1     1     A     1
2     2     B     2
3     3     0     3
4     4     A     4
5     5     B     5
6     1     0     6
7     2     A     7
8     3     B     8
9     4     0     9
10    5     A    10
11    1     B    11
12    2     0    12
13    3     A    13
14    4     B    14
15    5     0    15
```

As you can see the value "AB" doesn't appear in the data.frame.

So I have to use `drop=FALSE` when spreading the data:

``` R
 spread(df, blood, count, drop=FALSE)
  year  A  B AB  0
1    1  1 11 NA  6
2    2  7  2 NA 12
3    3 13  8 NA  3
4    4  4 14 NA  9
5    5 10  5 NA 15
```

So let's say there's an additional column `year2`:

``` R
df$year2 <- df$year * 2
spread(df, blood, count, drop=FALSE)

   year year2  A  B AB  0
1     1     2  1 11 NA  6
2     1     4 NA NA NA NA
3     1     6 NA NA NA NA
4     1     8 NA NA NA NA
5     1    10 NA NA NA NA
6     2     2 NA NA NA NA
7     2     4  7  2 NA 12
8     2     6 NA NA NA NA
9     2     8 NA NA NA NA
.....
```

We get for every combination of year and year2 a line in the resulting data.frame. That's no what I've expected to get.

So I tried to add the functionality in https://github.com/JerryWho/tidyr/tree/missingvalues.
Now I get

``` R
 spread(df, blood, count, drop=FALSE, other_col_as_one = TRUE)
  year year2  A  B AB  0
1    1     2  1 11 NA  6
2    2     4  7  2 NA 12
3    3     6 13  8 NA  3
4    4     8  4 14 NA  9
5    5    10 10  5 NA 15
```

Can I achieve this result with the orignal version of tidyr? Otherwise you can maybe add this functionality into the official version.

title: Rewrite crossing using vctrs thinking
crossing behaves differently with vectors and tibbles
description:
It appears that duplicate elements of vectors are dropped before generating permutations, but duplicate elements of tibbles are not. This is especially concerning in the case of vectors because it is likely to introduce silent errors when calculating permutation statistics (i.e. some of the data just won't be used in the calculation).

``` r
library(tidyverse)

x <- c(1, 2, 2)
z <- tibble(d = x)

y <- tibble(b = 4:6)

crossing(x, y)
#> # A tibble: 6 x 2

#> 1     1     4
```
