title: Animated gif in documentation
description:
## The gif

@apreshill made the best explanation for `tidyr::gather()` that I have ever seen:

![gather](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/209714/48026738-e9a06a80-e114-11e8-9a24-ecc8b37b8a53.gif)

Thank you, Alison! :100: 

The fundamental problem this gif solved for me is the confusion caused by the `key` and `value` arguments.

Before seeing this gif, I falsely (and instinctively) equated these things:
- the `key` and `value` arguments in `tidyr::gather()`
- the `id.vars` and `measure.vars` arguments in `reshape2::melt()`

This gif finally opened my eyes to the fact that `key` and `value` in `tidyr::gather()` are analogous to `variable.name` and `value.name` in `reshape2::melt()`. So many struggles :sob: 

Could we include this gif directly in the documentation on [this page][2]?

[2]: https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/gather.html

![untitled drawing](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/209714/48027537-0dfd4680-e117-11e8-89dc-331a718dc0d8.png)

Right now the gif is [posted on Twitter][1], but I'd like to see it in more places where people can find it while they're searching for information about `tidyr::gather()`.

[1]: https://twitter.com/WeAreRLadies/status/1059520693857996800

## A complaint about magical expressions

Also, I want to complain that the example in the documentation uses the naked words `stock` and `price` instead of `"stock"` and `"price"` as I would have expected. This is one of the magical things about R that was always difficult to accept as a beginner (and continues to be a challenge as a more experienced R user). It is difficult to accept that R will just *know* that `stock` should be turned into `"stock"` as a column name, instead of throwing an error because there is no `stock` variable defined anywhere, and there is no `stock` column in the input dataframe, either.

My expectation is this:

```
data %>% gather(stock, ...)
Error: object 'stock' not found
```

## A direct comparison to melt

Lastly, you might consider whether the documentation for `gather()` would be enhanced by showing a direct side-by-side comparison of the same operation executed  2 times, once by `gather()` and again by `melt()`. Personally, I would find it helpful. Others might find this confusing if they have never seen either function before, so it might not be a good idea.

Something like this:

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

mini_iris <- iris %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  slice(1)

# Let's gather all the measurements (except Species) into 1 column:
mini_iris %>% gather(key = flower_att, value = measurement, -Species)

# Now let's do the same thing again with reshape2::melt()
library(reshape2)

melt(
  data = mini_iris,
  variable.name = "flower_att",
  value.name = "measurement",
  id.vars = c("Species")
)
```

title: Using complete with a subset of levels silently drops observations
description:
Based upon the description of complete  its purpose is to add missing observations for specific combinations of variable values. I believe therefore it is not very intuitive for it to silently drop observations if certain levels are not present,  for example:

```
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

iris %>% 
    as_data_frame() %>% 
    mutate( Species = as.character(Species)) %>% 
    complete( Species = c("versicolor", "virginica"))
```

This code silently drops all observations with Species = setosa

I would propose either changing the function to use a full_join()  to ensure the original data is preserved or at the very least adding a warning/message so the user is aware that data has been lost. 

I am happy to make a PR if people agree this is a beneficial change.

title: Nesting tibbles after grouping by multiple factor variables produces NULL elements
description:
_Yesterday I submitted this by [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/54928621/nesting-tibbles-after-grouping-by-factor-variables-produces-null-elements-in-r), but it might belong here as well:_

I was reviewing some of my old R code when I stumbled upon several errors.

After running each line and playing around with my data I discovered that `nest()`ing tibbles `dplyr::group`(ed)`_by` factor variables produced one or more `NULL` elements.

Here an example with the mtcars data:

```
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

mtcars %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  select(cyl, carb, mpg) %>% 
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl),
         carb = factor(carb)) %>% 
  group_by(cyl, carb) %>% 
  nest()

# A tibble: 9 x 3
# cyl   carb  data            
# <fct> <fct> <list>          
#   1 6     4     <NULL>          
#   2 4     1     <tibble [5 x 1]>
#   3 6     1     <tibble [3 x 1]>
#   4 8     2     <NULL>          
#   5 8     4     <NULL>          
#   6 4     2     <tibble [6 x 1]>
#   7 8     3     <NULL>          
#   8 6     6     <NULL>          
#   9 8     8     <NULL> 
```


I thought `nest()` is taking factors `as.numeric()` and "getting confused" when different variables present same-named groups. But then I tried:

```
mtcars %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  select(cyl, carb, mpg) %>%  
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl) %>% as.numeric(),
         carb = factor(carb) %>% as.numeric()) %>% 
  group_by(cyl, carb) %>% 
  nest()
```

and got the same result as when nesting with non-factorial variables:

```
# A tibble: 9 x 3
# cyl  carb data            
# <dbl> <dbl> <list>          
#   1     2     4 <tibble [4 x 1]>
#   2     1     1 <tibble [5 x 1]>
#   3     2     1 <tibble [2 x 1]>
#   4     3     2 <tibble [4 x 1]>
#   5     3     4 <tibble [6 x 1]>
#   6     1     2 <tibble [6 x 1]>
#   7     3     3 <tibble [3 x 1]>
#   8     2     5 <tibble [1 x 1]>
#   9     3     6 <tibble [1 x 1]>
```

Compare with:

```
mtcars %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  select(cyl, carb, mpg) %>% 
  group_by(cyl, carb) %>% 
  nest()

# A tibble: 9 x 3
# cyl  carb data            
# <dbl> <dbl> <list>          
#   1     6     4 <tibble [4 x 1]>
#   2     4     1 <tibble [5 x 1]>
#   3     6     1 <tibble [2 x 1]>
#   4     8     2 <tibble [4 x 1]>
#   5     8     4 <tibble [6 x 1]>
#   6     4     2 <tibble [6 x 1]>
#   7     8     3 <tibble [3 x 1]>
#   8     6     6 <tibble [1 x 1]>
#   9     8     8 <tibble [1 x 1]>
```

Since my code used to work fine until last month, I wonder if `tidyr` was updated lately and the way of handling factor groups by `nest()` was changed?

Is it generally advisable not to nest data grouped by factor variables or rather not to `group_by()` on factor variables?

In the [issue ](https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/issues/554) mentioned by aosmith (stackoverflow), @hadley references to **`group_nest()`** which seems to resolve the problem (but it reorders the tibble!). Nevertheless, I still wonder why `nest()` is producing `NULL`...

```
mtcars %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  select(cyl, carb, mpg) %>% 
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl),
         carb = factor(carb)) %>% 
  group_by(cyl, carb) %>%
  group_nest() %>% 
  unnest %>% 
  all.equal(.,
            mtcars %>% 
              as_tibble() %>% 
              select(cyl, carb, mpg) %>% 
              mutate(cyl = factor(cyl),
                     carb = factor(carb)))

# [1] TRUE
```

title: gather() not able to properly handle direct referencing of cols from tibble's new name repair
description:
It looks like `gather()` is having some issues with the column names that come out of the name repair used in `tibble` 2.0.0+ (e.g., renaming `""` to `..1`, `..2`, etc):

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

x <- tibble(`..1` = 1, 
            `..2` = 2,
            x3 = 3)

# Gathering without specific reference works

x %>%
  gather(key = "col_name", 
         value = "value")
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   col_name value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>
#> 1 ..1          1
#> 2 ..2          2
#> 3 x3           3

# Gathering specifically referencing `..` colnames does not work

x %>%
  gather(key = "col_name", 
         value = "value",
         `..1`, `..2`, x3)
#> Error in .f(.x[[i]], ...): ..1 used in an incorrect context, no ... to look in

# But gathering specifically referencing non - `..` colnames does work

y <- tibble(x1 = 1,
            x2 = 2,
            x3 = 3)

y %>%
  gather(key = "col_name", 
         value = "value",
         x1, x2, x3)
#> # A tibble: 3 x 2
#>   col_name value
#>   <chr>    <dbl>
#> 1 x1           1
#> 2 x2           2
#> 3 x3           3
```

title: Order of columns causes nest() to drop some nests in the "data" list
description:
Trying to create a simple nesting of a tibble produces NULL in some of the produced `data` list.
---
This seems to only happen if, as in the example below, one of the variables we are nesting on (i.e., `z` below) is a factor. In the below example, if we move the factor `z` to be before `y` (the other variable we are nesting on) causes the second row to have a NULL.

Expected behavior: both approaches should produce the same output irrespective of column order in data.

Version: tidyr 0.8.2

```r
> tibble(x = letters[1:10], y = rep(1:2, each = 5), z = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:2], each = 5))) %>% nest(x)
# A tibble: 2 x 3
      y z     data            
  <int> <fct> <list>          
1     1 A     <tibble [5 × 1]>
2     2 B     <NULL>          
> tibble(x = letters[1:10], z = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:2], each = 5)), y = rep(1:2, each = 5)) %>% nest(x)
# A tibble: 2 x 3
  z         y data            
  <fct> <int> <list>          
1 A         1 <tibble [5 × 1]>
2 B         2 <tibble [5 × 1]>
```

title: problems with nesting by a factor when some levels are not present
description:
This works fine:
```r
library(tidyverse)
mtcars %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(cyl2 = factor(cyl, c(4L, 6L, 8L))) %>% nest(-cyl2)
## # A tibble: 3 x 2
##   cyl2  data              
##   <fct> <list>            
## 1 6     <tibble [7 x 11]> 
## 2 4     <tibble [11 x 11]>
## 3 8     <tibble [14 x 11]>
```
However, this does not:
```r
mtcars %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(cyl2 = factor(cyl, c(2L, 4L, 6L, 8L))) %>% nest(-cyl2) 
## # A tibble: 3 x 2
##   cyl2  data              
##   <fct> <list>            
## 1 6     <tibble [14 x 11]>
## 2 4     <tibble [7 x 11]> 
## 3 8     <NULL>  
```
When there are additional levels in a factor for which there is no data, attempting to nest by this factor introduces `NULL` values. Even worse, the nesting IDs do not match what actually gets nested:
```r
mtcars %>% as_tibble() %>% mutate(cyl2 = factor(cyl, c(2L, 4L, 6L, 8L))) %>% nest(-cyl2) %>% slice(1) %>% unnest(data)
```

Note that `cyl` and `cyl2` do not match in the second case.

title: Add type-based replacement option to replace_na.data.frame
description:
I am suggesting that type-based replacement be added as an option to `replace_na.data.frame` method. Specifically, in addition to being able pass a list of variable names and replacement values to the `replace` parameter, add functionality to pass a list of variable types and replacement values.

I think this is useful because I, and I assume other users, have use cases where they may have too many variables to list individually and have different replacement values dependent on variable type.

Below is an example of what I am talking about.

---

Assume we have `tbl` as:

```r
tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  w = c(1L, 2L, NA), 
  x = c("A", "B", NA), 
  y = c(TRUE, FALSE, NA), 
  z = c(1, 2, NA)
) 

> tbl
# A tibble: 3 x 4
      w x     y         z
  <int> <chr> <lgl> <dbl>
1     1 A     TRUE      1
2     2 B     FALSE     2
3    NA NA    NA       NA
```

And we want to replace `NA` values based on variable type using something like:

```r
new_tbl <- replace_na.data.frame(
  tbl,
  replace = list("integer" = 0L, "character" = "none", "double" = 0, "logical" = FALSE), 
  by_type = TRUE
)
```

And we return: 

```r
> new_tbl
# A tibble: 3 x 4
      w x     y         z
  <int> <chr> <lgl> <dbl>
1     1 A     TRUE      1
2     2 B     FALSE     2
3     0 none  FALSE     0
```

---

If you feel this may be a useful addition, I am happy to make a pull request following the guidelines (styling, tests, etc.). I have written the following as a possible design/implementation:

```r
replace_na.data.frame <- function(data, replace = list(), by_type = FALSE, ...) {
  stopifnot(is_list(replace))
  
  if (!by_type) {
    replace_vars <- intersect(names(replace), names(data))
    
    for (var in replace_vars) {
      check_replacement(replace[[var]], var)
      data[[var]][!is_complete(data[[var]])] <- replace[[var]]
    }
    
  } else {
    replace_types <- intersect(lapply(data, typeof), names(replace))
    replace_vars <- names(data)[lapply(data, typeof) %in% replace_types]
    
    for (var in replace_vars) {
      for (type in replace_types) {
        if (typeof(data[[var]]) == type) {
          check_replacement(replace[[type]], type)
          data[[var]][!is_complete(data[[var]])] <- replace[[type]]
        }
      }
    }
  }
  
  data
}
```

Any feedback on the above would be greatly appreciated. I want to ensure consistency in design and implementation, so I am definitely very flexible on both.

title: Column names differ depending on the version of R using spread
description:
I'm getting different column names depending on the R version installed starting with 3.5.0 when using `spread`.

```r

xmlforecast <- xml2::read_xml("ftp://ftp.bom.gov.au/anon/gen/fwo/IDQ11295.xml")

areas <-
  xml2::xml_find_all(xmlforecast, ".//*[@type='location']")
xml2::xml_find_all(areas, ".//*[@type='forecast_icon_code']") %>%
  xml2::xml_remove()

extract_values <- function(y) {
  values <- xml2::xml_children(y)
  attrs <- unlist(as.character(xml2::xml_attrs(values)))
  values <- unlist(as.character(xml2::xml_contents(values)))
  
  time_period <- unlist(t(as.data.frame(xml2::xml_attrs(y))))
  time_period <-
    time_period[rep(seq_len(nrow(time_period)), each = length(attrs)), ]
  
  sub_out <- cbind(time_period, attrs, values)
  row.names(sub_out) <- NULL
  return(sub_out)
}

parse_areas <- function(x) {
  aac <- as.character(xml2::xml_attr(x, "aac"))
  
  # get xml children for the forecast (there are seven of these for each area)
  forecast_periods <- xml2::xml_children(x)
  
  sub_qld <-
    lapply(X = forecast_periods, FUN = extract_values)
  sub_qld <- do.call(rbind, sub_qld)
  sub_qld <- cbind(aac, sub_qld)
  return(sub_qld)
}

qld <- lapply(X = areas, FUN = parse_areas)
qld <- as.data.frame(do.call("rbind", qld))

names(qld)

qld <- tidyr::spread(qld, key = attrs, value = values)

names(qld)
```

With R 3.4.3 the names are:
```r
c("aac", "index", "start-time-local", "end-time-local", "start-time-utc", 
"end-time-utc", "\"air_temperature_maximum\", \"Celsius\"", "\"air_temperature_minimum\", \"Celsius\"", 
"precipitation_range", "precis", "probability_of_precipitation"
)
```

And with R 3.5.0 the names are

```r
c("aac", "index", "start-time-local", "end-time-local", "start-time-utc", 
"end-time-utc", "type = \"air_temperature_maximum\", units = \"Celsius\"", 
"type = \"air_temperature_minimum\", units = \"Celsius\"", "precipitation_range", 
"precis", "probability_of_precipitation")
```

It appears to be platform independent.

I've written a check into the function to overcome this issue, https://github.com/ropensci/bomrang/blob/devel/R/get_precis_forecast.R#L239, is there something more appropriate?

title: fill() `...` description is misleading
description:
According to the docs, `fill()` supposedly fills on all columns if none are selected. But this is not the case:

``` r
library(tidyr)

df <- data.frame(Month = 1:5, Year = c(2000, rep(NA, 4)))
fill(df)
#>   Month Year
#> 1     1 2000
#> 2     2   NA
#> 3     3   NA
#> 4     4   NA
#> 5     5   NA

fill(df, Year)
#>   Month Year
#> 1     1 2000
#> 2     2 2000
#> 3     3 2000
#> 4     4 2000
#> 5     5 2000
```

Created on 2018-08-07 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

It is written this way because it inherits that parameter from `gather()`, which does select all if none are specified.

I like the idea of filling all columns if none are specified, so maybe you could use the following.

``` r
fill2 <- function (data, ..., .direction = c("down", "up")) 
{
  quos <- rlang::quos(...)
  if(rlang::is_empty(quos)) {
    fill_cols <- names(data)
  } else {
    fill_cols <- unname(tidyselect::vars_select(names(data), !!! quos))
  }
  
  .direction <- match.arg(.direction)
  fillVector <- switch(.direction, down = tidyr:::fillDown, up = tidyr:::fillUp)
  for (col in fill_cols) {
    data[[col]] <- fillVector(data[[col]])
  }
  data
}

df <- data.frame(Month = 1:5, Year = c(2000, rep(NA, 4)))
fill2(df)
#>   Month Year
#> 1     1 2000
#> 2     2 2000
#> 3     3 2000
#> 4     4 2000
#> 5     5 2000
```

Here's the clean version without `::`'s.

<details>

```r
fill.data.frame <- function (data, ..., .direction = c("down", "up")) 
{
  quos <- quos(...)
  if(is_empty(quos)) {
    fill_cols <- names(data)
  } else {
    fill_cols <- unname(tidyselect::vars_select(names(data), !!! quos))
  }
  
  .direction <- match.arg(.direction)
  fillVector <- switch(.direction, down = fillDown, up = fillUp)
  for (col in fill_cols) {
    data[[col]] <- fillVector(data[[col]])
  }
  data
}
```

</details>

title: crossing() removes NA from factor levels
description:
``` r
library(tidyr)
packageVersion("tidyr")
#> [1] '0.8.0.9000'
x_fac <- factor(c(1, NA), exclude = NULL)
levels(x_fac)
#> [1] "1" NA
x_cross <- crossing(x_fac)
levels(x_cross$x_fac)
#> [1] "1"
```

The root of this seems to be in `ulevels()`:
```r
ulevels(factor(c(1, NA), exclude = NULL))
#> [1] 1    <NA>
#> Levels: 1
```

Adding `exclude = NULL` in `factor()` inside `ulevels()` solves the issue (and passes all current tests).

If this is an unintended behavior, I am ready to make a PR.

In a few separate occasions I've been dealing with dataframes like the following:

title: Clean up json key-value pair columns
description:
It's fairly common to receive a CSV where one of the data elements is a character string which actually represents JSON text. This case comes up frequently when sourcing data from a NoSQL database or an RDBMS like PostreSQL that supports json/jsonb as a native column type.

In these scenarios, it'd be convenient to be able to transform the json text into a data.frame without using the other elements of the original CSV. In some ways, this is a classic unnest() problem where each value in a column actually represents multiple columns or rows of data.

This was first reported by @earino on Twitter:
https://twitter.com/earino/status/968544763430387712

Some complications to note: most JSON will not likely be a simple key-value pair set and contain several levels of nested attributes.

IMO the "right" approach would `unnest` the JSON resulting in "long" data, where the key-value pairs result in key-value columns. The user can choose to `spread` from there.

title: complete() on factors with NA level
description:
`complete()` produces a warning and converts your factor to a character vector if you call it on a factor with an explicit `NA` level:

```r
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

tibble(a = factor("x",
                  levels = c("x", "y", NA),
                  exclude = NULL)) %>%
    complete(a)
#> Warning: Column `a` joining factors with different levels, coercing to
#> character vector
#> # A tibble: 3 x 1
#>   a    
#>   <chr>
#> 1 x    
#> 2 y    
#> 3 <NA>
```

I'm not sure yet whether it's a good idea to have `NA` as a level in my factor in the first place, but this doesn't seem right.

title: Allow separate to fill with specified value
description: Currently, if you are separating into n columns but you have fewer than n separated items, you have to choose between warning the user, filling in from the left or filling in from the right. It would be nice to be able to avoid the warning and specify to fill with NA, or 0, "whatever"... or whatever. Is there a reason this isn't the current functionality?

title: Enhancing complete/expand to work with tables in database
description:
It would be really great to use the complete verb with a data.frame that is sitting in database.

such as:

```
total_counts = tbl(con, 'SOMETHING.TOTALCOUNTS')
total_counts %>%
  complete(Race, Gender, SmokingStatus, fill = list(num_total = 0))
```

Right now it throws the error:

```
Error in UseMethod("complete_") : no applicable method for 'complete_' applied to an object of class "c('tbl_dbi', 'tbl_sql', 'tbl_lazy', 'tbl')"
```

title: Different behavior for nest
description:
Here, the first three codes produce the same desired output (`iris` nested by `Species`) whereas the fourth one doesn't.

```
library(tidyverse)

iris %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  nest()

iris %>% 
  group_by(Species) %>% 
  nest()

iris %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  nest(-Species)

iris %>% 
  nest(-Species)
```

```
> identical(nest(as_tibble(iris), -Species), nest(group_by(iris, Species)))
[1] TRUE
> identical(nest(as_tibble(iris), -Species), nest(iris, -Species))
[1] FALSE
```

title: FR: separate() not a character but a vector
description:
There is a great tidyr::separate() function. I couldn't find a similar function in tidyverse when the target column is a list of vectors, not a character. The best way to solve it [that I found](https://community.rstudio.com/t/split-a-column-each-element-is-a-vector-to-multiple-columns/14009)  isn't obvious and quite complex

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
tribble(
    ~a,
    1:3,
    1:3 * 10) %>%
    `[<-`(, c('d', 'e', 'f'), map(transpose(.$a), unlist))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>   a             d     e     f
#>   <list>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 <int [3]>     1     2     3
#> 2 <dbl [3]>    10    20    30
```

It could be a special case of ```separate(sep = NULL)``` and I think it is a very intuitive name for the function but probably is a messy design decision. 
Such a function requires a complement version as ```unite()```

title: Performance of nest-map-unnest idiom
description:
*@danilinares commented on Oct 1, 2018, 1:18 PM UTC:*

I posted this question in StackOverflow that I think it might be of your interest:

[https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52591801/programming-using-the-tidyverse-speed-issues?noredirect=1#comment92118537_52591801](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/52591801/programming-using-the-tidyverse-speed-issues?noredirect=1#comment92118537_52591801)

We released the package quickpsy a few years ago (paper in the R journal paper). The package used R base functions, but also made an extensive use of functions of what was called at that time the Hadleyverse. We are now developing a new version of the package that mostly uses functions from the tidyverse and that incorporates the new non-standard evaluation approach and found that the package is much much slower (more than four times slower). We found for example that purrr::map is much slower than dplyr::do (which is deprecated):

library(tidyverse)

system.time(
mtcars %>%
group_by(cyl) %>%
do(head(., 2))
)

system.time(
mtcars %>%
group_by(cyl) %>%
nest() %>%
mutate(temp = map(data, ~head(., 2))) %>%
unnest(temp)
)
We also found that functions like pull are very slow.

We are not sure whether the tidyverse is not meant to be used for this type of programming or we are not using it properly.

*This issue was moved by [lionel-](https://github.com/lionel-) from [tidyverse/purrr#555](https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/555).*

title: nest() looses group_by() groups
description:
Apparently, using `tidyr::nest()` let's the `data.frame` forget it's grouping variables (see my [SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/53855897/4139249)). I'm not sure if this _is_ an issue, I just thought I'd post this here (my question [has been answered on SO](https://stackoverflow.com/a/53856537/4139249)).


``` r
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tidyr)

mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  nest() %>%
  groups()
#> NULL

```
The groups are gone. In order to use the grouping variables within a `map()` function call, for example, I need to reset the groups again. 

``` r
mtcars %>% 
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  nest() %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  mutate(wt_mean = map_dbl(data,~mean(.x$wt)/cyl))
#> # A tibble: 3 x 3
#> # Groups:   cyl [3]
#>     cyl data               wt_mean
#>   <dbl> <list>               <dbl>
#> 1     6 <tibble [7 x 10]>    0.520
#> 2     4 <tibble [11 x 10]>   0.571
#> 3     8 <tibble [14 x 10]>   0.500

Created on 2018-12-20 by the [reprex package](http://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.0).

```

title: complete() sets some decimal values to NA()
description:
Hi together,

I started a [discussion in the RStudio community forum](https://community.rstudio.com/t/complete-sets-some-values-to-na/16547/5) since I spotted an unusual behavior of `complete()`. Here is a reproducible example:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
dat <- tibble(group = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"), 
              beta = c(0.012, 0.013, 0.014, 0.012, 0.013, 0.014), 
              D = c(0.174, 0.16, 0.158, 0.204, 0.182, 0.164))
dat
#> # A tibble: 6 x 3
#>   group  beta     D
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 A     0.012 0.174
#> 2 A     0.013 0.16 
#> 3 A     0.014 0.158
#> 4 B     0.012 0.204
#> 5 B     0.013 0.182
#> 6 B     0.014 0.164
dat %>% complete(nesting(group), beta = full_seq(beta, 0.0005, tol = 5*1e-03))
#> # A tibble: 10 x 3
#>    group   beta      D
#>    <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 A     0.012   0.174
#>  2 A     0.0125 NA    
#>  3 A     0.013  NA    
#>  4 A     0.0135 NA    
#>  5 A     0.014   0.158
#>  6 B     0.012   0.204
#>  7 B     0.0125 NA    
#>  8 B     0.013  NA    
#>  9 B     0.0135 NA    
#> 10 B     0.014   0.164
```

<sup>Created on 2018-10-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>

Note that, beside the NA's which are introduced correctly for each intermediate step (i.e. 0.0125 and 0.0135), the values for 0.013 were set to NA as well. 

A workaround is to get rid of decimal numbers by multiplying the original D values and transforming them back afterwards:

``` r
library(tidyverse)
dat <- tibble(group = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B"), 
              beta = c(0.012, 0.013, 0.014, 0.012, 0.013, 0.014), 
              D = c(0.174, 0.16, 0.158, 0.204, 0.182, 0.164))
dat %>%  
    complete(nesting(group), beta = full_seq(beta*1e3, 0.0005*1e3) / 1e3)
#> # A tibble: 10 x 3
#>    group   beta      D
#>    <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#>  1 A     0.012   0.174
#>  2 A     0.0125 NA    
#>  3 A     0.013   0.16 
#>  4 A     0.0135 NA    
#>  5 A     0.014   0.158
#>  6 B     0.012   0.204
#>  7 B     0.0125 NA    
#>  8 B     0.013   0.182
#>  9 B     0.0135 NA    
#> 10 B     0.014   0.164
```

<sup>Created on 2018-10-18 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.2.1)</sup>


We couldn't not find the source of this behaviour but from my point of view it is an important issue since it might silently remove values from your data set.

EDIT: Might be related to [issue #2432 of dplyr](https://github.com/tidyverse/dplyr/issues/2432)

title: In separate an into= column name can be NA to not generate that column
description:
In the example below, modified from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48255809/to-change-tabular-data-to-a-different-format-in-r/48256012#48256012 , the `X` column is a junk column that just contains the second underscore delimiter for those rows that have it.  If the `separate` statement would allow `NA` or `""`, say, as a column name with the meaning _do not generate a column for that component_ then the `select(-X)` could have been omitted and the `separate` statement would become `separate(variable, c("CurveGroup", NA, "suffix"), sep = 5:6, fill = "right")` .  Not only would this reduce the code by one line but it would also eliminate the need to generate a junk name for a column that is subsequently dropped.

```
DF <- structure(list(pos = 1:2, BZ_SP = c(-300000L, 0L), BZ_SP_m1 = c(2L, 
  0L), BZ_SP_m2 = c(3L, 0L), CL_SP = c(2540544L, -118621L), CL_SP_m1 = c(1L, 
  3L), CL_SP_m2 = c(2L, 4L)), .Names = c("pos", "BZ_SP", "BZ_SP_m1", 
  "BZ_SP_m2", "CL_SP", "CL_SP_m1", "CL_SP_m2"), 
  class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, -2L))

DF
##   pos   BZ_SP BZ_SP_m1 BZ_SP_m2   CL_SP CL_SP_m1 CL_SP_m2
## 1   1 -300000        2        3 2540544        1        2
## 2   2       0        0        0 -118621        3        4

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

DF %>%
   gather(variable, value, -pos) %>% 
   separate(variable, c("CurveGroup", "X", "suffix"), sep = 5:6, fill = "right") %>% 
   select(-X) %>%
   spread(suffix, value)
```

giving:

```
  pos CurveGroup      V1 m1 m2
1   1      BZ_SP -300000  2  3
2   1      CL_SP 2540544  1  2
3   2      BZ_SP       0  0  0
4   2      CL_SP -118621  3  4

```

title: gather_if (feature request)
description:
I want `gather_if()` in order to gather columns of a certain type (e.g., numeric).
Here is my implementation of `gather_if()` based on `select_if()` .

```r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(rlang)

gather_if <- function(data, .predicate, key = "key", value = "value", ..., na.rm = FALSE, convert = FALSE, factor_key = FALSE) {
  vars <- dplyr:::tbl_if_vars(data, .predicate, rlang:::caller_env(), .include_group_vars = TRUE)
  gather(data = data, key = key, value = value, vars, ..., na.rm = na.rm, convert = convert, factor_key = factor_key)
}
```

Testing `gather_if()`

title: create a spread function for multiple variables
description:
I often have to do a spread over more than one variable.
I've found [this](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/29775461/how-can-i-spread-repeated-measures-of-multiple-variables-into-wide-format) stackoverflow question that does solves this problem for me.
I was wondering why the spread function doesn't allow this or why there isn't a spread_at function.
Below I've written a function that works for me:

```
##' Spread a key-multiple values pair across multiple columns
##' 
##' 
##' @param .data a data frame.
##' @param key the column that will be spread
##' @param value the columns that are collected
##' @return the new dataframe
##' @author Robert Reijntjes \email{r.reijntjes@lumc.nl}
##' @references \url{https://stackoverflow.com/questions/29775461/how-can-i-spread-repeated-measures-of-multiple-variables-into-wide-format}
##' @examples 
##' set.seed(10)
##' dat <- data_frame(
##'   Person = rep(c("greg", "sally", "sue"), each=2),
##'   Time = rep(c("Pre", "Post"), 3),
##'   Score1 = round(rnorm(6, mean = 80, sd=4), 0),
##'   Score2 = round(jitter(Score1, 15), 0),
##'   Score3 = 5 + (Score1 + Score2)/2
##' )
##' dat2=dat %>% spread_at(Time, c(Score1,Score2,Score3))
##' dat2=dat %>% spread(Time, starts_with("Score"))
##' @keywords summary
##' @export
spread_at <- function(data,key,value, fill = NA, convert = FALSE,
                           drop = TRUE)
{
  key_enq = enquo(key)
  value_enq = enquo(value)
  if (length(value_enq)==1) {
    data=data %>% spread_(key,value, fill, convert, drop)
  } else {
    data=data %>% gather(gatKey,gatVal,!!value_enq) %>%
      unite(uniteKey,c(!!key_enq,gatKey),sep="_") %>%
      spread(uniteKey,gatVal, fill, convert, drop)
  }
  data
}
```

title: Feature Request: separate_rows() to support fill for unequal length vectors
description:
He

This one here works nicely. 

```r
df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:3,
  y = c("a", "d,e,f", "g,h"),
  z = c("1", "2,3,4", "5,6"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

separate_rows(df, y, z, convert = TRUE)
```

however that here fails (uneven on the first element):


```r
df <- data.frame(
  x = 1:3,
  y = c("a", "d,e,f", "g,h"),
  z = c("1,2", "2,3,4", "5,6"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

separate_rows(df, y, z, convert = TRUE)
```

It would be really helpful if `separate_rows()` could get an option to handle uneven length vectors in the separate columns like the `separate()` function wich handles uneven lengths just filling up.

All the best

title: Allow unnest with list columns of differing lengths?
description:

If the user requests an unnesting of one list column from a dataframe with multiple, `unnest` will fail if the number of elements differs. Would it be possible for `unnest` to copy the other list columns, just as it copies values from standard, atomic columns?

In particular, the current behavior means `unnest` doesn't work with `sf` data, since the `geometry` column is already a list column. 

```r

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf")) %>% 
  slice(1:3) %>%
  select(NAME) %>%
  mutate(y = strsplit(c("a", "d,e,f", "g,h"), ","))

nc
```

title: Performance issue when nesting dates
description:
I find that nesting data that contains dates is quite slow and I get a major performance improvement by "manually" nesting the first of two groups using a loop.

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
tmp <- crossing(a = 1:30,
                b = 1:30,
                value = as_date(1:1000)) 

# This first one is an indirect way
# to nest the data.frame
system.time({
  tmp2 <- map(unique(tmp$a), function(.a){
    tmp %>% 
      filter(a == .a) %>% 
      group_by(a, b) %>% 
      nest()
  }) %>% 
    bind_rows()
})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    1.69    0.04    1.73
                                        
# This is much slower
system.time({
  tmp3 <- 
    tmp %>% 
    group_by(a, b) %>% 
    nest()
})
#>    user  system elapsed 
#>    3.70    1.73    5.58
                                        
identical(tmp2, tmp3)                   
#> [1] TRUE
```

I find that the crunching time increases linearly for both the usual and "manual" nesting methods; as in, the gap continues to widen.

title: Column type disappears in a nested empty tibble
description:
Let's say we have this `tibble`

```r
cats_and_dogs <- tibble(
    animal = c("dog", "dog", "cat", "cat"), 
    name = c("Bailey", "Lucy", "Tigger", "Chloe"),
    age = c(9, 4, 7, 2)
    )
```
We can easily obtain the nested version with `nest`
```r
by_animal <- nest(cats_and_dogs, -animal)

print(by_animal)
#  A tibble: 2 x 2
#   animal             data
#    <chr>           <list>
# 1    dog <tibble [2 x 2]>
# 2    cat <tibble [2 x 2]>

print(by_animal$data[[1]])
#  A tibble: 2 x 2
#     name   age
#    <chr> <dbl>
# 1 Bailey     9
# 2   Lucy     4
```

In this case all the column types are preserved. This is not the case when we handle an empty `tibble` (but with types defined for each column).

```r
cats_and_dogs_empty <- tibble(
    animal = character(),
    name = character(),
    age = double()
)

by_animal_empty <- nest(cats_and_dogs_empty, -animal)

print(by_animal_empty)
#  A tibble: 0 x 2
#  ... with 2 variables: animal <chr>, data <list>

print(by_animal_empty$data)
# list()
```
While I would have expected that the type of the nested columns would have been preserved like
```r
# A tibble: 0 x 2
# ... with 2 variables: name <chr>, age <dbl>
```
I am not sure if this kind of behavior is in the scope of `tidyr` but I believe it is pretty useful for large legacy code development where types can be important.

title: Behavior of empty nest call without groups.
description:
By default, `nest` operates on all non-grouped columns. Therefore, these are equivalent:

```
mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% nest()

mtcars %>% group_by(cyl) %>% nest(everything())
```

Without grouping, I would therefore expect to get a 1x1 tibble with the complete data in that cell. Instead it returns the original dataframe with a `data` filled with 1x0 tables. These are therefore not equivalent:

```
mtcars %>% nest()

mtcars %>% nest(everything())
```

This can be inconvenient in programming when a grouping of `NULL` can be supplied (i.e. no grouping).

Would it make sense to by default always nest all non-grouping variables?

title: Function for un-nesting column-embedded data.frames
description:
Is there space in tidyr for an `unnest_df()` function, equivalent to `unnest()` for embedded data.frames (like those obtained via jsonlite)?

```
require(jsonlite); require(tidyverse)

unnest_df = function(x, keep_parent_names = TRUE){
  df_cols = sapply(x, class) == 'data.frame'
  cmnd = paste('cbind(', paste0(paste0('x[,', 1:ncol(x), ifelse(!df_cols, ', drop=FALSE]', ']')), collapse=', '), ')')
  d = eval(parse(text = cmnd))
  if(!keep_parent_names) return(d)
  f = !names(d) %in% names(x)
  names(d)[f] = paste0(rep(names(x)[df_cols], unlist(sapply(x, ncol))), '.', names(d)[f])
  d
}

j = '[{
"date": "2017-06-12T00:00:00",
"pets": { "cats": 13, "dogs": 5 },
"colour": "red",
```

title: complete() does not use factor levels if no data
description:
complete() has behavior advertised as follows: 

> For factors, the full set of levels (not just those that appear in the data) are used.

However, this seems to only be the case so long as you have at least one record.  A few workarounds are less than optimal in my opinion, and it would be quite helpful for this functionality to work with an empty data.frame
 
```
options <- factor(c('a','b','c'))

df <- data.frame(column=character(), column2=character()) 
levels(df$column) <- options; levels(df$column2) <- options;

## Does not work - though I would expect it to
df %>% complete(column, column2)

## Works - nice if you have options readily available
df %>% complete(column=options, column2=options)

## Works - based on factors, and a bit tedious
df %>% complete(column=factor(levels(column),levels=levels(column)),column2=factor(levels(column),levels=levels(column)))



## With data, things work fine:
df <- data.frame(column=c('a'),column2=c('b'))
levels(df$column) <- options; levels(df$column2) <- options;

## Does not work above - works here
df %>% complete(column, column2)
```

title: separate() right edge fixed position splitting is off by 1
description:
According to the documentation for the `sep` argument:

> If numeric, interpreted as positions to split at. Positive values start at 1 at the far-left of the string; negative value start at -1 at the far-right of the string.

However, to split the right-most character into a new column, `sep`must be set to -2. Reproducible example:

```
library(tidyverse)

df <- expand.grid(group = c("alpha", "beta"),
                  dimension = c(1, 2),
                  stringsAsFactors = F) %>%
        tbl_df() %>%
        mutate(gr_dim = paste0(group, dimension))


# splits the one left most character
df %>%
  separate(gr_dim, sep = 1, into = c("gr", "dim"))

# creates two columns, one of which is the original column, the other blank
df %>%
  separate(gr_dim, sep = -1, into = c("gr", "dim"))

# splits the two left-most characters
df %>%
  separate(gr_dim, sep = 2, into = c("gr", "dim"))

# splits the one right-most character
df %>%
  separate(gr_dim, sep = -2, into = c("gr", "dim"))
```

title: spread with bit64::integer64 fails with missing combination
description:
There is problem with integer64 vector (from bit64 package, but originated in data retrieved via odbc package) and tidyr::spread.
 
Missing values are replaced by large value.
 
It's related to known (?) behavior of bit64 package, e.g.: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/21627741/fread-fails-with-missing-values-in-integer64-columns
or bit64 package documentation:

> further limitations
> • subscripting non-existing elements and subscripting with NAs is currently not supported. Such
> subscripting currently returns 9218868437227407266 instead of NA (the NA value of the underlying
> double code). Following the full R behaviour here would either destroy performance
> or require extensive C-coding. 
 
```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(bit64))

ex_df <- data_frame(id = c(1, 1, 2, 2), var = c("A", "B", "A", "B"), val = as.integer64(1:4))

ex_df
#> # A tibble: 4 x 3
#>      id   var             val
#>   <dbl> <chr> <S3: integer64>
#> 1     1     A               1
#> 2     1     B               2
#> 3     2     A               3
#> 4     2     B               4

# With all combination it's ok
ex_df %>% spread(var, val)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id               A               B
#> * <dbl> <S3: integer64> <S3: integer64>
#> 1     1               1               2
#> 2     2               3               4

# after removing one of them isn't ok:
ex_df %>% slice(-1) %>% spread(var, val)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id                   A               B
#> * <dbl>     <S3: integer64> <S3: integer64>
#> 1     1 9218868437227407266               2
#> 2     2                   3               4

# forcing fill doesn't change anything
ex_df %>% slice(-1) %>% spread(var, val, fill = as.integer64(0))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id                   A               B
#> * <dbl>     <S3: integer64> <S3: integer64>
#> 1     1 9218868437227407266               2
#> 2     2                   3               4

# NA in data stays NA:
ex_df %>% slice(-1) %>% mutate(val = na_if(val, 4)) %>% spread(var, val)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 3
#>      id                   A               B
#> * <dbl>     <S3: integer64> <S3: integer64>
#> 1     1 9218868437227407266               2
#> 2     2                   3              NA
```

title: Selecting columns in gather dependent on vector class
description:
When selecting columns with a data expression, a warning is given when using `c(x, y)`, but not when using an `x:y` expression.

Using the example from the help page:

```R
library(dplyr)
# From http://stackoverflow.com/questions/1181060
stocks <- tibble(
  time = as.Date('2009-01-01') + 0:9,
  X = rnorm(10, 0, 1),
  Y = rnorm(10, 0, 2),
  Z = rnorm(10, 0, 4)
)
```

Then using the first form gives a warning:

```R
stocks %>% gather(stock, price, c(2,3,4))
```

> Warning message:
In if (!is.finite(x)) return(FALSE) :
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used

While using the second one, results in no warnings:

```R
stocks %>% gather(stock, price, 2:4)
```

As far as I can tell, the only difference is the class of the vector specifying the columns: being a numeric vector in the first case and a more specific integer vector in the second one.

title: Column silently dropped when its name conflicts with value col name in gather.data.frame()
description:
`gather.data.frame()` computes which columns to gather using [this snippet](https://github.com/tidyverse/tidyr/blob/master/R/gather.R#L110).

```r
  quos <- quos(...)
  if (is_empty(quos)) {
    gather_vars <- setdiff(names(data), c(key_var, value_var))
  } else {
    gather_vars <- unname(tidyselect::vars_select(names(data), !!! quos))
  }
```

When the user doesn't provide a `...` argument, the gather columns are computed to be anything that's not `key` or `value`. This logic works when there's no existing column having the same name as `value`. If there is, that column would be silently dropped from the gathering.

I've produced a simple reprex below to illustrate.

``` r
packageVersion("tidyr")
#> [1] '0.7.0'

library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

XYZ <- data.frame(
  X = rnorm(2, 0, 1),
  Y = rnorm(2, 0, 2),
  Z = rnorm(2, 0, 4)
)

gather(XYZ, name, value)
#>   name      value
#> 1    X  0.1051179
#> 2    X  1.4617993
#> 3    Y -0.9121167
#> 4    Y  2.5378557
#> 5    Z -2.1496032
#> 6    Z -2.4815070

gather(XYZ, name, Y)
#>            Y name          Y
#> 1 -0.9121167    X  0.1051179
#> 2  2.5378557    X  1.4617993
#> 3 -0.9121167    Z -2.1496032
#> 4  2.5378557    Z -2.4815070
```

``` r
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(tibble)

berries <- fruit[31:33]
tibble(berries) %>%

#> 1        fig  <NA>
```

title: Add unfill(), the inverse of the fill() function
description:
Here’s a request for an `unfill()` function, which should do the inverse of what `fill()` does. This is useful for formatting data frames for final output, where one often wants to avoid repeating values (see http://blog.darkhorseanalytics.com/clear-off-the-table for a nice illustration).

For example, it should turn `x` into `x_blank` (here NA values are shown as empty cells):

```
 x  x_blank
 A  A
 A        
 A        
 B  B
 B        
 C  C
```

Here’s a proof-of-concept implementation that works on _vectors_:

``` r
unfill_vec = function(x, direction = c("down", "up")) {
  if (direction[1] == "down") {
    x[which(x[-1] == x[1:(length(x) - 1)]) + 1] = NA
  } else {
    x = rev(unfill(rev(x), direction = "down"))
  }
  x
}
```

For the tibble `df = tibble(x=c("A","A","A","B","B","C","C"))`, running `df %>% unfill(x)` should give the same output as:

``` r
df %>% mutate(x = unfill_vec(x))
```

Note that ‘unfilling’ is **not** the same as simple ’deduplication’, as shown here:

``` r
df2 = tibble(x = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "C", "C", "A"))
df2 %>% mutate(x_unfill = unfill_vec(x),
               x_dedup = ifelse(!duplicated(x), x, NA))
```

This results in:

```
      x x_unfill x_dedup
  <chr>    <chr>   <chr>
1     A        A       A
2     A     <NA>    <NA>
3     A     <NA>    <NA>
4     B        B       B
5     B     <NA>    <NA>
6     C        C       C
7     C     <NA>    <NA>
8     A        A    <NA>
```

‘Unfilling’ is really a type of _untidying_, so perhaps there’s a better package than `tidyr` for it? On the other hand, `tidyr` _does_ contain `spread()`, which is also an untidying function and the inverse of `gather()`.

title: Issue with complete and grouped_df
description:
With a regular ungrouped data.frame, using a factor or a character variable when using `complete` gives the same results. When using grouped_df with character it doesn't generate any new values, because (I suspect) it only looks for unique character values that exist within each group, not across the whole data.frame. I believe (could be wrong) that using a character variable in `complete` for a grouped data.frame will always return the same data.frame, which sort of defeats the purpose of `complete`.

``` R
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

df <- data.frame(stringsAsFactors=FALSE,
                 v1=c(1,1,2,3,4),
                 v2=c("A","B","B","A","C"), 
                 v3=rnorm(5,0,1))

df %>% complete(v1, v2) # works

df %>% mutate(v2=as.factor(v2)) %>% complete(v1,v2) # works

df2 <- df %>% group_by(v1) 

df2 %>% complete(v1, v2) # doesn't really work

df2 %>% mutate(v2=as.factor(v2)) %>% complete(v1,v2) # works
```

I  can see that this may not be a bug per se since it isn't immediately clear what the intended behavior of `complete` is when used with `group_by`, but there should probably be a note in the documentation about how the two interact.

Thanks

title: unnest inconsistent when (a) naming new column and (b) list-col has length-one entry
description:
```R > df1 <- tibble(a = "foo", b = list(c("bar", "baz"))) > df2 <- tibble(a = "foo", b = list(c("bar"))) > df1 # A tibble: 1 x 2 a b 1 foo !> df2 # A tibble: 1 x 2 a b 1 foo ``` Now, when `unnest`ing `b` _without_ specifying the new column's name, the output is consistent between `df1` and `df2`: ```R > unnest(df1, b) # A tibble: 2 x 2 a b 1 foo bar 2 foo baz > unnest(df2, b) # A tibble: 1 x 2 a b 1 foo bar ``` But when specifying that the new column take a new name, the nested column remains around _only_ for the case where the list-col entry has length one: ```R > unnest(df1, new_b = b) # A tibble: 2 x 2 a new_b 1 foo bar 2 foo baz > unnest(df2, new_b = b) # A tibble: 1 x 3 a b new_b 1 foo bar ``` Note that the last `unnest` call retains the original column `b`. Smells like a (minor) edge-case bug.

title: 0.7.0 breaks programmatic specification of column numbers in gather()
description:
Updating from 0.6.1 to 0.7.0 has broken code where column ranges are specified using variable names rather than integers (e.g. start:end instead of 1:4). Not sure if this change was intentional or not, but being able to specify those numbers programmatically (e.g. with ncol()) is really convenient and I would hate to lose it. MRE:

```{r}
library(tidyr)

# Make the data set
dat = data.frame(Genus = 'Escherichia',
					SP1 = rep(10,10),
					SP2 = rep(5,10),
					SP3 = rep(17,10))

# Make the data frame long. This works
dat %>% gather(Species,Count,2:4) -> dat_long

# Specify columns more programmatically. This used to work but now doesn't.
st = 2
dat %>% gather(Species,Count,st:ncol(dat)) -> dat_long

# This also fails, but more excitingly:
st = 1
dat %>% gather(Species,Count,(st+1):ncol(dat)) -> dat_long
```

title: feature request: separate_n to create arbitrary number of columns
description:
`separate` forces us to specify all the new column names. With `separate_n`, it is possible to specify a prefix, assuming that we'll generate the maximum number of columns according to the delimiters present in data. 

New parameters are `prefix` and `sep_col`. 
Column names will be given by `<prefix><sep_col><number>`.

What do you think?

Draft:

```r
separate_n <- function(data, col, prefix, sep = "[^[:alnum:]]+", sep_col = '',
                       convert = FALSE, fill = 'warn', remove = TRUE) {
  col_str <- deparse(substitute(col))
  if (missing(prefix)) prefix <- col_str
  ncol <- max(stringr::str_count(data[[col_str]], sep)) + 1L
  nzero <- ncol %/% 10 + 1L
  txt_print <- sprintf("%%s%%s%%0%dd", nzero)
  columns <- sprintf(txt_print, prefix, sep_col, seq_len(ncol))
  separate_(data, col_str, columns, sep = sep,
            remove = remove, convert = convert,
            fill = fill)
}
```

Example:

```r
library(tidyr)
d <- tibble::tribble(
  ~a, ~b,
  'a,e,c,r,g,4,5,6,7,8,31', 1,
  'a,e,r,g', 1,
  'a,e,c,r,g', 1,
  'a,c,r,g', 1,
  'a,e,c,r,g', 1,
  'a,e,r', 1
)

d %>% 
  separate_n(a, 'a', fill = 'right')
```

Result:

```
# A tibble: 6 × 12
    a01   a02   a03   a04   a05   a06   a07   a08   a09   a10   a11     b

3     a     e     c     r     g  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>     1
4     a     c     r     g  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>     1
5     a     e     c     r     g  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>  <NA>     1
```

title: Feature request: Fill only limited number of rows
description:
It would be handy to have an option for the fill function to fill only a limited number of NAs with the previous entry, not the entire NA block. The background is data from measurement instruments recording a value at irregular times which is, however, valid for a limited time period only (e.g. 220 seconds), not until the next timestamp (row) in the data frame.

Currently I do this with a rowwise approach (see below), which is rather slow, obviously. 

```
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

  #generate time series data
  #Note that in reality the interval between two timestamps is irregular, i.e. between 500- 700 s
  data <- bind_cols(
    data_frame(td=seq(from = ymd_hm("2010-01-01 00:00"), 
                                     to = ymd_hm("2010-01-31 23:59"), 
                                     by = 612)),
    as_data_frame(replicate(3,runif(4377))))
        
  #expand with valid measurement periods, then complete
  data2 <- data %>%
    rowwise() %>%
    mutate(temp = list(seq(from = td, to = td + seconds(220), by = 1))) %>%
    unnest() %>%
    select(td = temp, everything(), -td) %>%
    complete(td = full_seq(td,1)) 
```


I have found another approach which might be faster, but not very clean/elegant, either (see http://stackoverflow.com/questions/37972673/fill-a-limited-number-of-values-tidyr-fill).

I would love to be able to tell fill to only fill the next 220 rows after a non-NA entry and leave all others untouched:

```
data2 <- data %>%
    complete(td = full_seq(td,1)) %>%
    fill(V1:V3,nmax = 220)
```

title: unnest_cols
description:
A common use case for me in `mutate` or `summarize` is to call a function that returns a vector that is greater than length 1 but less than length(input). I wrote this helper function for this usecase. It takes a list column produced by, for example, a `summarize` call to `list(quantile(x))`, and expands it into multiple columns.

There are of course many ways to approach colwise operations like this. I'm posting this here to primarily to stimulate discussion. If there is interest, I would be happy to submit a PR.

First an example of the function in action:
```
# example
data("ToothGrowth")
# setup data
df <-  ToothGrowth %>%
  group_by(dose) %>%
  summarize(len = list(len))

# unnest_cols in action
df %>% mutate(quantile = map(len, quantile)) %>% unnest_cols("quantile")
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>    dose        len  `0%`  `25%` `50%`  `75%` `100%`
#>   <dbl>     <list> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1   0.5 <dbl [20]>   4.2  7.225  9.85 12.250   21.5
#> 2   1.0 <dbl [20]>  13.6 16.250 19.25 23.375   27.3
#> 3   2.0 <dbl [20]>  18.5 23.525 25.95 27.825   33.9
```

This is the function definition that produced the output above. I imagine an official version would be more robust.
```
library(tidyverse)
unnest_cols <- function(df, cols, col_names = NULL) {

  if (!is.null(col_names) && length(cols) > 1 && (!is.list(col_names)))
    stop("col_names must be supplied as a named list")

  for (col in cols) {
    original_order <- names(df)
    lc <- df[[col]] # list col to unnest
    max_len_of_l_elems <- max(map_dbl(lc, length))
    default_nms <- paste(col, 1:max_len_of_l_elems, sep = "_")
    nm <- if (is.list(col_names))
      col_names[[col]]
    else
      col_names

    if (is.null(nm)) {
      nm <- unique(map(lc, names))
      if (length(nm) != 1) {
        warning("not all element names of list col are identical")
        nm <- default_nms
      } else if (is_not_null(nm[[1]])) {
        nm <- paste(col, nm[[1]], sep = "_")
      } else
        nm <- default_nms
    }
    for (i in seq_len(max_len_of_l_elems))
      df[[nm[i]]] <- simplify(map(lc, i)) %||% list_along(lc)
    df[[col]] <- NULL
    # preserve order
    where_col <- which(col == original_order)
    new_order <- c(head(original_order, where_col - 1),
                   nm,
                   tail(original_order, length(original_order) - where_col))
   df <- df[new_order]
  }
  df
}
```
A final version would need to be smarter about names and error checking. A companion `nest_cols`, might make sense also (a version of `unite` that applies a  rowwise `list` instead of `paste`).

title: Consider adding a drop_na verb
description:
[forwarded from https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/1797 as per @hadley: "This feels more like a tidyr verb to me."]

pandas has the [pandas.DataFrame.dropna()](http://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/generated/pandas.DataFrame.dropna.html) which lets you drop rows which have NAs in it but also let you specify subset of columns (-> `subset`) to be looked at for NAs.

A similar dplyr verb would be 

``` R
drop_na <- function(data, ...){
    if (missing(...)){
        f = complete.cases(data)
    } else {
        f <- complete.cases(select_(data, .dots = lazyeval::lazy_dots(...)))
    }
    filter(data, f)
}
```

Examples: 

``` R
> df <- data.frame(a=c(1,2,3,4,NA), b=c(NA,1,2,3,4), ac=c(1,2,NA,3,4))
> df %>% drop_na(a,b)
  a b ac
1 2 1  2
2 3 2 NA
3 4 3  3
> df %>% drop_na(starts_with("a"))
  a  b ac
1 1 NA  1
2 2  1  2
3 4  3  3
> df %>% drop_na()
  a b ac
1 2 1  2
2 4 3  3
```

title: Feature request: Support for list variables in ``crossing``
Entire enclosing environment gets saved with nested ggplots / lms
description:
I don't really know in which package to complain about this. 

The hadley many-models approach (nest-mutate-map) is very powerful, but has been wreaking havoc on my memory (when using multidplyr) and disk usage when saving. The problem is that several classes carry about their calling environment, even data which is not directly used. To illustrate:

```
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
iris_big <- iris %>% as.tbl() %>%  
  mutate(iris = rep(list(iris), NROW(.)))

# Add a list column of ggplots
iris_big <- iris_big %>% 
  mutate(plot = iris %>% map(function(x){
    x %>% ggplot(aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) + geom_point()
  }))

# Size in memory is reasonable
object.size(iris_big)
#2759016 bytes
save(iris_big, file = "tmp.RData")
file.size("tmp.RData")
# Size on disk is reasonable
# [1] 104370 (4% of memory used)

# Now add some extra junk that's not used in the plots
iris_big2 <- iris_big %>% 
  mutate(plot = iris %>% map(function(x){
    Seatbelts_big <- Seatbelts %>% data.frame() %>% as.tbl() %>%  
      mutate(Seatbelts = rep(list(Seatbelts), NROW(.))) 
    # This isn't relevant to the plot but gets caught up
    x %>% ggplot(aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) + geom_point()
  }))

# Size in memory is reasonable (but when calling this using multidplyr it isn't)
object.size(iris_big2)
#2759016 bytes
save(iris_big2, file = "tmp.RData")
file.size("tmp.RData")
# Size on disk is huge.
#5358755 (194% of memory used)
```

R-core folks recommend creating new environments whenever creating these objects, but this is certainly not a user-friendly solution. See: http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/Model-object-when-generated-in-a-function-saves-entire-environment-when-saved-td4723192.html

Hope this helps!

title: Extending gather to work with pair-wise variables
description:
I am putting this function here that provides a generic function similar to `tidyr::gather` that works with **pairs** of variables or columns. I am hoping it would be useful for others, but it is still a rough extension to `gather`.

The motivation for this function is that I have several statistics, for which each can be further summarized into pairs of statistics-of-statistics. It is easy to get this data into a **wide** format, but I wish to transform it into the **long** format, ideal for e.g. `ggplot2`.

A dummy example:

```
(bla <- data.frame(group=letters[rep(1:3, each=3)], cor=1:9, bias=11:19, mse=21:29))
  group cor bias mse
1     a   1   11  21
2     a   2   12  22
3     a   3   13  23
4     b   4   14  24
5     b   5   15  25
6     b   6   16  26
7     c   7   17  27
8     c   8   18  28
9     c   9   19  29
```

The desired output would be as following, calculating the group-wise mean and standard deviation of `cor`, `bias`, and `mse`:

```
   group  stat    sd  mean
1      a   cor     1     2
2      b   cor     1     5
3      c   cor     1     8
4      a  bias     1    12
5      b  bias     1    15
6      c  bias     1    18
7      a   mse     1    22
8      b   mse     1    25
9      c   mse     1    28
```

As said, getting into wide format is easy:

```
bla %>% group_by(group) %>% summarise_each(funs(mean, sd), cor, bias, mse) 
Source: local data frame [3 x 7]

   group cor_mean bias_mean mse_mean cor_sd bias_sd mse_sd
  (fctr)    (dbl)     (dbl)    (dbl)  (dbl)   (dbl)  (dbl)
1      a        2        12       22      1       1      1
2      b        5        15       25      1       1      1
3      c        8        18       28      1       1      1
```
## The function

I called the function `gather2`, not that inventive. It is still rather rough and I am yet to figure how to apply the `select` functions (`starts_with`, etc.) for it.

```
gather2 <- function(data, key, values, key_values, ..., na.rm=FALSE, convert=FALSE, factor_key=FALSE) {
  pairs <- list(...)
  stopifnot(length(values) == length(pairs))
  stopifnot(all(sapply(pairs, length) == length(key_values))) ## all have to be same length

  gather_cols <- do.call(cbind, pairs)

  by_names <- setdiff(colnames(data), unlist(pairs))
  ren <- structure(gather_cols[,1], .Names=key_values)
  res <- select(data, -one_of(gather_cols[,-1])) %>% 
    rename_(.dots=ren) %>%
    gather_(key, values[1], key_values, na.rm=na.rm, convert=convert, factor_key=factor_key)
  for (i in 2:length(values)) {
    ren <- structure(gather_cols[,i], .Names=key_values)
    res <- select(data, -one_of(gather_cols[,-i])) %>% 
      rename_(.dots=ren) %>%
      gather_(key, values[i], key_values, na.rm=na.rm, convert=convert, factor_key=factor_key) %>%
      outer_join(res, res2, by=c(key, by_names))
  }
  res
}
```

The argument `key` is as in `gather`; `key_values` are the variable names holding the values (eq. to `value` in `gather`). `values` are the names of the "pairs", where the names of the gathered columns are replaced with this.
The columns to gather (`...`) are given in pairs, corresponding to to `values`.

**Demonstration**:

```
# As above
bla %>% group_by(group) %>% summarise_each(funs(mean, sd), cor, bias, mse) 
Source: local data frame [3 x 7]

   group cor_mean bias_mean mse_mean cor_sd bias_sd mse_sd
  (fctr)    (dbl)     (dbl)    (dbl)  (dbl)   (dbl)  (dbl)
1      a        2        12       22      1       1      1
2      b        5        15       25      1       1      1
3      c        8        18       28      1       1      1

# Pair-wise gathering
 bla %>% group_by(group) %>% summarise_each(funs(mean, sd), cor, bias, mse) %>%
  gather2('stat', c('mean','sd'), c('cor','bias','mse'), c('cor_mean','bias_mean','mse_mean'), c('cor_sd','bias_sd','mse_sd'))
Source: local data frame [9 x 4]

   group  stat    sd  mean
  (fctr) (chr) (dbl) (dbl)
1      a   cor     1     2
2      b   cor     1     5
3      c   cor     1     8
4      a  bias     1    12
5      b  bias     1    15
6      c  bias     1    18
7      a   mse     1    22
8      b   mse     1    25
```

I still desire to make it more automagic, such as using the special functions for `select`, or allowing to use patterns to define arguments.

title: as_data_frame_matrix: "envir" argument in getS3method
description:
It seems like `envir` is not a valid argument in `utils::getS3method` in R version 3.2.4. Couldn't find a specific mention of when this was added to `R.utils`, but unless there is something wrong with my R install I suppose this warrants a version bump for the R in `DESCRIPTION`. 

`getS3method` is only used on one line however, so it might be a better idea to just add an `if` statement for older versions of R (where envir is not an argument) and something like this:

``` R
get("as_data_frame.matrix", envir = asNamespace("tibble"))
```

title: Unnesting behaviour depends on dimension of data frame to be unnested
description:
The output of unnesting differs depending on the dimensions of the data frame to be unnested. (For more context on when one might encounter this issue see #197)

``` r
library("dplyr")
library("tidyr")
library("purrr")
library("broom")

data <- data_frame(
    name = c("Alex", "Alex", "Alex", "Tim", "Tim", "Tim"),
    year = c(1990, 1991, 1992, 1990, 1991, 1992),
    height = c(160, 165, 170, 120, 134, 150),
    weight = c(50, 52, 53, 48, 48, 52)
)

## 6   Tim  1992    150     52

# nest
data <- nest(data, year, height, weight)

data
## name           data
## (chr)          (chr)
## 1  Alex <tbl_df [3,3]>
## 2   Tim <tbl_df [3,3]>
```

Here we build two different linear models (`model_A` and `model_B`) that differ in that the former will estimate the intercept and the slope and the latter only the slope.

``` r
# build two different linear models
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    model_A = map(.$data, ~lm(year ~ height, data = .)),
    model_B = map(.$data, ~lm(year ~ height + 0, data = .))
```

When the data frame is unnested on a particular column, but contains multiple other nested columns, then there seems to be a different behaviour depending on the number of rows of the nested data frames in the column to be unnested.

In case there is more than one row (`tidy_model_A` - where we have a slope and intercept), the other nested columns are dropped. However, in case there is only one row (`tidy_model_B`), the other nested columns are not dropped.

``` r

  mutate(tidy = map(model_A, tidy))

## 4   Tim      height 6.656805e-02 2.562205e-03 2.598076e+01 2.449142e-02

tidy_model_B <- data %>%
  mutate(tidy = map(model_B, tidy))

tidy_model_B
## name           data model_A model_B               tidy
## (chr)          (chr)   (chr)   (chr)              (chr)
## 1  Alex <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm> <data.frame [1,5]>

tidy_model_B %>%

```

I wonder whether either `tidy_model_A` should be:

``` r

tidy_model_A
##   name          data  model_A model_B        term     estimate    std.error    statistic      p.value
##  (chr)          (chr)    (chr)   (chr)      (chr)        (dbl)        (dbl)        (dbl)        (dbl)
## 1  Alex <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm> (Intercept) 1.958000e+03 9.557251e-12 2.048706e+14 3.107423e-15
## 2  Alex <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm>      height 2.000000e-01 5.790501e-14 3.453933e+12 1.843174e-13
## 3   Tim <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm> (Intercept) 1.982036e+03 3.464698e-01 5.720659e+03 1.112843e-04
## 4   Tim <tbl_df [3,3]> <S3:lm> <S3:lm>      height 6.656805e-02 2.562205e-03 2.598076e+01 2.449142e-02

```

Or `tidy_model_A` should be:

``` r

tidy_model_B
## name    term estimate std.error statistic      p.value
## (chr)   (chr)    (dbl)     (dbl)     (dbl)        (dbl)

```

Is this behaviour designed? Sometimes it is nice to test different models (e.g. fixing the intercept) and then this difference in behaviour makes it difficult to do it programmatically.

title: variable behaviour when unnesting tables containing multiple nested columns

- spreading of data frames with nested columns returns an error.

In the following reproducible example I tried to give some context with a situation where one might encounter this. Specifically, in the example I try to summarise the output from different linear models that were based on different formulas. Perhaps there is a better way to do the same thing?

Is this behaviour designed? Sometimes it is nice to test different models (e.g. fixing the intercept) and then this difference in behaviour makes it difficult to do it programmatically.

title: complete() also changes existing data, not only missing data
description:
The help page for `complete()` makes it look the function can be used to add missing combinations of data, but in fact it also _changes existing data_.

Example code:

```
library(tidyr)
d = data.frame(id=c(1,1,2,2),
               day=c("mon","tue","tue","wed"),
               x=c(7,NA,6,5))
d
```

This outputs

```
  id day  x
1  1 mon  7
2  1 tue NA
3  2 tue  6
4  2 wed  5
```

Running the `complete()` function on this with `id` and `day` as columns to expand, I would expect a row for ‘id 1, day wed’ and a row ‘id 2, day mon’ to be added, with a custom value of `x`. However, it actually also changes the existing `x` value for ‘id 1, day tue’. That is

```
complete(d, id, day, fill=list(x=-99))
```

returns

```
     id    day     x
  (dbl) (fctr) (dbl)
1     1    mon     7
2     1    tue   -99
3     1    wed   -99
4     2    mon   -99
5     2    tue     6
6     2    wed     5
```

instead of

```
     id    day     x
  (dbl) (fctr) (dbl)
1     1    mon     7
2     1    tue    NA
3     1    wed   -99
4     2    mon   -99
5     2    tue     6
6     2    wed     5
```

Note that the `fill` argument is described in the help file as

> A named list that for each variable supplies a single value to use instead of NA for missing combinations.

However, it’s used for _existing_ combinations too, not only missing combinations.

So this is either a bug in the implementation or in the help file. IMHO, the behaviour described in the help file is much more useful than the current behaviour. (When I found this bug, I was using the `complete()` function for some data where the described behaviour of the `fill` argument would be _very_ useful, but the actual behaviour wasn’t useful at all.)

title: separate with fill = "left" reverses column order
description:
When `fill = "left"`, not only do NA values get filled in from the left, but the columns are filled in reverse order. Example:

``` r
library(tidyr)

d <- data.frame(x = c("1-2-3", "2-3", "3"))

# I understand this behavior
separate(d, x, c("a", "b", "c"))
#> Warning: Too few values at 2 locations: 2, 3
#>   a    b    c
#> 1 1    2    3
#> 2 2    3 <NA>
#> 3 3 <NA> <NA>

# here, surprised that 3 and 2 are reversed:
separate(d, x, c("a", "b", "c"), fill = "left")
#>      a    b c
#> 1    1    2 3
#> 2 <NA>    3 2
#> 3 <NA> <NA> 3
```

I think this is undocumented since the docs for fill only say that NAs are filled from the left, not that the values will be reversed. I also think the most common use case would be splitting a column where there is an optional first value (like either a `d/m/y` date or an `m/y` date) and can't think of a use case where reversing the order _only_ when there aren't enough values would be helpful.

It seems like changing it would be a [straightforward change here](https://github.com/hadley/tidyr/blob/master/src/simplifyPieces.cpp#L31), but I don't know if this is desired behavior. I'm happy to PR it myself.

description:
As directed (https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/1800), I'm posting this question here.

What's the best way to do this variation on nesting a data frame? I didn't want to use `tidyr::nest()` because I didn't want the other variables buried in data frames -- I wanted them as individual list columns. Sthg like this:

``` r
library(dplyr)

  group_by(cyl) %>%
```

``` r
library(purrr)
```

title: separate doesn't work on first grouped column when more than one column in group_by
description:
In a dataframe where two column names are passed to `group_by`, the `separate` function will not find the first column name (but will find the second one). 

Here's an example...

```
df <- data.frame(the_num = 1:30,
        the_chr1 = rep(sapply(1:10, function(i) paste(sample(c(letters,LETTERS),3),collapse="")),3),
        the_chr2 = sapply(1:30, function(i) paste(sample(c(letters,LETTERS),3),collapse="")))
```

And so if we attempt to pipe together a few functions, and then `separate` the contents of the first column in the `group_by`, which in this example is `the_chr1`, here's what happens:

```
library(dplyr); library(tidyr)
```

title: Spread should work with drop=FALSE and fill=NA and create columns (not rows) from empty factor levels
description:
Short description

The function `id` fails to consider the possibility that it's input is a data frame containing (or only including) factors with zero length members.  As does the function `id_var`, called by `id`.  This causes problems for the spread function, which should be able to handle these cases and generate named empty columns.  This further causes problems for dplyr, which can result in missing column names (that should have been generated by the factor transformation) in later stages in the pipe.  Instead the name is bound to some other thing in the global scope and the script (or shiny app) will error or otherwise fail.

---

Long description

In the following non empty example

```
data.frame(U=c("foo","bar")[c(1,1,2,2)],K=factor(letters[c(1:2,1:2)],levels=letters[1:2]),V=c(1:2,1:2)) %>% spread(K,V)
```

We get a data frame (like) with columns "a", "b".

```
    U a b
1 bar 1 2
2 foo 1 2
```

Now assume I know it has "a" and "b", and in later steps I consume "a" and "b" in e.g. mutate, or ggvis.

What if there is no data?

```
data.frame(U=c("foo","bar")[c()],K=factor(letters[c()],levels=letters[c(1:2)]),V=numeric()) %>% spread(K,V)
```

This produces the following:

```
[1] U
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```

Which then goes horribly wrong if I try to consume "a"

```
> .Last.value %>% mutate(zep = a)
Error: unsupported type for column 'zep' (CLOSXP, classes = function)
```

What happened here?  It pulled 'a' form the environment - in fact it's using `shiny::a` - a function to produce html.

Ideally, `drop=FALSE` should address this - by creating columns for factor levels that don't exist in the data.  

But right now that doesn't work - drop=FALSE does something different - it fills in missing data...

I can't even make this work properly, to produce an example, but never mind.

title: separate() upset by tbl_dfs with x.1 column naming convention
description:
Apologies if this is a dupe, or should be for dplyr. The following behavior chokes spread(). Here's a convoluted 'reprex':

``` R
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

s <- summarise(
  group_by(iris, Species), 
  sepal_l = mean(Sepal.Length), sepal_w = mean(Sepal.Width),
  petal_l = mean(Petal.Length), petal_w = mean(Petal.Width)
)

# The result of gather()
gather(s, Species, value)
# Source: local data frame [12 x 3]
# 
#       Species Species.1 value
#1      setosa   sepal_l 5.006
#2  versicolor   sepal_l 5.936
#3   virginica   sepal_l 6.588
# ... (abridged by br)

# This is the problematic call
separate(
  gather(s, Species, value),
  Species.1, c("part", "orient"), sep = "_"
)

# Error in matrix(unlist(pieces), ncol = n, byrow = TRUE) : 
#   'data' must be of a vector type, was 'NULL'

```

In similar-ish cases (https://github.com/hadley/dplyr/issues/860, https://github.com/hadley/tidyr/issues/51) ungrouping seemed to help. However, here only calling data.frame() on the data does.

``` R
separate( # Same error as above
  ungroup(gather(s, Species, value)),
  Species.1, c("part", "orient"), sep = "_"
)

separate( # Same error as above
  gather(ungroup(s), Species, value),
  Species.1, c("part", "orient"), sep = "_"
)

separate( # This works
  data.frame(gather(s, Species, value)), 
  Species.1, c("part", "orient"), sep = "_"
)

# Desired result:
#       Species  part orient value
#1      setosa sepal      l 5.006
#2  versicolor sepal      l 5.936
#3   virginica sepal      l 6.588
#4      setosa sepal      w 3.428
# ... (abridged by br)
```

Comparing objects that work and those that don't, the the x.1 renaming convention for duplicate column names (in this case Species.1) seems to be the only difference. The tbl_df _shows_ Species.1 as the column name, but seems to represent it as 'Species' internally, when unclassed. 'Species.1' is the `col` parameter in the problematic call to spread().

``` R
# e.g.
a <- gather(s, Species, value); b <- data.frame(a)
unclass(a); unclass(b)
```

title: Should gather default to character instead of factor for the key column?
description:
`gather` currently dispatches to `reshape2::melt`, and the resulting key column is of type `factor`, unless `convert=TRUE` is specified, in which case it’s converted to another type, depending on the actual data.

This default makes sense if the resulting table is used with modelling functions, but not much else. In particular, a very common workflow for me is to use `gather` followed by `inner_join`, e.g. (where `counts` is a gene expression experiment consisting of several libraries, and `col_data` is the experiment’s column data, in Bioconductor parlance, i.e. describes the experiments):

``` r
counts = gather(counts, Library, Count) %>% inner_join(col_data, by = 'Library')
```

This invariably yields a warning from `inner_join`:

> joining factor and character vector, coercing into character vector

And while harmless, it’s a bit annoying, especially as this is usually in a knitr document and I don’t want to clutter my output.

`convert=TRUE` isn’t really what I want: For instance, I almost always want the result to be of type `character`, regardless of the actual data format.

Am I right in thinking that using `factor` rather than `character` as the type of the key column is more for historical reasons than actually due to a hard advantage? Would it make sense to change the default?

key - The bare (unquoted) name of the column whose values will be used as new column headings.

value - The bare (unquoted) name of the column whose values will populate the cells of the resulting data table in the new columns.

Refine as needed, but, something like this when describe keys and values in tidyr will help a lot of folk have an easier time with the spread (and perhaps other) helpfiles.

`extract_numeric2 <- function(x, which_one = 1){`
`num <- str_trim(gsub("[^0-9.-]+", " ", x))`
`num <- strsplit(num," ")`
`as.numeric(sapply(num,"[",which_one))`
`}`

`extract_numeric2("49b30ea1ee66f66bbb05b6e5c728942566345f33",2) =  30`.

title: tidying key-value pair columns
description:
### Synopsis

Many (biology) file formats / databases will have columns containing `key=value` pairs separated (`;`). Which are useful for storing (some obs may have many attributes, others may have none...) but not for working with. To work with them it is most convenient to tidy:

from:

``` r
df
#> Source: local data frame [1 x 1]
#> 
#> attributes
#> 1 ID=enriched_region_1;Name=ACF1;Dbxref=modEncode:5056
```

to:

``` r
#> Source: local data frame [1 x 3]
#> 
#> Dbxref                ID Name
#> 1 modEncode:5056 enriched_region_1 ACF1
```

**I am going back and forth between these two forms all the time and perhaps it's general enough that there should be a `tidyr` roundtrip set of functions for it?**

These would operate on a column of a `tbl` and take `inter` and `intra` (key value) separators. i.e. for the above:

``` r
df %>%
  tidy_key_val_col(attributes, inter_sep = ';', intra_sep = '=')
```
### A minimal example:

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

df <- data_frame(attributes = "ID=enriched_region_1;Name=ACF1;Dbxref=modEncode:5056")

#> Source: local data frame [1 x 1]
#> 
#> attributes
#> 1 ID=enriched_region_1;Name=ACF1;Dbxref=modEncode:5056
```

To tidy this up the general pattern is to:

``` r
df %>% 
  mutate(attrs = stringi::stri_split_fixed(attributes, ';')) %>% 
  unnest(attrs) %>% 
  separate(attrs, c("attr_var", "attr_val"), '=') %>% 
  spread(attr_var, attr_val) %>% 
  select(-attributes)
#> Source: local data frame [1 x 3]
#> 
#> Dbxref                ID Name
#> 1 modEncode:5056 enriched_region_1 ACF1
```
